status: draft for owner review; not applied
built_by: five domain readers, one corpus miner (counts in traditions where the reader is "corpus miner"), one completeness critic; entries merged by normalised term

label_when: Alone on its own line, or line-initial followed by a numeral, ordinal, '.', ':', '.--', '--' or an em-dash, usually before a block of lyric; 'Last Verse' / '3rd Verse' standing above a stanza in sheet music and songsters.
In anthem and psalter printings: a one-word line or prefix that alternates with 'Full.' or marks the antiphonal sides of the choir. This is NOT the stanza sense of 'verse'.
Line-initial italic '_Verse._' or '_Ver. Chor._' followed by text (in an anthem this means the soloist sings, then the chorus). Alone, or followed by a numeral.
sung_trap: 'Verse' is a common sung/recited noun ('Verse, crown'd with ivy', 'Verse calls them forth; tis verse that gives', 'Verse and nothing else have I to give you' all occur in the corpus). Sung when it is followed by a comma plus more words in the same syntactic line, takes an article/possessive ('my verse', 'this verse'), or carries a verb. Label only when it stands with nothing but a number/ordinal and punctuation.
'verse' is sung in lyrics about poetry. Distinguish it from the harness's own [VERSE n] staging tags, which are structural, not apparatus to strip. Decani/Cantoris are never sung.

'verse' is sung in 92 rows across 50 files ('both of verse and of prose'); 'Verse Heroick,' (Durfey) is sung. Do not confuse with Watts's 'Ver. 165.', which is a scripture verse reference, not a section label.
traditions: Sheet music and Tin Pan Alley, music-hall songsters, gospel songbooks, college/glee songbooks, minstrel songsters; rarely in poetry.
Anglican verse anthems (Purcell, Gibbons); pointed psalters (Cathedral Psalter)
Herrick 6 rows (anthem settings); 47,934 [VERSE n] marks. Expected in Tin Pan Alley ('Verse', 'Refrain') and music hall ('Extra verse', 'Encore verse').
examples: Verse. / My song shall be alway of the loving-kindness of the Lord
_Verse._ My God, I'm wounded by my sin,  (eng_british_robert_herrick.txt)

label_when: Alone on a line with a numeral or ordinal; also inside editorial directions ('Repeat the first stanza', 'Omit stanzas 3 and 4'); as a title word 'Stanzas' / 'Stanzas written in...' it is a heading.
Alone with a numeral, or inside editorial prose ('Canto I. stanzas i.-v.').
sung_trap: Almost never sung; a line beginning 'Stanza' with ordinary syntax is still a direction ('Repeat the first stanza to complete the tune.' occurs in the corpus and is apparatus). Only a self-referential poem line ('this stanza shall...') inside metre is lyric.

There are 0 label rows. All 10 mid-line hits are editorial prose staged as lyric ('The first stanza of this song was the composition of a ...'), so the word inside a long prose sentence marks the whole line as apparatus. It is rarely sung, but in self-referential songs it can be.
traditions: Collected poems, anthologies, hymnals (directions), Byron/Shelley 'Stanzas' titles.
10 rows / 6 files, all prose leaks (Byron, Lovelace and others). 'Stave' is expected in Dickens-style carol books and songsters.
examples: STANZAS WRITTEN IN DEJECTION, NEAR NAPLES
3. Seven sheets, Canto I. stanzas i.-v., being the commencement of the  (eng_british_lord_byron.txt)

label_when: Alone on a line (any case, with or without '.' ':'); or line-initial followed by '.--', '--', '.', ':' and then lyric (Burns: 'Chorus.--We are na fou'), in which case strip only the prefix and keep the following words as lyric; or with a qualifier ('of Spirits', 'after each verse').

Alone on a line, or line-initial followed by '.', ':', '.—' or '--' and then sung text on the same line. Strip only the prefix: 'Cho. THEN UNDERSTAND YOU NOT' and 'Choir.--O Tibbie, I hae seen the day' (corpus) keep the text after the prefix. 'Chorus of X' is a label even inside a title.

Line-initial, followed by '.--', '--', '—', ':', '._' or a period plus spaces, with verse after it: strip only the prefix and keep the rest as sung. Alone on a line, followed by '.' or ':' or nothing: the whole line is a label.
sung_trap: Sung as a noun inside a lyric line ('the heavenly chorus', 'join in the chorus', 'Fit choristers of Nature'). Sung when preceded by an article/adjective/preposition or followed by a verb/lowercase continuation without dash punctuation. Note 'Cho.' line-initial followed by text in caps (Elizabethan madrigal printings: 'Cho. THEN UNDERSTAND YOU NOT') is a label + lyric.

'chorus' is sung in lyrics about singing ('the birds' sweet chorus', 'join in the chorus, boys'). It is sung when lowercase, mid-sentence, or governed by a verb or article within the metrical line. A dramatic poem's CHORUS: prefix (Shelley's Hellas) is a label even though everything after it is sung.

'chorus' occurs mid-line as a sung word in 68 rows across 42 files ('Listen to me, and then in chorus gather'). Treat it as a label only at line start with label punctuation, never mid-line. The bare word followed by a comma or by lowercase verse is sung.
traditions: All song printings: songsters, Burns/Scots collections, sheet music, gospel hymnals, college songs, shanties, minstrel, music hall, G&S libretti, Greek-model verse drama (Shelley, Swinburne).
every libretto; Greek-style verse dramas (Shelley, Swinburne, Arnold); songsters; sheet music; gospel hymnals; Lovelace; Burns

162 lyric rows / 19 files. Burns 79, Herrick 28, Waugh 10, Browning 9, Shelley translations 8, Bradbury 5, Lovelace 5, Gay 4, Watts-Dunton 4. Also 881 [CHORUS] marks plus 257 apparatus [CHORUS]. Expected throughout G&S, music hall, Tin Pan Alley and gospel hymnals.
examples: Chorus.--My heart's in the Highlands, my heart is not here,
Chorus.--For auld lang syne, my dear,  (eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt)

label_when: Alone on a line or line-initial followed by '.', ':', '.--', '--' before lyric; in gospel hymnals 'Ref.' printed once after stanza 1; in 1890-1929 sheet music 'Refrain' or 'Waltz Refrain' over the chorus block.
Line-initial with '.--', ':' or a period, or alone on a line.
sung_trap: 'refrain' is also a verb ('refrain from tears', 'I cannot refrain') and a poetic noun ('a sad refrain', 'the old refrain'). Sung when it has an article/possessive, is followed by 'from', or sits mid-line in metre. Label only when bare with punctuation.
The verb 'refrain' is sung in 35 rows across 27 files ('Then if you refrain, he is at you again'). Treat it as a label only at line start with label punctuation.
traditions: Gospel hymnals (Sankey, Bliss), Tin Pan Alley sheet music, Burns's abbreviated refrain cues, art-song texts.

1 lyric row (Burns 'Refrain.--To daunton me'); 1,240 [REFRAIN] marks. The Otterbein Hymnal (47 hymn files) prints 'Cho.--' and 'Ref.--'. Expected in gospel hymnals and Tin Pan Alley, where 'Refrain' is the standard chorus heading.
examples: Refrain.--To daunton me, to daunton me,
Refrain.--To daunton me, to daunton me,  (eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt)

label_when: Alone on a line above a repeated line-group, or line-initial with '.--'/':' before it; in medieval-carol editions a 'Burden' set at head and repeated after each stanza.
Alone on a line, or line-initial followed by '.--' or ':'.
sung_trap: 'burden' is a very common sung noun ('the burden of my woe', 'lay down my burden'); 'o'ercome/owercome' is a Scots verb and noun ('the owercome o' the sang'). Sung when syntactically embedded (article, possessive, verb).
Sung as a noun in 103 rows across 66 files ('The burden of woe that his spirit was breaking'). The word is never a label mid-line.
traditions: Medieval/Tudor carols (Early English Text Society, Wright), Elizabethan songbooks, Shakespeare songs ('Burthen dispersedly'), Scots songs.
0 lyric-row labels; 1,614 [BURDEN] marks, 1,580 of them as apparatus. Expected in carol, ballad and Elizabethan song collections.
examples: [BURDEN] / Miserere Domine.  (eng_british_adelaide_anne_procter.txt; the burden text itself is sung)

label_when: Alone on a line, often all-caps, with a roman/arabic numeral, before a block; in verse drama it alternates with 'Chorus'.
A line-initial prefix, alone or followed by '.'/':' and a Roman numeral; used where two halves of a chorus alternate.
sung_trap: Never sung.
Never sung.
traditions: Shelley (Hellas, Prometheus Unbound), Swinburne (Atalanta), Milton (Samson), choral cantata texts.
Shelley (Hellas, Prometheus Unbound); Swinburne (Atalanta); Milton's Samson Agonistes tradition; Victorian cantatas; Gilbert's Princess Ida
examples: SEMICHORUS I. / Life may change, but it may fly not;

label_when: Alone on a line or as a bracketed/parenthetical heading over a rapid-delivery passage in music-hall and G&S printings; 'Patter Song' as a number heading.
Alone as a heading, or line-initial with ':' or '.'. In G&S it is a centred heading over a number.
sung_trap: 'patter' is a sung verb/noun for rain and feet ('Patter, patter, on the beck', 'Patter on the window-pane' both in the corpus). Sung when followed by comma + same word, preposition, or a subject; label when bare with optional punctuation or parentheses.

The word is sung inside the patter itself ('This particularly rapid, unintelligible patter / Isn't generally heard', Gilbert) and in 'Patter on the window-pane' (Jane Taylor). Do not treat it as a label mid-line or when followed by a preposition.
traditions: Music hall, G&S libretti, comic opera, coon-song and minstrel sheet music, Victorian comic songsters.
5 [PATTER] marks plus 3 apparatus (Gilbert, Ruddigore). Expected heavily in G&S (PG 808) and music hall, where 'Patter' often introduces SPOKEN prose that must not be counted either.
examples: PATTER: Now, ladies, you've heard of my troubles...
--- TITLE: PATTER-TRIO: My eyes are fully open ... (Ruddigore, Act II)  (eng_hall_ws_gilbert.txt)

label_when: Alone on a line with optional ':' or '.'; inside brackets. Effectively absent from pre-1929 printed lyrics (a Tin Pan Alley sheet labels only Verse and Chorus/Refrain); a hit almost certainly comes from a modern editor or transcriber.
sung_trap: 'bridge' is very often sung ('London Bridge', 'the bridge of sighs', 'over the bridge'); 'release' is sung ('release me'). Label only bare, capitalised, with nothing else on the line.
traditions: Modern editorial overlays on Tin Pan Alley/jazz-age songs; not native to the period printings.

entries.term: Pre-chorus / Post-chorus / Hook / Outro (modern section names)
label_when: Alone on a line, optionally in brackets or with ':'. Expected count in 1600-1929 printings is zero; any occurrence indicates later editorial apparatus.
sung_trap: 'hook' is sung ('by hook or by crook', 'fish-hook'); 'lift' and 'climb' are common sung verbs. Label only bare and alone.
traditions: None native; check only as contamination from modern transcriptions.

entries.term: Introduction / Prelude / Symphony / Ritornello (instrumental opening or between-verse passage)
label_when: Alone on a line or in parentheses/brackets in songbooks and sheet-music texts, marking bars with no words; in Moore's Melodies/Thomson's Scottish Airs 'Symphony' between stanzas. In collected poems 'Prelude'/'Introduction' as a heading above verse whose body IS lyric (keep the body, mark the heading).
sung_trap: 'symphony' sung ('the symphony of the spheres'); 'prelude' and 'interlude' sung as nouns ('life's brief interlude'). Also 'Prelude' can be a poem's real title. Treat as label when bare with optional numeral/punctuation; treat as title when it is the item's TITLE line.
traditions: Georgian/Victorian sheet songs, Thomson/Moore/Haydn-Beethoven Scottish settings, opera libretti, Longfellow ('Prelude' to Voices of the Night), Wordsworth ('The Prelude' is a book title, not a section).

label_when: Alone on a line between parts of a poem sequence or verse drama, sometimes numbered; the following verse is lyric.
sung_trap: Sung as a noun mid-line ('a sweet interlude'). Label only when bare.
traditions: Victorian/Edwardian poem sequences (Swinburne, Meredith's sequences, Heine translations 'Lyrical Intermezzo').

entries.term: Vamp / Vamp till ready / Till ready
label_when: Alone on a line or parenthesised before verse 1 (or before a repeat) in music-hall and Tin Pan Alley texts; it instructs the accompanist and is never text.
An italic music-direction line or parenthetical in sheet-music lyric transcriptions.
Alone on a line at the head of a sheet song or between verse and refrain, or bracketed inside the refrain where the voice stops and the band plays.
sung_trap: 'vamp' is a 1910s-20s sung noun/verb ('the vamp of Savannah', 'she's a vamp'). Sung when it has an article/subject or sits inside metre; label when bare or with 'till ready'.
'vamp' is a sung noun in 1910s-20s songs ('She's a vamp'), and 'break' is common ('break my heart'). A cue only when it is parenthesised/italic, or the phrase 'till ready'.

'vamp' is a sung noun in 1910s-20s songs about a seductress ('She's a vamp from Broadway', 'Vamp of Savannah') and a verb ('to vamp a girl'). 'Break' is ubiquitous: 'break of day', 'my heart will break', 'Slow broke the gray cold morning'. 'Fill' is sung ('fill the cup'). These are labels only when free-standing (optionally with 'till ready' or a bar count), in brackets, or in italics, with no subject or object.
traditions: Music hall, vaudeville, Tin Pan Alley sheet music, ragtime songs.
Tin Pan Alley; music hall; ragtime song sheets
Tin Pan Alley, ragtime, jazz-age and music-hall sheet music, vaudeville professional copies

entries.term: Break / Breakdown / Dance / Walk-around / Clog / Stop-time
label_when: Alone on a line or parenthesised after a chorus, marking wordless dance/instrumental bars; as a heading 'Walk-Around' over a minstrel finale whose text is lyric.
sung_trap: 'break' is one of the most common sung words ('Break, break, break', 'break of day', 'my heart will break'); 'dance' and 'jig' are frequently sung. Label only when bare (optionally parenthesised) or in 'after each verse' directive phrasing.
traditions: Minstrel songsters (Christy's, Bryant's), vaudeville, coon songs, music hall, Tin Pan Alley.

label_when: Alone on a line in march-song and dance-song sheet music, where 'Trio' is the third strain (often the sung chorus); keep the words under it.
sung_trap: 'strain' is a very common sung noun ('Repeat th' exulting strain', 'a dying strain', 'sing a joyful strain' all occur in the corpus); 'trio' rarely sung ('a trio of maids'). Label only when bare with ordinal/punctuation. 'Trio' as a VOICE ensemble number is a separate entry.
traditions: Sousa-era march songs, college/military songs, two-step and waltz songs, band-song sheets.

entries.term: Coda / Codetta / Tag / Ending / Last time
label_when: Alone on a line, or with 'To' / 'al' navigation; barbershop 'Tag' over the final repeated phrase.
Alone on a line as a section heading of a sheet song, or line-final in brackets ('To Coda'). 'Tag' alone above a final repeated phrase is barbershop, music-hall and ragtime usage.
sung_trap: 'tag' sung ('rag, tag and bobtail'); 'ending' sung ('a happy ending', 'never-ending'). Label only when bare or with ordinal/navigation words.

'coda' and 'tag' rarely appear in lyrics. 'Tag' as a game or verb ('play at tag', 'tag along') is sung inside a sentence. A poem section headed 'Coda' (Victorian sequences) is a recited section whose heading is still a label (section-name domain); its text is recited and counted.
traditions: Sheet music, barbershop quartet arrangements (1910s-20s), art songs.
sheet music, Tin Pan Alley and music-hall professional copies, barbershop arrangements, art-song cycles

label_when: Alone on a line or parenthesised before/after alternative words for different passes; also printed above split final lines.
sung_trap: 'last time' and 'the first time' are common sung phrases ('for the last time'). Label only when bare/parenthesised and not inside a metrical sentence.
traditions: Sheet music, gospel hymnals, college songbooks.
examples: (2nd time) And then we'll all go home.

entries.term: Reprise / Repeat Chorus / Chorus as before
label_when: Alone on a line or after the last stanza instructing to sing previously printed words; in libretti 'Reprise' heading over shortened repetition (body is lyric).
sung_trap: 'Repeat' opens real sung lines ('Repeat the sounding joy', 'Repeat the joyful sound', 'Repeat with us the pledge', 'Repeat a' her jokes' are in the corpus). Direction only when its object is a section noun (chorus, verse, stanza, strain, lines) or a number, or the line is bare 'Repeat.'
traditions: Songsters, hymnals, music hall, G&S, operetta and musical comedy.

label_when: A chorus/refrain incipit ending in '&c.' (often indented, often after a 'Chorus' label) means 'sing the whole chorus again'. Mark the cue as a repeat pointer, not new lyric lines.
sung_trap: The incipit words themselves are genuine lyric; only the '&c.' and the implied expansion are apparatus. An 'etc.' inside a comic patter line can be spoken text, rare.
traditions: Burns/Scots collections, Southern war songsters, Christmas carol books, Moore, broadsides (63 corpus files carry '&c.').
examples: CHORUS. Christmas knows a merry, merry place, &c.

entries.term: Repeat marks: bis / ter / twice / Rep.
label_when: Parenthesised or trailing at line end, or alone on a line; it multiplies the preceding line(s).
sung_trap: 'twice' is sung ('think twice', 'twice as sweet'). Treat as apparatus only when parenthesised, at line end after punctuation, or bare. 'bis' and 'ter' are never sung in English.
traditions: Songsters, Scots collections, French-derived art songs, minstrel songs, hymnals.

entries.term: Da Capo / Dal Segno / Fine / al Fine / al Coda
label_when: Alone on a line or at line end (after punctuation, often italic or parenthesised); 'Fine' marks where the D.C./D.S. pass stops.
sung_trap: 'Fine' is a very common English sung word ('Fine knacks for ladies', 'Fine flour press'd down', 'Fine for a soger' all occur line-initially in the corpus). Navigation 'Fine' is bare, usually italic/parenthesised or paired with D.C./D.S. on the page; anything followed by a noun or within metre is lyric.
traditions: Sheet music, glee and part-song books, hymnals with repeated refrains, ballad-opera airs.

label_when: Alone on a line or line-initial with '.'/'--' before a declaimed passage in libretti, cantatas, oratorio wordbooks; often paired with a character name.
Alone on a line or with a following dash/speaker name, before declaimed lines.

Alone on a line as a sub-heading in a cantata, libretto or song; in Burns's 'The Jolly Beggars' the corpus already marks each one as apparatus ('Recitativo', alternating with 'Air', eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt:4167-4587). Always a label.
sung_trap: Never sung.
Never sung. The recitative TEXT that follows is sung and stays counted.

The word is never sung. The lines under it ARE sung (recitative is sung text), so count them. Do not treat 'recitative' as 'spoken'. 'Melodrama' (spoken over music) is the exception: its lines are spoken; see the Spoken entry.
traditions: G&S libretti, ballad opera, oratorio/cantata wordbooks (Handel), Georgian theatre songs, Burns's 'Jolly Beggars' (Recitativo).
Handel/Haydn/Mendelssohn oratorio wordbooks (Messiah, Creation, Elijah); Purcell; ballad operas; G&S ('Recit.' in Pinafore and Sorcerer); cantatas
cantatas, oratorio and opera libretti, ballad operas, Burns's cantata, Gilbert & Sullivan libretti, concert-song sheets

label_when: Alone on a line, parenthesised, or line-initial with ':'/'.--' before speech; the words after it are recited text (counts as recited lyric only if the corpus counts recited text - flag the label regardless).
sung_trap: 'Spoken' line-initial with ordinary syntax is lyric ('Spoken in fear with sense of need' in the corpus) or a prologue heading ('Spoken by Miss Fontenelle on her Benefit Night' is a heading). Label only when bare/parenthesised or with colon/dash.
traditions: Music hall, vaudeville, coon songs, Tin Pan Alley, prologues/epilogues in theatre, Burns's occasional addresses.

variants: AIR.—Tune, "Over the Hills and far away."
label_when: Alone on a line, numbered with roman/arabic numerals (ballad opera numbers its airs: 'AIR I.' to 'AIR LXIX.'), often followed by a tune name ('Air XXXI. Cobbler's End'); 'AIR--"X"' giving the tune is a tune designation (meter-or-tune domain; this corpus hoists it into TITLE).

Alone on a line, or line-initial and followed by a Roman/Arabic number, a full stop, an em-dash/double hyphen, or 'Tune'/'To the tune of' plus a quoted tune name; usually capitalised or small caps; comes directly before a stanza, often right after a speaker prefix (MACHEATH. / AIR XXII.).
A line, or a parenthetical under the title, that starts with Air/Tune/To the tune of/Melody and then gives a quoted or italic tune name; it never rhymes with the stanza.

LINE-INITIAL 'Air' (or 'AIR', 'Old Air', 'Irish Air') followed by '--', ':', '.--' or ' - ' plus a tune name, between title and text or hoisted from there. In Moore and Scots collections this is near-universal. The corpus hoists these into [air: X] and keeps some as '# APPARATUS: AIR—“_Jenny’s Bawbee_.”'. In old American tunebooks 'Air' is also the name of the MELODY PART (Treble/Air/Tenor/Bass); that use is a voice-part label.
sung_trap: 'air' is extremely common in lyric ('the air was still', 'castles in the air', 'a merry air'). Label only when it heads a line with a numeral/tune name/punctuation and no verb.

'air' is a very common sung noun (breeze, sky, melody, bearing): 'Air with no breath of earth to stain it' (corpus), 'the morning air', 'a merry air'. Treat it as a label only when it is the first word, capitalised, and followed by a number, a full stop/dash with nothing else from the sentence, or a tune name. If a verb or a lowercase continuation follows ('Air, that ...', 'Air with ...'), it is sung.
'To the tune of the fife and drum' can be a sung line. It is a label only when it opens the block before stanza 1 and the rest of the line is a quoted title.

'air' is an extremely common sung word, and LINE-FINAL 'Air:' with a colon is sung: 'Is better than heavy Air:' (eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt:467), 'And Vanish into Air:', 'To my Native Country Air:', 'Mind Lovers no more, than the Birds of the Air.', 'Whose various sweets perfume the Air.' Restoration printing capitalises nouns, so capital 'Air' proves nothing. The label is LINE-INITIAL, followed by tune-delimiting punctuation, then a quoted, italic or title-cased name, and stands outside the stanza block. A sung 'air' is preceded by an article, preposition or adjective and ends a rhyming line.
traditions: Ballad opera (Beggar's Opera, Love in a Village), songsters, Scots/Irish collections ('Air--'), Moore's Melodies, Dowland/Campion ayre books.

John Gay's Beggar's Opera and Polly; 18th-c. ballad operas (Love in a Village, The Quaker's Opera); Elizabethan/Jacobean ayre books (Dowland, Campion); Burns/Moore song collections giving the tune; Civil War songsters ('air:')
Burns (corpus: Tune--"The Dragon of Wantley."); Moore's Irish Melodies; broadsides; American Civil War and political songsters; temperance and campaign songbooks
Moore's Irish Melodies, Scots song collections, Civil War and political songbooks, parlour sheet songs, Victorian anthologies, songsters
examples: AIR XVI. Tune, Over the Hills and far away. / Were I laid on Greenland's coast,
"--- TITLE: Lesbia Hath a Beaming Eye  [air: Nora Creina]" (hoisted from 'Air--Nora Creina'); trap: "Is better than heavy Air:"

entries.term: Song (as a number or embedded-song heading)
label_when: Alone on a line (often caps) above an embedded lyric in a play, novel, masque or libretto; or 'Song--Character' in libretti; or 'Song I./II.' within a sequence.

Alone on a line, or a capitalised heading followed by a full stop, a dash plus a character name, or a number. In a play, masque or novel it is inserted between prose or blank verse and the lyric that follows.

A line-initial number, or 'No.'/'Song'/'Hymn'/'Psalm'/'Air' with a number, that heads an item (often together with its title, which belongs in the title field). In libretti and vocal scores 'No. N' numbers the musical items.
sung_trap: 'song' is constantly sung ('sing a song', 'a song of sixpence'). Label only when bare with punctuation/numeral/character name; a line 'Song.' inside a poem refers to an embedded song heading.
'Sing me a song', 'Song of the shirt', 'my song is done' are sung. A label is one word (plus a number or name), capitalised, and has no verb or article governing a following noun phrase that rhymes.

'Psalm' or 'Hymn' as a title word in a sung line ('Sing a psalm of praise') is not followed by a numeral. 'Air' with a numeral (ballad-opera numbering) is apparatus; 'air' as a noun in a lyric ("the summer air") is sung.
traditions: Shakespeare/Jonson/Fletcher plays, masques, G&S libretti, Scott/Tennyson embedded songs, Blake's 'Song', songsters ('Comic Song').

masques and plays with inserted songs (Jonson, Dryden, Sheridan); G&S libretti; music-hall and Tin Pan Alley sheet-music subtitles; verse dramas (Shelley, Tennyson's The Princess, Browning's Pippa Passes)
Hymnals, psalters, Herrick's Hesperides (numbered), ballad operas (Beggar's Opera 'Air I.'), G&S vocal scores and libretti, songsters
examples: SONG.—RALPH. / The nightingale / Sighed for the moon's bright ray
181. A DIALOGUE BETWIXT HORACE AND LYDIA

entries.term: Duet / Trio / Quartet / Quintet / Sestet / Ensemble (vocal-number headings)
label_when: Alone on a line or followed by '--' and character names, heading a number in libretti/cantatas; the body is lyric.
Alone on a line, or followed by a dash or parentheses with the performers' names; capitalised; before the first sung line of the number.
sung_trap: Rarely sung ('a trio of maids from school' - G&S sings 'Three little maids'); 'sestet' also a sonnet division (rarely printed). Label only when bare or with character names.
Rarely sung, though it can appear in a lyric about singing ('we sang a duet'). A lowercase or mid-sentence use is sung.
traditions: G&S libretti, operetta, musical comedy, glee clubs, oratorio wordbooks.
G&S; Balfe, Wallace, Benedict English operas; ballad operas; Victorian drawing-room songs; Moody & Sankey gospel songbooks ('Duet or Semi-chorus')
examples: DUET—MABEL and FREDERIC. / Ah, leave me not to pine

entries.term: Finale / Opening Chorus / Closing Chorus / Tableau
label_when: Alone on a line in libretti, musical-comedy and pantomime wordbooks; body under it is lyric.
A heading line, often with an act reference.
sung_trap: 'curtain' and 'finale' sung only as ordinary nouns mid-line ('the grand finale of the night'). Label only when bare/caps.
'finale' is occasionally sung figuratively ('the grand finale of our days'), always lowercase mid-line. It is separate from the navigation word 'Fine' (repeat domain).
traditions: G&S, comic opera, musical comedy, pantomime, minstrel-show finales.
G&S; operetta; musical comedy; ballad opera ('Air LXIX. Finale' style)
examples: FINALE, ACT I. / Oh, happy the lily

label_when: Alone on a line with a numeral/ordinal; 'SCENE.--' followed by setting prose (the prose is a stage direction, not lyric).
Under or after a song lifted from a play or opera, identifying its location; alone on a line, often italic or parenthesised.
sung_trap: 'act' and 'scene' are common sung words ('act your part', 'the scene was fair'); 'number' sung. Label only with numeral/ordinal or caps with dash.
In a libretto, 'Act I.' / 'Scene.--' heads a section (section-name domain), not a citation; neither is sung.
traditions: G&S libretti, operetta, ballad opera, masques, verse drama, minstrel-show programmes.
Shakespeare songs in anthologies, Elizabethan dramatic lyrics, ballad-opera and G&S extracts, Beggar's Opera airs

entries.term: Solo / Soli / Tutti / All / Leader / Shantyman (call-and-response part labels)
label_when: Alone on a line or line-initial followed by '.', ':', '--' before the part it assigns (spirituals: 'Solo. -- Sin's rooster's crowed' in the corpus). Strip the label, keep the text.
Alone on a line, or line-initial followed by '.'/':'/'--' and a performer name or voice type (corpus Morris 'SOLO--SOPHIA.').
sung_trap: 'All' is one of the commonest sung words; 'men', 'women', 'people', 'crew' are common sung nouns. Label only when the word stands bare (with punctuation) at line start and the remainder is a full lyric line, or alone on its own line; 'All' followed by lowercase continuation in metre is lyric.
'solo' is rarely sung ('she sang a solo sweet'); it is sung only lowercase mid-line.
traditions: Spirituals and jubilee songbooks, sea shanties, work songs, gospel, hymnals (responsive), glee books, libretti.
gospel hymnals (Moody & Sankey Sacred Songs and Solos); oratorio; libretti; sheet music; shanties
examples: Solo.--Sin's rooster's crowed, Ole Mahster's riz,

entries.term: Voice-part names (Treble / Counter / Tenor / Bass / Air / Soprano / Alto)
variants: Air (= melody line in four-part tunebooks)
label_when: Alone on a line or at line start before a voice's words in tune-books and part-song books; 'Air' in American shape-note books names the melody part.
A prefix or heading designating which voice sings the following line(s), or a stave/part label in tunebooks and part-books. Single letters S. A. T. B. appear in choral word-sheets as prefixes.
sung_trap: 'air', 'bass', 'treble' sung as ordinary words ('the bass of heaven's deep organ', 'treble' in 'treble joy'). Label only when bare with punctuation at line start in a part-book layout.

'bass' (also the fish, and confusion with 'base'), 'treble' (adjective: 'treble joy'), 'tenor' ('the even tenor of their way'), 'air' and 'counter' are common sung words. Sung when lowercase or inside metrical syntax; a label only when capitalised, followed by '.'/':' and either at line start before a line it governs or alone. Single letters S./A./T./B. conflict with initials ('A.' article, 'R. Burns'); require the run of other part letters nearby, or 2+ spaces after.
traditions: Shape-note tunebooks (Sacred Harp, Southern Harmony), New England tunebooks, glee/part-song books, Victorian anthems.
oratorio and anthem wordbooks; Tudor/Jacobean part-books; shape-note tunebooks (Sacred Harp, Southern Harmony); glee books; gospel quartet books
examples: TENOR.  Hark! from the tombs a doleful sound.
Bass. / Thus saith the Lord of Hosts

entries.term: Decani / Cantoris / Full / Verse (Anglican anthem sides)
label_when: At line start or in margins of anthem/chant wordbooks, assigning lines to choir sides or to solo ('Verse') vs whole choir ('Full').
sung_trap: 'full' is common sung adjective ('full of grace'); 'Verse' see Verse entry. Label only at line start as bare abbreviation with '.' or in the margin.
traditions: Anglican cathedral anthem wordbooks, chant books, Tudor/Restoration anthems.
examples: Dec. O Lord, open thou our lips.

label_when: Alone on a line (all-caps 'HE.'/'SHE.' occur 6 times each in the corpus) or line-initial before the lyric line; alternate through a dialogue song.

Line-initial pronoun or role word, capitalised, followed by '.' or '. -' and then the sung line (corpus Moore 'He. -     When he looks for honey-dew'; Burns 'Both. For a' the joys, &c.'); it alternates line by line or stanza by stanza.
sung_trap: 'He' and 'she' line-initial are constantly sung ('She walks in beauty'). Label only when the word stands alone with a full stop/colon (or caps + period) and no verb follows on that line.

'He', 'She' and 'Both' are among the commonest line-initial SUNG words ('He came to my window', 'Both were young'). Prefix test: the word is followed directly by a full stop (or '. -'/':') and then a capital letter starting a new sentence. 'He.' / 'She.' as a complete sentence never occurs in sung English. Any continuation without the full stop is sung.
traditions: Dialogue songs and duets in songsters, Burns ('Duncan Gray' style), Scots and Irish courting songs, Elizabethan dialogues, music hall duets.
Burns duets; Moore; 18th-c. dialogue songs (Playford, D'Urfey); pastoral eclogues; music-hall duets; drawing-room duets
examples:
SHE.
O tell me, Johnny, will ye be true?
She. -    Is to waves that wander near,

entries.term: Dialogue / Eclogue / Pastoral / Idyl (poem-type and division headings)
label_when: Alone on a line as a heading or numbered division ('Eclogue I.', 'The Shepherd's Calendar, Januarye. Aegloga prima'), or as the title. The corpus also has '[Gothic: Eclogue.]' (13 lines) where a blackletter heading leaked into the text.
sung_trap: 'pastoral' and 'dialogue' rarely sung as nouns/adjectives ('a pastoral strain'). Label only as bare heading or with numeral.
traditions: Spenser, Drayton, Pope, Virgilian translations, Burns ('dialogue' songs), Tennyson ('English Idyls'), Theocritus translations.

entries.term: Question / Answer / The Answer / The Reply (ballad, broadside and dialogue divisions)
label_when: Alone on a line between two halves of a broadside or poem pair ('The Answer.' after 'The Question.'), or as title of a companion poem; 'Q.'/'A.'/'Echo.' line-initial in catechism, riddle and echo poems.
Line-initial abbreviation with a full stop followed by text (corpus Herrick 'Ans. Heat ye to cool ye.').
sung_trap: 'Answer me, answer me!' and 'Reply, reply!' are genuinely sung (both in the corpus); 'echo' is common sung word. Label only when the word has an article-title form ('The Answer'), stands alone with a full stop, or is line-initial 'Q.'/'A.'/'Echo.' followed by a separate utterance.
'A.' is ambiguous with the article 'A' (sung 'A lass ...'). Prefix only when 'A.' has a full stop and 2+ spaces or a capitalised new word follows. 'Answer' is a sung verb ('Answer me, love').
traditions: Broadside ballads, Pepys/Roxburghe ballads, Elizabethan answer poems (Marlowe/Raleigh), riddle songs, catechism hymns, echo poems (Herbert).
Herrick; catechetical hymns; Sunday-school dialogue songs; Watts's Divine Songs for children
examples: Ans. Heat ye to cool ye.

entries.term: Part / The First Part / Part the Second (poem, ballad, hymn divisions)
variants: Second Part, to the same tune
_The Second Part, To the same Tune._
label_when: Alone on a line with a numeral or ordinal, or 'the First/Second Part' phrasing; in Watts and other hymnals followed by a metre ('Second Part. C. M.' occurs in the corpus); in broadsides 'The Second Part. To the same tune.'
Alone on a line, followed by a roman, arabic or ordinal numeral or 'the First/Second', optionally followed by a metre code. Also as 'The Second Part' heading a broadside's second half.
sung_trap: 'part' is very common sung ('Part in peace!', 'Part of the morning light', 'Part your joined lips', 'Part, or the whole of Thee' all line-initial in the corpus; also 'we must part'). Label ONLY when it carries a numeral/ordinal or the formula 'the [ordinal] part' and no verb/object, typically alone on its line.

'part' is sung in 655 rows across 229 files ('Yes, we must part'), and line-initially as a verb ('Part in beryl at the bow'). Treat it as a label only when no verb or object follows and a numeral or ordinal is present.
traditions: Broadside and garland ballads, Child/Percy ballads, Watts and Wesley hymnals, metrical psalters (Ps. 119 in parts), long narrative poems (Coleridge's Ancient Mariner 'Part I'-'Part VII').

5 lyric rows / 2 files (Calverley 2, Watts 3), plus TITLE lines (Watts 'Part the second', Coleridge 'Part Iii') and apparatus (Lady Anne Barnard 'PART II.', Durfey). Expected in broadside ballads ('The Second Part. To the same tune') and songsters.

variants: Hymns. Book 2. Composed on Divine Subjects.
label_when: Alone on a line with numeral or ordinal; often followed by a verse or prose argument.
Alone, followed by a numeral, as a division heading. A descriptive subtitle may follow on the same line or the next.
sung_trap: Italian 'canto' ('I sing') inside an Italian line is lyric; English sung use is negligible.
'book' is sung mid-line (e.g. 'the blest volume'). 'Canto' is not sung in English verse. Treat them as labels only with a numeral and no verse continuation.
traditions: Scott (Lay, Marmion, Lady of the Lake), Byron (Don Juan, Childe Harold), Spenser, Dante translations.
Watts 'Book 2.' and 'Book 3.' (2 lyric rows); Carroll CANTO I-VII in TITLE lines; John André CANTO II and III as apparatus.

label_when: Alone on a line with numeral/ordinal; or as a hymnal division prefixing hymn numbers ('Hymn 2:58' = Book II, Hymn 58).
sung_trap: 'book' sung constantly ('the book of life'). Label only with numeral/ordinal and no other words.
traditions: Epic and long poems (Milton, Pope, Wordsworth, Cowper), Watts's Hymns in three Books, Spenser.

entries.term: Fit / Fitt / Fytte / Fitte (ballad and romance division)
label_when: Alone on a line with ordinal or numeral, or 'the [ordinal] Fit(t)' formula; also archaic spelling 'Fyrst'.
Alone, as 'Fit/Fytte the <ordinal>' or 'Fytte <numeral>', heading a section of a ballad or mock-ballad.
sung_trap: 'Fit' is one of the most frequent line-initial sung words in the corpus (over 30 lines: 'Fit for the place above', 'Fit to deck maidens' bowers', 'Fit emblem of your sons'); also 'a fit of...'. Label ONLY when followed/preceded by an ordinal or numeral with nothing else on the line, or in the caps formula 'FIT THE FIRST'.

'fit' is sung in 28 line-initial rows across 17 files ('Fit for the deed I had to do'), and Gilbert sings 'To let the punishment fit the crime' (6 rows). Carroll's mock-archaic 'Ye jawe of horse yt wyll not fytte' is sung.
traditions: Percy's Reliques, Child ballads (Chevy Chase, Gest of Robyn Hode), Carroll's 'Hunting of the Snark' (Fit the First ... Fit the Eighth), medieval romance editions.
1 apparatus row (Carroll, Hunting of the Snark 'Fit the fourth'). Expected in Percy-style ballad anthologies and Child-ballad printings.

entries.term: Passus / Duan / Branch / Gest (medieval and Ossianic divisions)
label_when: Alone on a line with numeral/ordinal or Latin ordinal.
sung_trap: 'branch' sung as a common noun. Label only with ordinal/numeral.
traditions: Piers Plowman editions, Macpherson's Ossian ('Duan'), Welsh-romance translations, Robin Hood gests.

entries.term: Section / Movement / Division / Number (generic numbered divisions)
label_when: Alone on a line with numeral/ordinal or the § sign.
sung_trap: 'movement' and 'section' sung as plain nouns ('every movement of her soul'). Label only with numeral/ordinal.
traditions: Long poems, cantata wordbooks, hymnal topic divisions, school songbooks.

label_when: Alone on a line (the corpus has bare 'I', 'II', 'III' lines), or line-initial before stanza text in hymnals/psalters ('1 Hark! the herald', '2 Christ, by highest heaven adored'), centered above sonnets in a sequence.
sung_trap: Roman 'I' alone may be a one-word sung line only in extremely rare cases; the pronoun 'I' line-initial is always followed by text. Ordinals ('First', 'Last') are sung when followed by words. Label when the numeral stands alone or prefixes text with only space/period separation in a numbered hymn/psalm layout.
traditions: All: hymnals, psalters, sonnet sequences, long poems, songsters, round books.

entries.term: Verse references in hymn/psalm headings (Ver. 3, v. 1-4)
label_when: Inside or directly under a psalm/hymn heading, citing scripture verses paraphrased; never sung.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Watts's Psalms of David Imitated, Scottish Psalter, Tate and Brady, Methodist hymnals.

entries.term: Strophe / Antistrophe / Epode (and Jonson's Turn / Counter-turn / Stand)
label_when: Alone on a line, numbered or not, in Pindaric odes and Greek-model choruses.
sung_trap: 'turn' and 'stand' are common sung verbs; label only when capitalised alone in an ode's divisional sequence.
traditions: Pindaric odes (Jonson, Gray 'The Bard', Cowley), Shelley/Swinburne/Arnold choral dramas, Milton's Samson, Horace translations (Epodes).

label_when: Alone on a line before the closing short stanza of a ballade, chant royal or other poem/sequence ('ENVOY' 6 times, 'L'ENVOI' once in the corpus).
sung_trap: 'envoy' as a messenger noun ('the king's envoy') sung mid-line; 'Prince,' opens the envoi text and IS lyric. Label only when bare.
traditions: Chaucerian ballades, Victorian ballades (Swinburne, Lang, Dobson, Henley), Kipling ('L'Envoi'), Spenser.

entries.term: Proem / Prologue / Induction / Exordium / Preface (opening divisions)
label_when: Alone on a line or as heading line, often followed by 'spoken by'/'to'; the verse body under it IS lyric (verse prologue), but a prose preface is apparatus in full.
sung_trap: Rarely sung; 'prologue' as noun in a line ('the prologue of the day'). Distinguish heading (bare/caps) from body.
traditions: Theatre prologues/epilogues (Burns, Garrick), Chaucer editions, Tennyson ('Prologue' to In Memoriam), Morris ('Apology'), Longfellow (Tales of a Wayside Inn 'Prelude'/'Interlude'/'Finale').
examples: PROLOGUE, SPOKEN BY MR. WOODS, ON HIS BENEFIT NIGHT

label_when: Alone on a line or as heading; '(Continued.)' / '(To be continued.)' are print artifacts between instalments.
sung_trap: Verse epilogues are lyric under the heading; 'P.S.' can open a sung line in comic letter-songs ('P.S. - I love you') - lyric when followed by metre in quotes/body. Label when bare.
traditions: Theatre epilogues, broadsides with sequels, periodical poetry, Browning ('Epilogue' to Asolando), Burns's verse epistles with 'Postscript'.

label_when: Alone on a line before a summary of a canto/book/poem. The heading is apparatus and, when the argument is prose (Milton), the WHOLE following paragraph is apparatus too; when it is a verse quatrain (Spenser), it is non-sung paratext but metrical - mark as argument, not lyric.
A prose paragraph (not lineated, not metrical) before or after a song, often italic or in smaller type, describing occasion, story or source. Entire paragraph is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'argument' rare in song ('Arguments and fair Intreats did I use' in corpus, lyric because embedded in a sentence).

Prose links in chantefable or recitation pieces, and spoken dialogue in libretti/minstrel sketches, are performed but not sung (speaker/dialogue domain decides). A spoken 'Recitation' in a music-hall song is performed text: flag it as spoken, not as editorial.
traditions: Spenser (Faerie Queene), Milton (Paradise Lost), Pope, Dryden translations, Scott, Blake ('The Argument' in Marriage of Heaven and Hell - verse, arguably lyric).
Percy, Scott's Minstrelsy, Burns, Moore, broadside long titles ('Shewing how ...'), Milton/Spenser-style arguments, songster introductions
examples: The following lines were written on the eve of the battle.

entries.term: Invocation / Dedication / Inscription / Address / To the Reader
label_when: Alone on a line or as heading; verse body below is lyric, prose dedication paragraph is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'address'/'dedication' sung as nouns ('with dedication true'); 'To ...' openings are often real titles. Label when bare or in the formula 'To the Reader'.
traditions: Collected poems, Byron (Don Juan 'Dedication'), Tennyson (Idylls 'Dedication'), Burns ('Address to the Deil' is a title), hymnals' prefatory verses.

entries.term: Conclusion / Close / The End / Finis / Explicit (end markers)
label_when: Alone on a line after the last stanza or between parts ('The Conclusion' introducing a final section, 'FINIS' printed as colophon); 'End of the First Part'.
sung_trap: 'end' and 'the end' are sung phrases ('world without end', 'till the end'); 'close' sung ('at the close of day'); 'Conclusion' rarely sung. Label only when bare on its line (often caps/centered) or in 'End of ...' / 'Here endeth' formulas.
traditions: Broadsides ('FINIS'), garlands, chapbooks, medieval text editions ('Explicit'), Victorian books ('THE END'), sheet music ('Fine').

label_when: Alone on a line inside a long psalm/hymn marking a point where singing may stop; occurs 37 + 5 + 5 times in eng_hymn_watts.txt.
Alone on a line between stanzas of a long psalm or hymn (corpus Watts: 37 'PAUSE.', 5 'PAUSE I.', 5 'PAUSE II.', 1 'PAUSE III.'); it marks a point where the congregation may stop.
Alone, in caps, with an optional roman numeral, between stanzas of a long psalm or hymn. It marks where a congregation may stop when singing in portions.
sung_trap: 'pause' sung as verb/noun ('pause, my soul', 'without a pause'). Label only when bare and caps/with numeral.
'pause' is a sung verb/noun ('Pause, my soul! adore and wonder', 'without a pause'). A label only as a one-word capitalised line, optionally with a Roman numeral.
'pause' is sung in 104 rows across 63 files ('And the heart must pause to breathe'). Treat it as a label only when it stands alone in caps.
traditions: Isaac Watts's Psalms and Hymns, and hymnals reprinting them (Dwight, Rippon, Methodist and Baptist collections).
Isaac Watts; Doddridge; 18th-19th-c. Dissenting and American hymnals derived from Watts
48 lyric rows / 1 file (eng_hymn_watts.txt). Expected in other Watts and Rippon-type hymnals.

label_when: Alone on a line or as hymnal item heading, with number (arabic or roman, sometimes roman 'C.' = 100) and often metre/tune; also cross-references 'As the 149th Psalm' (metre pointer).

A heading with a number or Roman numeral, often with a metre tag (L.M., C.M., S.M. — meter domain) and a verse-reference line ('Ver. 1 2 3.' — corpus Watts, x87, which lists the psalm verses paraphrased). The 'Ver.' line is always apparatus.
sung_trap: 'psalm' sung in lyric ('sing a psalm', 'A Psalm of Life' is a title). Also a corpus direction 'Psalm, by adding the two following lines to every stanza' is editorial. Label when followed by number/numeral; direction when it has a verb about how to sing.

'psalm', 'hymn' and 'anthem' are sung nouns ('Sing a hymn of gladness', 'raise the psalm'). A label when it is followed by a number/Roman numeral, a 'Part', or alone with a full stop. Do not confuse 'Ver.' (verse reference) with the harness tag '[VERSE n]'.
traditions: Metrical psalters (Sternhold and Hopkins, Tate and Brady, Scottish Psalter 1650, Bay Psalm Book), Watts, hymnals.
Watts (Psalms of David Imitated; Hymns and Spiritual Songs); Wesley; Tate & Brady; Bay Psalm Book; Scottish Psalter; every hymnal
examples: Ver. 1 2 3. / Thy mercies fill the earth, O Lord

label_when: Alone on a line with number or book:number (both forms in the corpus: 'Hymn 77.', 'Hymn 3:28. 1st. S. M.'), often with metre.

A line made of hymn or psalm number, optional part or version ordinal ('1st.', '2d.', '3d.', 'First Part', 'Second Version') and a meter label, in heading position. The whole line is apparatus. The corpus has these lines in eng_hymn_watts.txt, e.g. 'Hymn 3:26. 1st. L.M.' (line 11514), 'Psalms 51:2. Second Part. L. M.'
Line-initial 'Hymn' or 'Psalm' plus a number, optionally followed by a metre or tune reference.
sung_trap: 'hymn' sung as noun ('a hymn of praise'); 'Hymn to Intellectual Beauty' is a poem title. Label when numbered; title when it names an addressee.
None sung. The ordinals '1st.', '2d.' here mean first or second version of a psalm, not a 1st-time/2nd-time navigation; do not merge the two readings.
'hymn' is sung in 75 mid-line rows ('Thy lustrous soul, then harp and hymn'). A heading needs a digit right after the word.
traditions: Watts (three books), Wesley, Olney Hymns, Sankey, all denominational hymnals.
Watts's Psalms and Hymns, Wesley's Collection, Rippon, Dobell, Tate & Brady, American reprints, Scottish Psalter (versions)
19 rows / 1 file (Watts). 'No. N' numbering is expected in songsters.

entries.term: Version / Another / The Same / Second Set (alternate-text divisions)
label_when: Alone on a line in psalters, songbooks and Scots collections introducing an alternative text of the preceding item.
sung_trap: 'another' and 'the same' are frequent sung openers ('Another year is dawning', 'the same sweet face'). Label only when the line is bare (with full stop) or in a formula ending in 'version/metre/set/of the same'.
traditions: Scottish Psalter (second versions), Watts ('Another'), Burns/Johnson's Scots Musical Museum, Elizabethan miscellanies ('Another of the same').

label_when: Alone on a line as heading of the closing praise stanza ('Doxology.' in the corpus). The stanza body ('Praise God, from whom all blessings flow') IS sung.
A heading line before a final trinitarian stanza or prose ascription.
sung_trap: 'Gloria' is sung in macaronic carols ('Gloria in excelsis Deo', 'Gloria tibi Domine!' in corpus); 'Glory be to the Father' is sung text in chant books. Label when bare heading; sung when the line continues the Latin/English text.

The doxology TEXT under the heading ('Praise God, from whom all blessings flow', 'Glory be to the Father, and to the Son') IS sung and stays counted. Strip only the heading. 'Glory be to the Father' printed as the first words of a stanza is sung, not a label.
traditions: Protestant hymnals, Anglican chant books, Watts, Ken's hymns, Methodist collections.
Ken's Morning/Evening Hymn; Methodist and Baptist hymnals; Anglican chant books; Watts appendices
examples: DOXOLOGY. / Praise God, from whom all blessings flow;

label_when: Label only in heading formulas ('Threefold Amen', 'Dresden Amen', 'Alleluia' as a section heading in a hymnal topic index) or a parenthesised/marginal 'Selah' in a psalm printing.
It is apparatus only in headings or notes ('Threefold Amen.', 'The Amen may be omitted'), as a bracketed/parenthesised editorial optional marker in hymnal word editions, or in a rubric.

It is apparatus as a closing formula when the edition prints it outside the stanza (centred, small type, under the tune) in a WORDS-ONLY collection that does not sing it, or in reading anthologies of hymns as poems. A note such as 'Omit Amen' is always apparatus. Policy: in hymnals (Hymns A&M 1861 on) the final 'Amen' is SUNG to the tune's plagal cadence and should count; tag it rather than delete it.

Almost never a label. Flag it only when a hymnal prints an optional final 'Amen' set apart (italic, in brackets, or 'Amen' on its own under the last stanza with a note), and then annotate it as optional-sung rather than removing it.
sung_trap: These words are normally SUNG: the hymnal 'Amen' printed after the last stanza is set to music; 'Hallelujah' refrains are lyric; 'Selah' in a verse paraphrase may fill metre. Keep as lyric unless it is a heading formula or a bracketed/marginal mark outside the metre.

Amen is USUALLY SUNG: 'Amen, Amen:' (corpus Guiney), 'Amen, amen, say I.' (Rossetti), 'Amen.' as the final line of a hymn in Victorian hymnals. Default to sung. Exceptions: 'Amend' (sung word starting with the same letters); headings naming an Amen setting; and an Amen the editor printed in brackets as optional — keep it but flag it for the policy decision rather than counting it automatically.

'Amen' inside stanzas ('And all the people said Amen', 'Amen, so let it be', spiritual refrains 'Amen, Amen') is sung text. The final 'Amen' after a hymn in a music edition is sung too. It is apparatus only when the source explicitly treats it as a liturgical close or rubric, as in 'Omit Amen' or a bracketed 'Amen' in a reading text.
All 12 line-initial and 36 mid-line corpus occurrences are sung ('Amen, Amen:' Guiney x3; 'Amen! Amen!' Burns; 'Hallelujah! Amen.').
traditions: Hymnals, psalters, gospel songs, Anglican chant, spirituals.
Hymns Ancient & Modern (every hymn ends Amen); English Hymnal; Catholic hymnals; gospel songs (seldom)
hymnals (Victorian Anglican and later), gospel songbooks, spirituals, psalters, devotional poetry collections
12 line-initial rows / 8 files plus 36 mid-line rows / 19 files; hymn and secular files.
examples: And crown him Lord of all. / Amen.
"Amen." (centred under the last stanza of a Hymns A&M hymn)

entries.term: Liturgical section names (canticles, mass and office parts)
label_when: Alone on a line as the heading of a liturgical item or section in hymnals, chant books, anthem wordbooks and carol books.
sung_trap: The Latin incipit often IS the sung first line ('Te Deum laudamus', 'Kyrie eleison', 'Venite, exultemus'); 'Recessional' is also Kipling's poem title; 'anthem' and 'chant' are sung nouns ('the national anthem', 'chant a lay'). Label when bare and capitalised as a heading; sung when it continues as text in the metre or is followed by more words of the canticle.
traditions: Anglican/Episcopal hymnals, Catholic hymnals, carol books (macaronic), chant books, Wesleyan collections.

label_when: Line-initial before a short line in litanies and office texts; strip the marker, keep the text.
Single-letter V./R. (or ℣/℟) at line start before alternating sentences in prayer books, litanies and office books; full words as headings.
A single-letter V./R. or the symbols at line start in litanies and responsorial hymns, or role names (Minister/People) as speaker labels.
sung_trap: 'V.'/'R.' cannot be sung; 'Response' as noun rarely sung. Ambiguity: 'V.' as roman five before a stanza is numbering, not versicle - disambiguate by alternation with 'R.'.

Single-letter 'V.' and 'R.' are also speaker initials (corpus Lovelace 'V.   Touch thy dead wood' is a character, not a versicle) and attribution initials ('R. Burns'). Both are apparatus prefixes, but R. followed by a surname is attribution (other domain). Check for an alternating V./R. pair to call it liturgical. The response text itself is sung or said and stays counted.
Jean Ingelow's '_V_.' is the Vicar (a speaker). Single capital letters also occur as initials. Treat V./R. as versicle and response only when they alternate in a liturgical item.
traditions: Book of Common Prayer-style litanies, Catholic office books, responsive readings in Protestant hymnals.
Book of Common Prayer (Litany, Suffrages); Roman Breviary and Missal translations; Sarum primers; Anglo-Catholic office books; 19th-c. American responsive hymnals
0 in the corpus. Expected in hymnals with litanies and in carol-service books.
examples:
V. O Lord, open thou our lips.
R. And our mouth shall show forth thy praise.
V. O Lord, show thy mercy upon us. / R. And grant us thy salvation.
(expected) V. O Lord, open thou our lips. / R. And our mouth shall show forth thy praise.

label_when: Alone on a line as a heading or numbered carol in a collection ('CAROL XII.'), or as a title.
sung_trap: 'Noel'/'Nowell' and 'wassail' are very frequently SUNG refrain words ('The First Nowell', 'Noel, Noel, Noel'); 'carol' sung as verb ('the larks carol'). Label only when numbered or bare heading at item top; a 'Nowell' line inside or after a stanza is burden lyric.
traditions: Carol books (Sandys, Husk, Bramley and Stainer, Oxford), broadsides, Tudor carol MSS editions.

entries.term: Round / Catch / Canon / Glee / Madrigal / Part-song (vocal-form headings)
label_when: Alone on a line as heading of an item, frequently with voice count ('Round in 3 parts'), or numbered ('Catch XII.'); entry numbers 1. 2. 3. inside a round mark where each voice enters (numbering, not lyric).
A heading line or subtitle.

As a heading or subtitle ('A Round for three voices'), or inline numerals, asterisks or signs placed before words where each voice enters. The entry numerals or signs are apparatus; the words are sung once each.
sung_trap: 'round' is one of the most frequent sung words ('all around', 'round the old tree' in corpus); 'catch', 'glee', 'canon/cannon' are common sung words. Label only when bare heading or with voice-count/numeral qualifier.

'round' is extremely common in sung text ('Round the old tree', 'All round my hat', 'go round'). A label only as a one-word capitalised line, or as 'Round for N voices'. Any preposition/adverb use is sung.

'round' is a very common sung word ('round her paddles dies away', 'Weave a circle round him thrice', 'all the year round', 'a round of pleasure'). 'catch' is a sung verb ('catch the wind'), and 'canon' is a sung or recited noun in hymns and poems. They are labels only as a heading or subtitle, typically 'A Round' or 'Round for N voices', or alone on a line before the text, or after the title as a genre tag. Entry numerals ('1.', '2.', '3.') in rounds must not be read as stanza numbers.
traditions: Ravenscroft, Playford, Catch Club collections, glee books, school/children's songbooks, Elizabethan madrigal books, G&S ('Madrigal' numbers in Mikado and Ruddigore).
Playford; school and Sunday-school songbooks; Victorian children's books
Ravenscroft and Hilton catch books, Playford, glee clubs, school songbooks, nursery collections ('Three Blind Mice'), Restoration catches

entries.term: Song-genre headings (Ballad / Ballade / Lay / Ditty / Roundelay / Air / Lyric / Chanson)
label_when: Alone on a line as the item heading or as a numbered division ('Ballad I.'); generic headwords when used as the whole title ('SONG', 'A BALLAD') signal that the item has no other title.
sung_trap: Many are sung words ('a lay of old', 'lay me down' - 'lay' is a common verb; 'sing a ballad', 'lullaby, baby' is the sung refrain of lullabies). Label only when the line is the heading/title; 'Lullaby' as refrain within stanza is lyric.
traditions: Songsters, anthologies, Victorian art-song texts, Scott ('Lay of the Last Minstrel'), Macaulay ('Lays of Ancient Rome'), Gaelic boat songs in English.

entries.term: Fixed verse-form headings (Sonnet, Rondeau, Rondel, Roundel, Triolet, Villanelle, Sestina, Pantoum, Ghazal, Rubai, Haiku)
label_when: Alone on a line as heading (with or without numeral or 'To ...' dedication), or as a heading in a sequence; Shakespeare's sonnets are often headed by a bare roman numeral (numbering).
sung_trap: 'sonnet' as noun in lyric ('a sonnet to her eyebrow'); 'couplet' rarely. Treat as heading when the whole line is the form-name (+ numeral/dedication); lyric when embedded in a sentence.
traditions: Collected poems (Shakespeare, Milton, Wordsworth, Keats, Rossetti, Swinburne's roundels, Dobson/Gosse/Lang/Henley French forms), Fitzgerald's Rubaiyat, Imagist haiku (1910s), Edward Lear limericks (no heading normally).

entries.term: Occasional-genre headings (Ode, Elegy, Epigram, Epitaph, Epithalamium, Dirge, Threnody, Monody, Requiem, Complaint, Palinode, Impromptu)
label_when: Alone on a line as the item heading or a numbered division ('ODE.' and 'EPITAPH ON THE TOMB OF ...' occur in the corpus); 'Epitaph' and 'Impromptu' headings often precede a 2-6 line poem.
sung_trap: 'dirge', 'requiem', 'elegy', 'ode', 'complaint' and 'lines/verses' occur as nouns in sung lines ('sing a dirge', 'the requiem of the sea'). Treat as heading when the line consists only of the form-word plus 'on/to/written/for ...' heading formula, often caps; a lyric line has its own syntax and metre.
traditions: All poetic anthologies; Burns ('Epitaph for ...', 'Impromptu'), Gray, Collins, Tennyson ('Ode on the Death of the Duke of Wellington'), broadside elegies, gravestone-epitaph collections.

entries.term: Lament / Coronach / Keen / Caoine (Gaelic-tradition lament headings and cries)
label_when: Alone on a line as heading ('CORONACH' in Scott's Lady of the Lake, Canto III; 'Lament for Flodden'), or the Gaelic-titled heading 'Cumha ...'.
sung_trap: 'Lament' is a common sung verb ('Lament him, Mauchline husbands a'', 'Lament, lament, old abbeys', 'Lament in rhyme' all line-initial in the corpus); 'keen' is a common adjective ('Keen son of trade'); 'Ochone', 'Ullagone', 'Ululu' are sung lament cries - keep as lyric. Label only for the heading line (bare or 'Lament for/of ...' formula on its own line at item head).
traditions: Scots and Irish songs in English (Scott, Hogg, Moore, Mangan, Ferguson, Burns), Highland laments, Irish keening songs, Ossianic poems.

label_when: Alone on a line as heading or designation of a tune-song (Scots/Irish harp 'Port' tunes, mouth-music items), or 'Lilt:' line-initial before vocables.
sung_trap: 'lilt'/'lilting' are sung ('I've heard them lilting at our ewe-milking' in Flowers of the Forest; 'Lilting of tipsy blisses' in corpus); 'port' is sung as harbour/wine ('safe in port', 'a bottle of port'). The vocable lines that follow ('Hi rim o ro') are SUNG and must be kept. Label only for the bare heading/designation.
traditions: Scots and Irish collections, Hebridean song in translation (Kennedy-Fraser), Irish harp tune books (Bunting).

label_when: Alone on a line (often caps) dividing a pibroch-song or a canntaireachd text; the corpus already stages [URLAR], [SIUBHAL], [SIUBHAL n], [CRUNLUATH] as section tags, so any remaining printed occurrence in body text is apparatus.
sung_trap: None in English except 'Ground' ('upon the ground' is sung) and 'Doubling' ('doubling the cape'). Label only bare.
traditions: Pibroch songs and translations (Hogg, Scott, Gaelic song collections), piping tune books, canntaireachd.

entries.term: Gaelic and Welsh section terms in English printings (Fonn, Luinneag, Séis, Curfá, Rann, Ceathramh, Pennill, Englyn, Cytgan, Cywydd, Awdl)
label_when: Alone on a line or line-initial with ':' marking the chorus (Fonn, Luinneag, Séis, Curfá, Cytgan) or verse (Rann, Ceathramh, Pennill) in bilingual or translated collections; Welsh form names as headings.
sung_trap: These words do not occur as English sung words; inside a Gaelic or Welsh line they may be part of the text ('fonn' = 'tune/desire' in a Gaelic lyric). Label only when bare/with colon and the following text is the section.
traditions: Highland and Hebridean song books with English, Irish song books (Petrie, Joyce, Walsh), Welsh Melodies with English words (Brinley Richards, 'Songs of Wales'), Ossianic translations.
examples: Fonn:  Ho ro mo nighean donn bhoidheach,

label_when: Alone on a line (often caps, often after the last printed chorus) heading verses printed below the music; the verses themselves are lyric.
sung_trap: 'encore' could be shouted/sung in a theatre-themed song ('Encore! Encore!' as crowd cry) - lyric when inside metre or with exclamation repetition. Label when bare heading.
traditions: Music hall, vaudeville, Tin Pan Alley sheet music, G&S encore verses (topical additions), college songbooks.

label_when: Alone on a line as heading, or parenthesised 'Introducing ...' naming an interpolated song inside a medley/olio; each interpolated song title is a sub-heading.
sung_trap: 'medley' sung ('a medley of colour'); 'selection' rare. Label when bare heading or parenthesised 'Introducing'.
traditions: Minstrel olio programmes, music-hall medleys, glee club medleys, Tin Pan Alley medley sheets, songsters.

entries.term: Interpolated-song and segment headings in narrative poems (Song, Hymn, Chorus, Interlude inside a long poem)
label_when: Alone on a line within a long poem or prose-and-verse text, marking that the next lines are a sung inset (e.g., Tennyson's Princess 'Songs', Scott's ballads in Marmion). Keep the inset lines as lyric.
sung_trap: See Song/Hymn/Chorus entries: embedded syntax = lyric.
traditions: Scott, Tennyson, Morris, Longfellow, Browning, Victorian novels with embedded songs.
examples:
SONG.
The splendour falls on castle walls

label_when: Alone on a line or with a dash/parenthetical cast list.
sung_trap: Very rarely sung; a lowercase mid-line use is sung.
traditions: G&S (the Ruddigore patter-trio); oratorio (Elijah 'Lift thine eyes'); glee books; operetta

label_when: A heading line, often followed by the performers. In sheet music it is also a subtitle ('Quartette for Mixed Voices').
sung_trap: 'Sestet' is also a sonnet-section term (another domain) and is never sung. These words are almost never sung lyrics.
traditions: G&S; Victorian operetta; barbershop and male-quartet song folios; gospel quartet books; corpus Morris: 'The Maid of Saxony, quintette and chorus'

label_when: Alone on a line, or a speaker-style prefix ('ENSEMBLE.') before lines sung together.
sung_trap: Practically never sung in English lyric. It is a label wherever it is capitalised and stands alone or is followed by a full stop/colon.
traditions: G&S; French opéra-bouffe translations (Offenbach, Lecocq); Edwardian musical comedy
examples: ENSEMBLE. / Then hail the day that brings ...

label_when: A prefix or heading. In Anglican anthems 'Full.' alternates with 'Verse.' to mark the whole choir against soloists.
sung_trap: 'full' is a common sung adjective ('my cup is full'). It is a label only as a one-word line or a capitalised line-initial word followed by '.' and a new sentence, in anthem or oratorio printings.
traditions: Anglican cathedral anthem books (Boyce, Novello octavos); Handel oratorio wordbooks; Victorian choral festivals
examples: Full. / O give thanks unto the Lord

label_when: A heading or prefix before a solo number, often with a voice name.
sung_trap: 'Aria' is almost never a sung word in English; when it is lowercase inside a metrical line, it is sung.
traditions: oratorio and opera wordbooks; Italian opera translations (Bunn, Chorley, Oxenford); Victorian concert programmes
examples: AIR.—Soprano. / I know that my Redeemer liveth

entries.term: Cavatina / Cabaletta / Romance / Romanza / Canzonetta / Canzone / Ballata
label_when: A heading line or prefix before a solo number.
sung_trap: 'romance' is a common sung word ('the days of old romance'); 'canzonet' can be sung in poems about song. Treat it as a label only alone/capitalised with a full stop before a number, or followed by a performer name.
traditions: Italian/French opera in English translation; Balfe (The Bohemian Girl); Wallace (Maritana); Victorian parlour songs; Elizabethan canzonets (Morley)
examples: ROMANCE.—Thaddeus. / When other lips and other hearts

label_when: A heading before an extended dramatic number.
sung_trap: Never sung. Do not confuse it with 'Scene' (act/scene apparatus, which has its own sung trap).
traditions: Victorian English opera; concert songs (Mendelssohn 'Infelice')

entries.term: Overture / Introduction / Prelude / Entr'acte / Intermezzo / Interlude / Postlude / Symphony
variants: Symphony (in old sheet music = instrumental prelude/ritornello)
label_when: Alone on a line. These mark purely instrumental numbers or passages, so no sung text belongs to the label.
sung_trap: 'prelude', 'interlude' and 'symphony' are sung figuratively ('the symphony of the spheres', 'life's brief interlude'). Sung when lowercase in a rhyming line; a label when it is a one-word capitalised line, often italic or bracketed, between stanzas.
traditions: libretti; Moore's Irish Melodies and Victorian sheet music ('Symphony' between verses); hymnals with interludes; cantatas
examples: (Symphony.) / The harp that once through Tara's halls

label_when: A heading or parenthetical marking speech over the orchestra.
sung_trap: Never sung. The spoken text after it is declaimed. Keep it counted as recited only if corpus policy counts recited text (it does), and strip only the label.
traditions: G&S (Ruddigore ghost scene); Victorian stage plays with music; melodrama acting editions

label_when: A heading or subtitle line.
sung_trap: Rarely sung; it is sung only lowercase inside a rhyming line.
traditions: Offenbach in translation; Gondoliers-era operetta; drawing-room songs
examples: BARCAROLLE. / Beautiful night, O night of love

label_when: A heading line or subtitle.
sung_trap: In poem collections 'Madrigal' is frequently the TITLE (title domain, still not sung). As a word inside a lyric it is sung. The 'fa-la' syllables of a ballett are sung.
traditions: Elizabethan madrigal books (Morley, Weelkes, Wilbye); G&S Mikado 'Brightly dawns our wedding day' (MADRIGAL); Ruddigore; Victorian anthologies
examples: MADRIGAL. / Brightly dawns our wedding day

label_when: A heading or subtitle; in glee-club books, the first line under the title.
sung_trap: 'glee' is a very common sung noun ('with glee', 'mirth and glee'). A label only when capitalised alone, or 'Glee for N voices'. Lowercase 'glee' in a rhyme position is sung.
traditions: Georgian/Victorian glee-club books; Catch Club collections; college songbooks; Confederate songsters (corpus title 'THE CAVALIER'S GLEE')

label_when: A heading line or subtitle only.
sung_trap: 'catch' is a common sung verb ('Catch me, cowardly knaves, if you can!', 'Catch the last word of cheer', both corpus). A label only when a capitalised one-word line or followed by 'for N voices'.
traditions: Catch Club collections; Purcell catches; Playford; Victorian glee books
examples: CATCH. / Hark! the bonny Christ Church bells

label_when: A heading line.
sung_trap: 'canon' can be sung ('the Everlasting ... fix'd His canon'). Also watch the spelling confusion with 'cannon' (sung). Sung when lowercase or governed in syntax.
traditions: Tallis's Canon headings in hymnals; glee books
examples: CANON. / Glory to Thee, my God, this night

label_when: A heading, a subtitle in sheet music, or a number name in a libretto.
sung_trap: 'ballad' is sung in lyrics about songs ('a ballad sung of old'). 'The Ballad of X' is a TITLE. A label only alone, or followed by a dash/performer.
traditions: G&S; Victorian sheet music; Tin Pan Alley subtitles ('Ballad')
examples: BALLAD—JOSEPHINE. / Sorry her lot who loves too well

label_when: A heading line or subtitle before a number.
sung_trap: 'serenade' is a common sung word ('I'll serenade you'). Sung when it is a verb or noun inside a rhyming line; a label when alone and capitalised.
traditions: operetta; Victorian sheet music; poem collections (often as title)

label_when: A subtitle line under the title, or a number heading. In sheet music it is set in small caps above or below the title.
sung_trap: Not sung; at most 'song and dance' appears inside an idiom in a lyric (lowercase, mid-line).
traditions: music hall; Tin Pan Alley; minstrel and vaudeville songsters; G&S
examples: PATTER-SONG.—Major-General. / I am the very model of a modern Major-General

entries.term: Number / item numbering of musical numbers
label_when: Line-initial 'No.' plus a number, often followed by a number heading.
sung_trap: 'No.' at line start can be the sung word 'No' followed by a period ('No. I will not'). It is numbering only when a digit or Roman numeral follows immediately.
traditions: vocal scores; libretti with numbered numbers; oratorio wordbooks; Sankey/Bliss hymnals ('No. 123')

label_when: A one-word line, a parenthetical, a bracketed direction, or a sheet-music direction ('Dance' printed under the last bar). Typically italic.
sung_trap: 'dance', 'jig', 'reel', 'waltz', 'hornpipe' are common sung words ('Let us dance on the green', 'dance the hornpipe'). They are sung when inside a rhyming/metrical line, with verbs or objects. A label when parenthesised/bracketed, one-word, or an imperative to the performer ('Dance and exit').
traditions: G&S (Cachucha in Gondoliers, Pinafore hornpipe); music hall; minstrel songsters; pantomime; Tin Pan Alley ('Dance' bars)

label_when: A one-word or short line at the end of a scene/act, usually italic, parenthesised or bracketed.
sung_trap: 'curtain' and 'picture' are sung nouns ('the curtain of night', 'a picture no artist could paint'). Sung if inside a metrical line with syntax; a label as a one-word line, or 'Curtain.'/'Quick curtain.' after the last sung line.
traditions: G&S; melodrama; pantomime; musical comedy libretti; operetta acting editions

label_when: A heading line beginning with ACT/Act plus an ordinal or Roman numeral. Often followed by a scene-setting prose paragraph.
sung_trap: 'act' is a sung verb ('Act,--act in the living Present!', corpus Longfellow) and a noun ('the act of love'). A label only when it is followed by a numeral/ordinal and nothing else.
traditions: libretti; verse dramas (Byron, Shelley, Tennyson); ballad operas; masques

label_when: Line-initial SCENE/Scene followed by a number, a full stop or dash, or a location description (often italic prose with no rhyme). The whole description paragraph is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Scene of glory and dread!' (corpus Brownell) and 'the scene' are sung. Sung when it is followed by 'of'/a verb or sits inside a rhyming line; a label when followed by a numeral, '.—', or a place description.
traditions: libretti; verse dramas (Matthew Arnold Empedocles on Etna, corpus); masques; pastorals
examples: SCENE II.--Noon. A Glen on the highest skirts of the woody region of Etna.

variants: ENTER CYPRIAN, DRESSED AS A STUDENT;
label_when: Line-initial or bracketed/parenthesised/italic, followed by a capitalised character name, a direction abbreviation (R., L., R.U.E., C.), or an adverb, and ending with a full stop or closing bracket.
Line-initial 'Enter', or bracketed or italic 'Exit/Exeunt' with a character name. These are third-person stage verbs.
sung_trap: 'Enter! fear not the bars' and 'Enter at Freedom's porch' (corpus Stedman) are sung imperatives. Sung when followed by '!', an object/prepositional phrase ('into', 'at', 'in'), or sitting in a rhyming line; a direction when followed by a character name or stage position.

'Enter' is sung in 19 line-initial rows / 11 files ('Enter at Freedom's porch,', 'Enter every trembling heart.', 'Enter neither care nor fear.') and 'exit' mid-line in 7 ('I sigh, for thy exit is near;'). A label requires a character name and no second-person or imperative object.
traditions: libretti; ballad operas; verse dramas; acting editions; songsters reprinting stage songs
Lyric rows: Ingelow '_[Exit FRANCES._', Shelley 'ENTER CYPRIAN ...'. Bracket apparatus: Shelley Calderón 'Enter Moscon And Clarin.' etc. Expected in G&S and ballad opera.
examples: Enter SIR JOSEPH, with COUSIN HEBE and FEMALE RELATIVES.

label_when: A line-final or standalone direction, often with an unclosed opening bracket '[' (Shakespearean/18th-c. convention, corpus Gay: '[Exeunt.'). Italic, bracketed or parenthesised.
sung_trap: 'Exit bid to every woe' (corpus Clare) uses exit as a sung noun; 'Urceus Exit' is a title. Sung when it has syntax in a rhyming line. Note the unclosed '[' can collide with harness tags such as '[VERSE 2]': a bracket directive containing Exit/Exeunt/Manet/Enter is apparatus, while harness section tags are structural.
traditions: ballad operas (Gay); verse dramas; libretti; Ingelow dramatic poems (corpus)

entries.term: Aside / addressee, gesture and sound-cue parentheticals
label_when: Parenthesised or bracketed, usually italic, either after a speaker name ('_Mrs. Thorpe (aside)._' corpus) or on its own line. Typically a present-tense 3rd-person verb ('kneels', 'rising'), 'to'+addressee, or a sound cue; no rhyme or meter.
Bracketed or italic after a speaker name, before that speaker's line: '_Mrs. S_. (_aside_).'. Strip the speaker and the direction.
sung_trap: Parenthetical SUNG lines are common in the corpus: '(Hark to the thrush's trilling)', '(Hurry!)' as a ballad interjection, '(Butter and eggs and a pound of cheese)', '(Why, Jane, he'll set his pinafore afire!)'. Keep a parenthetical as sung when it rhymes or scans with the stanza, repeats as a refrain, is in 1st/2nd person, or is exclamatory. Strip it only when it is a 3rd-person stage verb, an addressee ('to X'), a sound/music cue, or the word aside/apart.

'Aside' is sung in 9 line-initial rows ('Aside the frozen Hebrides', 'Aside yon siller stream') and 149 mid-line rows / 72 files ('Dauntlessly aside she flings'). It is a label only in parentheses or brackets, or in italics next to a speaker.
traditions: libretti; verse dramas; music-hall songsters; comic songs; Ingelow and Browning dramatic poems
Jean Ingelow 8 rows; Shelley 'DAEMON [ASIDE]:'.
examples: _Mrs. T. (aside)._ Neighbours, there's one thing beats me.
_Mrs. S_. (_aside_).                  He takes no pride in us.  (eng_british_jean_ingelow.txt)

entries.term: Within / Without / Off / Behind the scenes
label_when: Parenthesised/bracketed, or attached to a speaker prefix ('CHORUS (within).').
sung_trap: 'within' and 'without' are very common sung prepositions ('within my heart', 'without the city wall'). Sung whenever governed in syntax inside a line; a direction only when standing alone in parentheses/brackets, or tagged onto a speaker prefix.
traditions: libretti; verse dramas (Tennyson, Browning); oratorio; cantatas
examples: CHORUS (within). / Hail, Poetry, thou heaven-born maid!

entries.term: Sings / They sing / All sing / Spoken
label_when: A parenthetical after a speaker name, a short line introducing a lyric inside prose or blank verse, or a sheet-music marker for spoken patter between verses.
sung_trap: 'Sing, sing, what shall I sing?' and 'she sings of love' are sung. 'sings' is a direction when parenthesised, attached to a speaker name (corpus 'Babette (sings)'), or when the line is just subject + sing(s) + colon/full stop with no rhyme. With 'Spoken' music-hall patter, strip the label only; the patter itself is recited text (keep it counted unless policy excludes spoken patter).
traditions: Dobson (corpus); music hall (Dan Leno, Marie Lloyd folios); Tin Pan Alley; novels and plays with inserted songs; Pippa Passes ('PIPPA sings')
examples: Babette (sings) / On the first of the Spring ...

entries.term: Hum / whistle / laugh / yodel as performance cues
label_when: Parenthesised or italic one- or two-word cues.
sung_trap: Vocables that ARE sung: 'Ha! ha! ha!', 'Tra la la', 'Tol-de-rol', 'Fal-de-ral', 'yo-ho' are lyric text. Strip only the cue word, never the printed syllables.
traditions: music hall; Tin Pan Alley; comic-opera laughing songs; minstrel songsters

label_when: A heading line before additional stanzas, often at the end of a sheet song or libretto number.

Alone on a line as a heading above verses printed after the main song, in music-hall and Tin Pan Alley sheets and in G&S libretti (the 'encore verses' of patter songs). The heading is apparatus; the verses under it are sung.
sung_trap: 'encore' can be sung ('they shouted encore!'). Sung inside a rhyming line; a label as a heading.

'Encore!' is occasionally sung as an exclamation in songs about the theatre ('They shouted encore!'). It is sung when it is inside quotation marks or a clause, and a label when it is a heading with 'verse(s)' or alone.
traditions: music hall; Tin Pan Alley; musical comedy; later G&S libretti with encore verses
music-hall, vaudeville, Tin Pan Alley, Gilbert & Sullivan and Edwardian musical comedy libretti

entries.term: As sung by / Sung by / Introduced by (performer credit)
variants: Sung by Mr. Braham at Drury Lane
label_when: A line under the title or at the head of the text, beginning 'As sung', 'Sung by', 'Sung with', 'Introduced', 'Written for', 'Performed'; contains a performer name or venue.
sung_trap: A sung line could begin 'Sung by the ...' only in narrative ballads; that would rhyme and continue in syntax.
traditions: songsters; broadsides; music hall; minstrel; Vauxhall/Ranelagh song sheets; Tin Pan Alley covers
examples: As sung by Mr. G. H. Macdermott at the London Pavilion.

label_when: A heading followed by a block of lines in the shape name + comma/parenthetical role (+ dotted leader + actor), typically before Act I.
sung_trap: Never sung; the whole block is apparatus.
traditions: libretti; ballad operas; verse dramas; masques
examples: DRAMATIS PERSONAE. / The Rt. Hon. Sir Joseph Porter, K.C.B. (First Lord of the Admiralty)

variants: (small caps rendered as caps or Title Case)
label_when: Line-initial, in capitals/small caps or italic, ending in '.' ':' '.—' or '--', either alone on a line or followed by the speech on the same line (corpus Lovelace 'CHA.  A slave! a fool!'). Speakers may also occur mid-line ('You must, lost fool, come in.    W.  Oh, let me in!'), usually after a run of spaces. The same name recurs at line starts throughout the piece and is often listed in Dramatis Personae.
