sung_trap: A vocative name opens many sung lines ('Maria, come ...', 'Polly, put the kettle on'). It is sung when it is followed by a comma, an exclamation, or a verb in the same sentence, or when it is part of the metre or rhyme. A one-word all-caps line in a poem can also be a TITLE (e.g. 'WESTMINSTER.'). Mid-line single capitals followed by '.' and 2+ spaces are speakers; 'R. Burns' and 'Mr.' are attribution/abbreviation, not speakers.
traditions: libretti; verse dramas (Shelley's Cyclops and Faust translations, Lovelace, Coleridge, Byron); ballad operas; pastoral dialogues; corpus (DAEMON:, CYCLOPS:, SILENUS:, JUSTINA:, CYPRIAN:, FAUST:)
examples: MEPHISTOPHELES: / I like to see the Old One now and then

label_when: A line-initial or parenthetical tag before the echoed word(s).

Bracketed or italic, or line-initial followed by '.' or ':', in front of a repeated fragment that a second group sings softly, as in glees, partsongs and echo songs. The fragment after the cue is sung.
'Echo.', 'Answer.' or '_Ans._' as a speaker label before the echoed words is a label. The echoed words themselves are sung.
sung_trap: The echoed WORD after the tag IS sung ('Echo. Love.'); only the tag is apparatus. 'echo' as a noun or verb in a line ('the hills echo') is sung.

'Echo' is sung constantly as a noun, verb or personification: 'And Echo answers', 'the echoes ring', 'Echo, sweet nymph'. It is sung when it has an article, verb or possessive, or sits mid-sentence. It is a cue when it is a lone capitalised token with '.', ':' or brackets, followed by a short repeat of the words just sung.

Barnes's '--_my dears_;' and '--_bad chaps_.' are the echo, so they are sung. 'echo' is sung in 204 mid-line rows / 92 files. Herrick's '_Ans._ Like and dislike ye.': strip '_Ans._' and keep the rest.
traditions: Elizabethan/Caroline echo poems (Herbert's 'Heaven'); masques; Victorian part-songs with echo choir
glee and part-song books, Elizabethan and Restoration echo songs, parlour songs, operetta
Herrick '_Ans._' 7, Barnes echo poem, Morris.

entries.term: Voice / Voices / Spirit etc. as speaker
label_when: Prefix at line start in caps/italic with '.' or ':'.
sung_trap: 'A voice cried in the wilderness' and 'Voices of the night' are sung. Prefix only when the word is followed by '.'/':' alone, or the '.'/':' is followed by a new line or a new capitalised sentence.
traditions: verse dramas (corpus: SPIRIT:, MORTAL:, DEATH:, GABRIEL:, RAPHAEL:); mystery plays; oratorio; cantatas; Tennyson's 'The Two Voices'
examples: A VOICE. / Come away, come away!

label_when: A prefix before recitative or narration in oratorio/Passion wordbooks.
sung_trap: Never sung.
traditions: Passion settings in English (Bach in translation, Stainer's Crucifixion); cantatas; school operettas
examples: EVANGELIST. / And when they had sung an hymn

label_when: A heading, often with 'spoken by' + actor.
sung_trap: The prologue text is recited verse and is counted under 'recited' policy; strip only the heading and the 'spoken by' credit. 'prologue' as a sung word is rare.
traditions: Restoration/Georgian theatre; ballad operas (The Beggar's Opera introduction); masques; burlesque

label_when: Line-initial speaker prefix in minstrel songsters, before patter or song cues.
A line that lists characters (names joined by commas or 'and'), often italic and centred under the title, or a cast list before a libretto.
sung_trap: Rarely sung, though 'bones' can be sung ('rattle the bones'); sung when inside a rhyming line.
Names joined by 'and' can open a sung line ('Mr. and Mrs. Discobbolos / Climbed to the top of a wall', Lear). A label has no verb and stands before the first verse.
traditions: American minstrel songsters (Christy's, Bryant's) — period printings
Apparatus: Barnes '_John and Richard._'; Gilbert performer list (also hoisted into TITLE); Shelley '[The Cyclops, Silenus, Ulysses; Chorus.]'. Expected in G&S libretti.
examples: INTERLOCUTOR. Mr. Bones, will you favour us with a song?

label_when: Line-initial prefix alternating lines in work songs, shanties, spirituals and lined-out psalmody.
sung_trap: 'All' prefix vs the sung 'All' (see All/Omnes). 'Leader' is sung in patriotic lyrics ('our gallant leader'). A prefix only when followed by '.'/':' and a new capitalised line.
traditions: shanty collections (Terry, Whall); Slave Songs of the United States (1867); Jubilee Singers books; Scottish/American lined-out psalmody; camp-meeting songbooks
examples: Solo: Oh, Shenandoah, I long to hear you, / Chorus: Away, you rolling river,

label_when: Line-initial and followed by '.', ':' or a parenthetical direction, then sung text or a new line. Tutti/Omnes are always labels.
sung_trap: 'All' begins very many sung lines ('All under the willow-tree', 'All alone on the hillside--', 'All round my hat' — corpus). It is a label only when written 'All.' / 'ALL.' / 'All:' / 'ALL (x).' with punctuation immediately after the word, followed by a capitalised new sentence or end of line. 'All,' (comma), or 'All' continuing into a noun or verb phrase, is sung. 'Together' is sung far more often than labelled; it is a label only as a capitalised parenthetical prefix.
traditions: G&S; libretti; verse dramas; shanties; gospel songs
examples: ALL. Hail, men-o'-war's men--safeguards of your nation!

label_when: A short parenthetical or heading over a stanza, verse or chorus.
sung_trap: 'in unison' / 'in harmony' are used figuratively in sung lines ('hearts in unison beat', 'sweet harmony'). Sung when inside a rhyming line with syntax; a label when parenthesised or alone.
traditions: hymnals (Hymns Ancient & Modern, English Hymnal); school songbooks; choral octavos
examples: (Unison.) / O God, our help in ages past

label_when: Line-initial, capitalised/small-caps, followed by '.'/':' or a parenthetical, before the line(s) that group sings. A stage-direction sentence may also name the group in capitals: '(The GIRLS attempt to waltz ...)' — corpus Morris.
sung_trap: 'Boys, keep away from the girls', 'Men of Harlech', 'Girls and boys come out to play', 'Women of England' are sung. Sung when followed by a comma (vocative), 'of', or a verb in the same clause; a label when followed directly by '.'/':' and a new sentence, or alone.
traditions: G&S; operetta; music hall; school cantatas; hymnals ('Men only' / 'Women only' verses)
examples: GIRLS. / How beautifully blue the sky,

entries.term: Congregation / Choir / People / Minister / Priest (service roles)
label_when: Line-initial prefix (often italic or red in service books) followed by '.'/':', or alone on a line (corpus Wordsworth 'PRIEST.').
sung_trap: 'O ye people, praise the Lord', 'the choir of angels', 'priest and king' are sung. A label only when followed by a full stop or colon and then a new sentence or a new line.
traditions: Book of Common Prayer; Methodist/Presbyterian hymnals with responsive readings; Catholic missals in English; Wordsworth's Ecclesiastical Sonnets (as dramatic tag)
examples: Minister. O Lord, open thou our lips. / People. And our mouth shall shew forth thy praise.

label_when: A heading or line-initial prefix before a short sentence sung before and after a psalm or canticle.
sung_trap: 'antiphon' is a rare sung word (Herbert's 'Antiphon' is a TITLE). 'Ant.' at line start could be the insect noun only in children's songs, never with a full stop and capitalised text in a hymnal.
traditions: Anglican office books; Roman Breviary in English; Herbert (titles); English Hymnal 'O come, O come, Emmanuel' printed with its antiphons
examples: Ant. O Wisdom, which camest out of the mouth of the Most High

label_when: A heading before the Venite or its antiphon.
sung_trap: Never sung.
traditions: Breviary translations; Anglican Mattins (Venite)
examples: Invitatory. The Lord is King: O come, let us worship.

entries.term: Canticle names / Latin incipits as headings
variants: Cant. 3. 2. (Song of Songs reference, corpus Watts)
The Song of the Three Children
label_when: An italic or capitalised Latin incipit, or 'Canticle'/'Song of X', alone on a line above the English text; or a scripture reference ('Cant. 4. 1 10 11 7 9 8.' — corpus Watts, which cites the Canticles/Song of Songs) under a hymn number.
sung_trap: Latin may itself be the sung text: 'Miserere Domine.' (corpus, refrain x6), 'Gloria in excelsis Deo' in carols, 'Adeste fideles'. It is sung when it recurs within or after stanzas, rhymes, or is followed by more Latin text lines; it is a label when it is a lone incipit heading followed by an English translation that begins with the same meaning. Also 'a great Te Deum' (corpus Procter) is a sung noun phrase.
traditions: Book of Common Prayer; Watts's Psalms & Hymns; cathedral service books; Catholic hymnals; Christina Rossetti and Procter devotional verse
examples: Nunc Dimittis. / Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace

label_when: A heading line, usually capitalised, before English or Latin text of that section.
sung_trap: 'Kyrie eleison', 'Gloria', 'Hosanna', 'Agnus Dei' are frequently the SUNG words themselves (a carol refrain 'Gloria in excelsis Deo'; 'Hosanna in the highest'). Sung when part of a stanza line, when repeated as a refrain, or when followed by more words of the text on the same line; a label when it is alone and followed by an English or full Latin text block that opens with different words or a translation.
traditions: Anglican Communion services; Catholic hymnals and Vesperals; Victorian Mass settings (Gounod, Mozart in English); Requiem translations
examples: AGNUS DEI. / O Lamb of God, that takest away the sins of the world

entries.term: Mass propers, sequences and Requiem sections
label_when: A heading line; also a hymnal 'use' line under the title ('Introit for Easter Day', 'Offertory Hymn').
sung_trap: 'Alleluia' is massively sung — it is a label only in the heading form 'Alleluia (verse).' or 'The Alleluia.' 'communion' and 'offertory' can be sung nouns in devotional hymns ('sweet communion'). 'Dies Irae'/'Stabat Mater' can be the first sung Latin words; apply the incipit rule (lone heading + translation = label).
traditions: English Hymnal; Hymns Ancient & Modern; Catholic hymnals; Anglican missals; Victorian translations (Neale, Caswall)
examples: Sequence. / Day of wrath! O day of mourning!

label_when: A heading line, or a 'use' line under a hymn title ('Office Hymn. Compline.').
sung_trap: 'matins', 'vespers', 'evensong' are sung nouns in poems ('the vesper bell', 'sweet evensong'). 'None.' is ambiguous with the sung pronoun 'None' ('None but the lonely heart'): label only in a list of hours or as a heading with a full stop and nothing else, in a breviary context. 'Prime' is also a sung adjective.
traditions: English Hymnal; Breviary translations; Anglican service books
examples: Office Hymn. Compline. / Before the ending of the day

entries.term: Church-year and topical section headings in hymnals
label_when: A heading line between hymns, usually capitalised, often centred, not part of any hymn's stanza; frequently followed by a hymn number.
sung_trap: 'Christmas', 'Easter', 'morning', 'evening', 'harvest' are common sung words ('Christmas comes but once a year'). A heading is a one- or two-word line set apart from stanzas, preceding a hymn number or title.
traditions: Hymns Ancient & Modern; English Hymnal; Methodist Hymn-Book; Plymouth Collection; Gospel Hymns 1-6; Watts (Book I/II/III)
examples: EASTER. / 134. / Jesus Christ is risen to-day

entries.term: Processional / Recessional / Introit hymn / Gradual hymn
label_when: A use heading above or below a hymn title.
sung_trap: Kipling's 'Recessional' is a TITLE (title domain). A sung occurrence is rare; lowercase inside a line is sung.
traditions: Episcopal and Anglican hymnals; festival service sheets

label_when: 'Selah' is a psalm-margin direction and an apparatus label when it is line-final or standalone and in italics/parentheses in KJV-derived metrical psalms. Hallelujah/Alleluia/Hosanna are labels only as section headings ('Hallelujah Chorus', 'Alleluia (verse)').
sung_trap: Hallelujah, Alleluia and Hosanna are almost always SUNG (refrains, gospel choruses). 'Selah' is occasionally sung in Victorian anthems that set it to music. Sung when it is inside a stanza line or rhyme; apparatus when it is a bracketed/italic one-word line after a prose psalm verse.
traditions: KJV-text anthems and chant books; gospel hymnals; spirituals; Handel wordbooks
examples: He is the King of glory. Selah.

entries.term: Collect / Lesson / Epistle / Gospel / Prayer (non-sung service items)
label_when: A heading line or an announcement formula in a service book, followed by prose (not stanzas).
sung_trap: 'grace', 'gospel', 'blessing', 'prayer' are among the commonest sung words ('Amazing grace', 'The gospel train', 'Sweet hour of prayer'). Sung when inside a metrical line; apparatus only as a heading or a liturgical formula ('Here endeth...'). 'Let us pray' inside a hymn stanza is sung. 'Grace' printed as a title over a sung table grace is a TITLE.
traditions: Book of Common Prayer; service books; Victorian school-hymn books (Graces); Burns 'Selkirk Grace' (title)

label_when: Chant/tone headings above psalms; and the pointing symbols scattered inside pointed psalm text (vertical bars, asterisks, daggers, accent ticks), which are print apparatus, not text.
sung_trap: 'chant' is a sung verb ('let us chant his praise'). The colon in a pointed psalm is real punctuation shared with text, so remove only the bar/asterisk/dagger pointing glyphs. 'Tone' is sung ('the tone of thy voice') unless it is followed by a numeral.
traditions: Cathedral Psalter; Anglican Chant Book; Plainsong Psalter; English Hymnal (Gregorian tones); Catholic Vesperals
examples: Tone VIII. 1. / O come, let us | sing un- | to the | Lord *

variants: Then shall be said or sung ...
At the Offertory may be sung
label_when: Italic or pilcrow-led prose directions, usually in the third person/subjunctive ('shall', 'may be'), between texts.
sung_trap: 'stand', 'kneel', 'all kneeling' can be sung ('Kneel at the cross'). Sung when inside a metrical line; a rubric when it is pilcrow-led, uses 'shall/may be said or sung', or is a one-word parenthesis.
traditions: Book of Common Prayer; hymnals with service sections; Catholic hymnals; Anglo-Catholic service books
examples: ¶ Then shall be sung or said this Hymn following.

label_when: A heading line within a chorus/ode, alone, with an optional numeral.
sung_trap: Never sung. Note that 'Ant.' here collides with 'Ant.' = Antiphon; both are apparatus.
traditions: Pindaric odes (Gray, Collins); Milton's Samson Agonistes; Shelley (Hellas); Swinburne (Atalanta); Arnold (Merope); Gilbert's Princess Ida
examples: STROPHE. / Before the beginning of years

label_when: Prefixes and headings in masque and pastoral dialogue texts; dance directions in italics.
sung_trap: Pastoral names are often vocatives in the sung text ('Come, Corydon', 'Damon, let us go'). Sung when they are followed by a comma or are part of the metre; a prefix when followed by '.' and a new sentence.
traditions: Jonson and Campion masques; Milton's Comus; Caroline pastoral songs (Lovelace, Herrick, Carew); Purcell's King Arthur
examples: First Shepherd. / Hark! the larks in the bushes

label_when: A speaker or performer prefix with an embedded parenthetical direction, ending in '.' or ':'. The whole prefix up to and including its closing punctuation is apparatus.
sung_trap: The text following on the same line after the prefix is sung. Do not strip past the prefix's closing '.'/':'/'.—'.
traditions: G&S; operetta; verse dramas
examples: PIRATE KING (to RUTH). / For some ridiculous reason, to which, however, I've no desire to be disloyal,

entries.term: Part divisions and Argument in oratorio and cantata wordbooks
label_when: A heading line with an ordinal or Roman numeral; 'Argument' is a prose plot summary block (all apparatus).
sung_trap: 'part' is sung ('we part at dawn', 'my part in this'). A label only when it is followed by a numeral or ordinal and nothing else; 'Argument' is sung only rarely, inside a line.
traditions: Handel, Haydn, Mendelssohn wordbooks; Victorian cantatas (Sullivan's Golden Legend, Elgar); Dryden's Alexander's Feast

variants: Repeat the first stanza to complete the tune.
N.B. The last two lines of each verse are repeated
The two last lines of every verse to be repeated
label_when: Alone on a line (often italic, bracketed, parenthesised or set flush right), or line-final after a sung line in brackets/parentheses, or line-initial and followed by a STRUCTURAL object: line(s), last, first, verse, stanza, chorus, cho., refrain, strain-number, a numeral, 'from *', 'ad lib', a dynamic. Also apparatus when it is a full prose sentence that addresses the singer about the tune ('to complete the tune').
sung_trap: 'repeat' is an ordinary verb in hymns and poems: 'Repeat the exulting strain' (eng_american_e_griswold.txt:20), 'Repeat the sounding joy', 'And thrice repeat' (Herrick), 'Repeat with us the pledge a century old!' (Whittier). It is sung when the object is a poetic noun phrase (strain, joy, sound, pledge, praise, name, accents), when the line scans and rhymes with the stanza, and when it carries no brackets or italics. 'Strain' is the hard case: 'Repeat the strain' can be a direction in tunebooks, where 'strain' means a musical section. Treat it as a direction only when it stands alone in brackets or italics, outside the stanza's meter.
traditions: hymnals and psalters (Watts, Wesley, gospel songbooks), songsters, broadsides, parlour sheet music, shape-note tunebooks, school songbooks
examples: "Repeat the first stanza to complete the tune." (eng_hymn_watts.txt:22516)

label_when: Line-final after a sung line, usually in parentheses or italics or after a dash, sometimes beside a brace '}' that groups the lines to be repeated. It is also apparatus as a token alone on a line right after the line(s) it doubles. It means: sing the preceding line or bracketed group twice (bis), three times (ter) or four times (quater).
sung_trap: These words are not English, so they are almost never sung. A Latin hymn line can contain 'ter' ('ter sanctus'). The letters can also sit inside a word ('Bistre', 'Tertian'). Match only a whole token with no letters attached. Do NOT expand the repeat into the counted text unless the project policy says so: the label is apparatus, and the line before it is sung once as printed.
traditions: French- and Italian-influenced song sheets, glee books, parlour songs, songsters, national anthems and Marseillaise translations, ballad operas

entries.term: twice / thrice / three times as a repeat count
label_when: Only when it is enclosed in parentheses or brackets, set in italic, or line-final after a comma or dash and outside the meter. It is also apparatus as a one-word line after a sung line. It is never apparatus when it is grammatically inside the sentence.
sung_trap: Very common sung words: 'Twice or thrice his roundelay' (Tennyson), 'Thrice, thrice, thrice blest!' (Willson), 'Haud up thy han', Deil! ance, twice, thrice!' (Burns), 'Twice forty times return'. They are sung when they modify a verb or noun in the line, are capitalised only at line start, or scan. A bare 'thrice' repeated three times in a lyric is sung emphasis, not a count. Treat it as a direction only with brackets, italics, or a lone token after the line's terminal punctuation.
traditions: songsters, broadsides, sheet music, hymnals, nursery song collections, ballad collections

label_when: Line-FINAL after the sung text, or alone on the next line, with no other words.
sung_trap: Line-INITIAL parenthesised numerals are usually speaker or voice numbers in dialogue poems and part-songs, not repeat counts: William Barnes's eclogues print '(1)', '(2)', '(3)' for speakers ('(2) The road, George, no.  There's na'r a road.', eng_hall_william_barnes.txt:7124), and a line can hold several of them ('(2) Do wag. (1) Do goo at last.  (3) Well done.'). Those belong to the speaker/voice domain. Line-final '(2)' can also be a footnote marker (number the footnote domain). Treat it as a repeat count only when the edition uses it consistently that way, or a key says so. 'x2' and '2x' are 20th-century usage only; they will not appear in pre-1880 printings, so a hit there is probably OCR noise.
traditions: late songsters, Tin Pan Alley lyric sheets, modern transcriptions of older songs, dialogue eclogues (as the trap)

entries.term: Repeat signs and their OCR forms
label_when: Any non-alphabetic token made of bars and colons at a line's start or end, or wrapping a span of words, in a text transcribed from engraved music. '§', '%', or a superscript 'S' placed before a word marks where D.S. returns to. '⊕' or 'Ø' marks the coda jump. An '*' paired with an instruction ('Repeat from *') is a navigation anchor.
sung_trap: None of these is sung. Danger lies in over-matching: a single '*' may be a footnote anchor or a hymnal 'may be omitted' mark; a row of asterisks is an omission/section divider (other domain); '|' may be Anglican chant pointing (see the chant pointing entry); and '§' may be an editor's section sign. Strip the token but keep every word it wraps; the wrapped words are sung.
traditions: OCR and e-text transcriptions of sheet music, shape-note tunebooks, gospel songbooks, school songbooks, music-hall professional copies

entries.term: &c. / etc. (abbreviated return of chorus or refrain)
label_when: Line-final after a few cue words, especially the first words of a chorus or refrain printed in full earlier ('Rise, rise, etc.', eng_american_john_w_paine.txt:21; 'Ah! years may come, &c.', Clough). The '&c.' token is apparatus. The cue words in front of it are the opening of a sung repeat and are sung. Annotate the line as an abbreviated return (the corpus already uses [CHORUS: abbreviated return, printed "&c." in the source]) and do not count '&c.' as a word.

Line-final (often italic) after a short incipit of a refrain/chorus already printed in full earlier in the same song, e.g. 'Over the Hills, &c.', 'Ca' the yowes, &c.', 'Look away, etc.'; or after a Chorus/Cho. label. The '&c.' token itself is never sung: it instructs 'repeat the rest of the refrain'. The incipit words before it are a cue for the full refrain (annotate the line as an abbreviated return, as the corpus already does with '[CHORUS: abbreviated return, printed "&c." in the source]'); count the incipit once at most, never as new lyric, and do not count '&c.' as a word.

Inside a title, Air/Tune line, by-line, imprint or prose note where it shortens a name, title or list ('Sung by Mr. Vance, &c.', 'Tune: O'er the muir, &c.', 'The Bonnie Lass, &c.' as a title, 'Printed and sold by J. Pitts, &c.'). The whole line is apparatus already; &c. adds nothing.
sung_trap: '&c.' is sometimes real text in comic, satirical and mock-learned verse: catalogue jokes such as 'Lords, Dukes, &c.', or 'see Mallet's Northern Antiquities, Herbert's Helga, &c.' inside a footnote (eng_british_felicia_hemans.txt:2437), where it is editorial prose. It is sung when it falls mid-line inside a list that rhymes, or when the rhyme needs the word 'etcetera' ('etc.' read aloud). It is a repeat cue when it ends a line that copies the start of an earlier chorus or stanza.

Spelled-out 'et cetera'/'etcetera' that scans and rhymes is sung (comic and patter songs: 'With his hat and his cane, et cetera'). '&c.' mid-line in a sung catalogue that the meter needs (a list in a comic song, 'pins, needles, laces, &c.' where the syllables are counted) is read aloud as 'et cetera'. Test: if deleting '&c.' leaves the line a syllable short or kills a rhyme, it was sung; if the words before it duplicate the opening of an earlier full refrain, it is a pointer.
Same as pointer entry: sung only when spelled out or metrically required inside a lyric line.
traditions: songsters, Burns and Scots collections, Civil War songbooks, broadsides, parlour songs, Byron ('Sons of Greeks, etc.')

Scots songbooks (Burns, Johnson's Museum, Jacobite Relics), D'Urfey's Pills to Purge Melancholy, 18th-c. songsters and garlands, broadsides, American songsters, minstrel and Civil War songbooks, hymnals (refrain cues), music-hall songbooks
All; especially broadside imprints, songster tables of contents, Burns tune lines

variants: Chorus to be repeated after each verse
label_when: Alone on a line, or in parentheses/italics at the end of a stanza, or as a footnote-style note after the first stanza. It tells the singer when to insert a chorus; it is not the chorus text. Any line that begins 'Chorus'/'Cho.' plus a navigation phrase (after, as before, same, twice, ad lib) is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'chorus' is a sung noun in many lyrics: 'the morning stars in chorus', 'Join in the chorus, boys!' (a music-hall line that IS sung), 'the birds' sweet chorus'. Such a line is sung when it is a full clause inside the meter with a verb other than repeat/after/as, and it rhymes. 'Chorus.--' or 'Chorus--' at line start followed by actual lyric words (Burns: 'Chorus.--My heart's in the Highlands') is a section label (section-name domain) plus sung text; split the label from the text.
traditions: songsters, minstrel books, Civil War collections, gospel songbooks, music-hall sheets, school songbooks

label_when: In parentheses, brackets or italics, alone on a line or flush right after a stanza (the corpus example sits at column ~46), or as a hymnal footnote keyed by '*'. The stanza the note governs stays sung text; only the note is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'omit' as a verb inside the lyric is rare but real in poems ('Nor omit the sacred rite'). It is sung when it has a lyric object, falls inside the rhyme scheme, and has no brackets.
traditions: Civil War songbooks, hymnals (Victorian and later), gospel songbooks, school songbooks

label_when: Alone on a line, line-final in parentheses/italics, or after the last line of a section of a da capo aria (Handel and ballad-opera libretti print 'Da Capo.' or 'D.C.' at the foot of the air's B section). Any standalone 'D.C.' with no other words in a song text is navigation.
sung_trap: In American songs 'D. C.' is often 'District of Columbia' ('Washington, D. C.', 'to D. C. we go'). That use sits inside a sentence and usually follows 'Washington' or a preposition. 'D.C.M.' and 'C.M.D.' are hymn METER labels (Double Common Metre), not Da Capo; check for the trailing 'M'. Initials 'D. C.' can also sign a poem or credit (a by-line, attribution domain). Treat it as navigation only when it is free-standing or line-final after a sung line, with nothing else in its phrase.
traditions: opera and oratorio libretti, ballad operas, glee and catch books, sheet music, shape-note and gospel songbooks, school songbooks

label_when: A free-standing token, or line-final after a sung line. The segno glyph or its OCR stand-ins ('%', '§', a stray 'S' or '$') can sit line-INITIAL on the line to return to; strip the glyph and keep the words.
sung_trap: 'D. S.' as a person's initials in signatures, dedications and by-lines (attribution domain). '%' and '$' in songs about money or prices ('two per cent') are rare but possible. A line-initial stray '$' or '%' in an OCR'd sheet-music lyric is a segno; one inside a sentence is text.
traditions: sheet music, gospel songbooks, music-hall and Tin Pan Alley professional copies, school songbooks

entries.term: Fine (end point of a da capo or dal segno repeat)
label_when: Alone on a line (often right-aligned and italic) between two sections, or line-final after a sung line in brackets or italics, or in the phrase 'al Fine'. It marks where the song ends on the da capo return.
sung_trap: 'fine' is a common sung English adjective and noun: 'Fine knacks for ladies, cheap, choice, brave and new' (eng_british_john_dowland.txt:48), 'Fine his nose, his nostrils thin', 'Fine flour press'd down', 'Fine for a soger', 'a fine old English gentleman', 'Fine Pears, quoth she'. It is sung whenever it modifies a following noun, takes a complement, or stands inside the meter. Treat it as a label only when it stands alone (with or without a period) with no syntactic link to the neighbouring lines, or in 'al Fine'. The capitalised single word 'Fine.' at the end of a section in a da capo song is the label. Do not confuse it with 'Finis' or 'The End' (end markers, another domain).
traditions: sheet music, libretti (da capo airs), gospel songbooks, school songbooks, glee books
examples: "Fine." (alone, after the refrain, before the verse that returns D.C.)

label_when: With an abbreviated ordinal (1st, 2nd, 2d, 3d), always apparatus. Spelled out ('First time'), apparatus only when line-initial followed by ':', '.', or '--', or in brackets or italics, and governing alternative words or a dynamic. Volta numerals '1.' and '2.' above alternative endings, transcribed inline, sit next to text that is sung only in that pass; keep the words and strip the numerals.
sung_trap: 'The first time ever I saw your face', 'For the second time I'm thine', 'first time I met you' are sung. The spelled-out phrase is sung when it is a constituent of a clause. A label is followed by a colon or dash, or bracketed, and has no verb attached.
traditions: sheet music, gospel songbooks, Tin Pan Alley and music-hall copies, school songbooks
examples: "2nd time: And the band played on."

entries.term: Last verse / Last time / Final chorus (pass-specific directions)
label_when: Alone on a line, or line-initial followed by ':', '.', or '--', or in brackets or italics, introducing text, a dynamic or a tempo change for the final pass. A label introducing ALTERNATIVE words for the final pass keeps those words as sung text.
sung_trap: 'last' and 'final' are common sung words: 'The last time I saw Paris', 'Slow spreading, strengthening long, at last', 'Do goo at last', 'the last verse of the song she sang' (a narrative poem). The phrase is sung when it sits inside a clause or the meter. It is a label when it is a free-standing heading without a verb, with a colon or dash or brackets.
traditions: gospel songbooks, sheet music, music-hall, school songbooks, hymnals

variants: Parts of this hymn may be sung separately
Verse 4 may be sung as a solo
The first and last verses may be sung together
label_when: A note in italics or small type above or below a hymn, or a footnote keyed with '*' or '†'. The note is apparatus; the stanzas are sung.
sung_trap: None sung; an English hymn never sings stanza numbers. Make sure the stanza numerals themselves are handled by the numbering domain.
traditions: Victorian and later hymnals, Church of Scotland and Methodist hymnals, school hymnals
examples: "(Verses 1, 2, 5 may be used as a short hymn.)"

entries.term: Segue / Attacca / Go on (theatre and suite continuity)
label_when: Alone on a line between numbers of a libretto or music-hall act, or bracketed at the end of a number.
sung_trap: 'Go on' and 'continue' are sung inside sentences ('Go on, go on, my bonny lad'). They are apparatus only when free-standing in brackets or italics between numbers.
traditions: comic opera and operetta libretti (Gilbert & Sullivan, Offenbach translations), music-hall and burlesque scripts, Broadway vocal scores

label_when: Any occurrence in a song text; it means a part is silent.
sung_trap: Not English; never sung.
traditions: sheet music, part-songs, operetta vocal scores, gospel quartets

label_when: Alone on a line, often in brackets, marking a passage with no words: e.g. 'Symphony' between stanzas in Moore's Irish Melodies or Scots song collections, and in 18th-c. song sheets. 'Prelude', 'Introduction' and 'Interlude' as standalone headings in sheet songs are apparatus.
sung_trap: 'symphony' is sung in Romantic lyric ('a symphony of birds', 'the spheres' symphony'), and 'prelude' and 'interlude' are poem titles and words ('this sweet prelude'). As TITLES of poems (Tennyson's 'Prelude', Whitman), these are the poem's title and its text is recited (title domain). The instrumental heading is a lone word with no article, placed between stanzas of a song text.
traditions: 18th-19th c. song sheets, Moore's Irish Melodies, Scots song collections (Thomson, Museum), parlour songs, hymnals ('Organ interlude'), operetta vocal scores

variants: Spoken by Miss Fontenelle on her Benefit Night, December 4th, 1793,
label_when: Line-initial followed by ':', '.', or '--', or alone on a line, or bracketed before a prose or verse passage, in minstrel and music-hall songsters (very frequent in Beadle's and Wehman's: 'Spoken.--Yes, and...'), Tin Pan Alley comic songs, and G&S (patter numbers). The corpus already has [PATTER] sections.
Line-initial 'Spoken:' or '(Spoken)', or a headnote sentence 'Spoken by <performer> ...'. In music hall, the prose that follows the cue is not sung either: mark the whole spoken block.
sung_trap: 'Spoken in fear with sense of need' is a sung hymn line. 'Spoken' is also part of TITLES and attributions: 'Prologue Spoken At The Theatre Of Dumfries' (Burns title) and 'Spoken by Miss Fontenelle on her Benefit Night' (eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt:18847, an occasion/attribution line, not a delivery label for a passage). It is sung when it is a participle in a clause; it is an occasion line when followed by 'by' plus a name or 'at' plus a place. 'Patter' is sung as a noun ('the patter of little feet', 'pitter-patter of the rain'). Policy flag: the text under a 'Spoken' label is performed but not sung. The task counts sung OR recited text, so annotate it as [SPOKEN] rather than delete it, and decide policy explicitly.
'Speaks not my love!' and 'Speaks thus,--' are sung (11 line-initial rows / 8 files). 'spoken' is sung in 71 mid-line rows ('With reverence be it spoken').
traditions: minstrel and comic songsters (1840-1900), music-hall, vaudeville, Tin Pan Alley comic and descriptive songs, Gilbert & Sullivan, recitation books
1 row (Burns prologue headnote). Expected heavily in music-hall songs (spoken patter between verses) and minstrel songsters.
examples: Spoken by Miss Fontenelle on her Benefit Night, December 4th, 1793,  (eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt)

label_when: Bracketed or italic, alone on a line or at a section head, telling voices to hum, often beside a hummed passage that has no words. In part-song and barbershop arrangements, 'Hum' is printed under the lower voices while the melody has words.
sung_trap: 'hum' is a common sung verb and noun: 'Hums the bee!' (Skipsey), 'To hear you sing, \'Ah, Hum di Hum!\'' (Lear), 'the hum of the city', 'Humming-birds and honey-bees'. Nonsense refrains 'hum-a-dum', 'Hum di hum' are sung vocables and count. It is a direction only when bracketed or italic and without syntax.
traditions: part-songs, glee books, barbershop and quartet arrangements, Tin Pan Alley, plantation and minstrel ensembles, operetta

label_when: Bracketed or italic, alone on a line or replacing a refrain pass. It tells the performer to whistle instead of singing.
sung_trap: Extremely common sung word: 'O Whistle, an\' I\'ll come to ye, my lad' (a Burns title and chorus), 'Oh whistle for the wind' (Kingsley), 'Quoth she, and whistles thrice' (Coleridge), 'He sprang to his sleigh, to his team gave a whistle' (Moore), 'the balls that whistled through'. It is a cue only when it has no syntactic role and is enclosed or free-standing, usually at the position where a refrain would be printed.
traditions: music-hall, vaudeville, Tin Pan Alley, minstrel songsters, comic songs

entries.term: Vocal-effect and delivery cues (laugh, sob, yodel, falsetto, sotto voce)
variants: Ha! ha! (printed in italics as a cue)
label_when: Bracketed or italic, inline or alone on a line, describing HOW a sound is produced, not words to sing.
sung_trap: Printed sung laughter, cries and vocables are sung text and count: 'Ha! ha! ha!', 'Hee! Hee!' (Barnes), 'Oh! oh!', yodel syllables 'Lay-ee-oo', 'Hic! hic!' in drinking songs when they are in the meter. Words like 'sigh', 'laugh', 'weep', 'shout' are sung verbs. A cue is bracketed or italic and in the third person or participle ('Laughs', 'Laughing'). The sung form is in the first/second person, or is the vocable itself, inside the meter.
traditions: music-hall, vaudeville, comic and descriptive songs, minstrel songsters, Tyrolean-style parlour songs, operetta libretti
examples: "I'm the man that broke the bank (Laughs) at Monte Carlo"

entries.term: Voice-part and ensemble assignment labels (Solo, Tutti, Unison, S.A.T.B.)
label_when: Alone on a line, or line-initial followed by '.', ':', '--', or '. --' (Lanier: 'Solo. --    Sin's rooster's crowed', eng_american_sidney_lanier.txt:104), or bracketed. Split the label from the sung text that follows it on the same line.
sung_trap: 'solo', 'all', 'full', 'harmony', 'unison', 'treble', 'bass', 'tenor', 'trio' are sung words: 'All people that on earth do dwell', 'We sing in full harmony', 'the tenor of his life', 'a trio of maidens', 'the bass of heaven's deep organ' (Milton), 'sing solo'. They are labels only at line start with a following '.', ':' or '--', or alone on a line, with no verb or article. 'All' line-initial with a period ('All. Hurrah!') in dialogue songs is a voice label. 'All' as the first word of a sung line ('All hail the power') has no punctuation after it. 'Ten.' (tenor) is an abbreviation trap for the numeral 'ten'.
traditions: part-songs, glees, hymnals, gospel songbooks, shape-note tunebooks (Treble/Counter/Tenor/Bass), operetta, plantation and spirituals collections, music-hall
examples: "Solo. --    Sin's rooster's crowed, Ole Mahster's riz," (eng_american_sidney_lanier.txt:104)

entries.term: All sing / All join (audience and company participation cues)
label_when: Alone on a line, italic or bracketed, before a chorus or round entry. In D'Urfey's Pills the corpus has '_All Sing._' as apparatus (eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt:10770 and following).
sung_trap: 'Now all together, boys!', 'Everybody's doing it', 'Let all together sing' are sung lines. Such a line is sung when it is a full clause inside the meter. It is a cue when it is italic or bracketed with no other syntax.
traditions: Restoration catches and drolls (D'Urfey), music-hall, community and school songbooks, college songbooks, minstrel walk-arounds

entries.term: Dance and stage-business directions in songs (Dance, Clog, Breakdown, Walk-around)
label_when: Bracketed or italic, or alone on a line, between or after stanzas, telling the performer to dance. Very frequent in minstrel songsters ('Dance.' after each verse, 'Walk-around' finales) and music-hall song-and-dance numbers.
sung_trap: 'dance' and its relatives are among the commonest sung words: 'Dance on, dance on, \'tis joy to see' (twice in the corpus), 'Dance, dance, my girl, the war-hawks scream', 'Dance to her chant', 'dance a hornpipe on the deck', 'They danced the reel', 'a merry jig'. They are sung inside clauses. They are directions only when bracketed or italic or alone, and in the imperative-free stage form ('Dance.', 'Dances off.'). Tune names containing these words ('The Swaggering Jig', 'Sailor's Hornpipe', 'Reel o' Tulloch') are tune designations; see the Air/Tune entries.
traditions: minstrel and dime songsters (1840s-1890s), music-hall, vaudeville, burlesque, Irish comic songs, Tin Pan Alley
examples: "(Dance.)" (after each verse of a minstrel song)

entries.term: Dance-rhythm and character headings (Waltz, March, Fox-trot, Tempo di ...)
label_when: Alone on a line at the head of a song (above stanza 1 or the refrain), or attached to an Italian or English tempo word ('Moderato (Blues tempo)'), or in parentheses after the title, or as a tune-type designation after 'Tune--' or 'Air--' in Scots collections ('Tune--Strathspey').
sung_trap: 'march', 'waltz', 'polka', 'blues', 'rag', 'lilt', 'reel', 'jig' are sung in lyrics: 'Slow be your march! the field is won!' (eng_british_felicia_hemans.txt:1435), 'Let\'s waltz', 'the Blues', 'Alexander\'s Ragtime Band', 'Doin\' the fox-trot'. They are sung when inflected or governed by a verb, article or possessive, or when they rhyme. They are labels when alone at the top of the song text, or glued to 'Tempo di'/'time'/'tempo', or in parentheses with nothing else.
traditions: parlour and sheet music (1840-1929), music-hall, Tin Pan Alley, ragtime and blues sheets, Scots and Irish song collections, operetta

label_when: Alone on a line (often italic or small caps) above stanza 1 or a section, or after the title or voice-part label, or in parentheses. These are Italian, so any free-standing occurrence in an English song text is apparatus. They often carry a metronome mark ('Andante ♩ = 72').
sung_trap: 'Grave' is an English sung word ('the silent grave', 'O Grave, where is thy victory?'). It is a tempo mark only when alone or with Italian modifiers and capitalised at the top of a section. 'Moderato' should not be confused with 'Moderator' (Carroll, 'To call a Moderator)', eng_british_lewis_carroll.txt:1713). 'Largo' and 'Presto' can appear in comic songs ('Hey presto!') inside a clause. 'Andante', 'Allegro' and others occasionally appear as section TITLES of poems (Browning-style musical titles, 'Allegro' after Milton's 'L\'Allegro'). Milton's 'L\'Allegro' is a poem title, not a tempo; treat it as title domain.
traditions: sheet music and parlour songs, art songs, hymnals (later 19th c. tune headers), gospel songbooks, operetta vocal scores, school songbooks

label_when: Free-standing on a line, or inline in italics or parentheses between sung words in transcriptions of sheet music, where an expression mark sits under the staff and lands in the text stream. Strip the token and keep the words around it.
sung_trap: These are not English, so they are rarely sung. 'dolce far niente' can be quoted in a lyric. 'Ten.' (tenuto) collides with 'ten' and with 'Ten.' (tenor). 'Port.' collides with 'port' (wine, harbour). 'Trem.' rarely appears in lyrics. An abbreviated mark ends in '.' and is often italic; the sung word is lowercase inside syntax.
traditions: sheet music, art songs, operetta vocal scores, gospel and school songbooks transcribed from notation
examples: "_dolce_ Sweet the hour when daylight dies"

entries.term: English tempo words (Slow, Slowly, Brisk, Lively, Moderately)
label_when: Alone on a line (often italic or with a period) at the head of a song or section, or in parentheses after a title or voice label. It has one to six words, no subject, no main verb, and does not fit the stanza's meter or rhyme. It often co-occurs with a metronome mark or a dance heading.
sung_trap: These are frequent sung adjectives and adverbs: 'Slow, solemn, stole:--', 'Slow be your march!', 'Slow rose the mist from the river', 'Slow to threaten, strong to move', 'Lively bright horror and amazing anguish', 'And it\'s "Lively, hearties, and let her go!"' (eng_american_j_w_palmer.txt:206), 'Fast falls the eventide', 'Bright be thy dreams'. They are sung when followed by a noun, verb or prepositional phrase that continues the sense, or when the line rhymes or scans with the stanza. A direction is a short phrase that ends the line, with no subject, set apart from the stanza block (above stanza 1, or between stanza and chorus), and often italic or parenthesised. Words such as 'Slowly.' alone on a line, preceded and followed by blank lines, are directions.
traditions: American and British parlour and sheet music, gospel songbooks, hymnals, school songbooks, music-hall, Tin Pan Alley, ragtime ('Not fast')

entries.term: English expression and character words (Tenderly, With spirit, Cheerfully)
label_when: Same position rule as the English tempo words: a lone adverb or 'With' plus an abstract noun, on its own line above or within a song text, in italic or parentheses, with no grammatical link to the stanza.
sung_trap: These words are sung in hymns and lyrics: 'Cheerfully on, through joy and woe;' (eng_british_adelaide_anne_procter.txt:1836), 'Gently, Lord, O gently lead us', 'Softly and tenderly Jesus is calling', 'Merrily, merrily shall I live now', 'With spirit and with understanding'. They are sung when followed on the same line by more words in the sentence, or when they open a stanza line that scans. A direction stands alone as the whole line or parenthetical and does not rhyme with anything.
traditions: parlour songs, gospel songbooks, hymnals, school and community songbooks, sheet music

entries.term: Tempo-change terms (Rit., Rall., Accel., A tempo, Pause, Hold)
label_when: Abbreviations with a period are always apparatus. Full English words are apparatus when bracketed or italic, alone on a line, or interleaved between sung words in a transcription from notation. A fermata glyph over a syllable OCRs as '^', '⌒' or '(^)', and those tokens are apparatus.
sung_trap: 'pause', 'hold', 'slower', 'faster', 'dying away' are sung: 'Pause, traveller, pause!', 'Hold the fort, for I am coming' (a gospel song TITLE and REFRAIN, sung), 'Slower and slower the wheel goes round', 'his voice dying away'. A cue such as 'heard gradually dying away at a distance' (eng_british_felicia_hemans.txt:1716, apparatus) is a stage description in italics in the third person; the sung form is part of the stanza's syntax and meter. 'Retard' as a lyric noun or adjective is rare but possible.
traditions: sheet music, gospel songbooks, hymnals, part-songs, operetta, school songbooks, dramatic poems with music cues

entries.term: Dynamic marks (p, pp, f, ff, mf, cresc., dim.)
label_when: Single-letter or two-to-three-letter lowercase tokens ('p', 'pp', 'mf', 'ff') standing as whole tokens at line start, between sung words or alone are always apparatus in an English lyric; no English sung word is spelled 'pp', 'ff', 'mf', 'sfz'. Abbreviations ending in '.' ('cresc.', 'dim.') are apparatus. Full English words ('Loud', 'Soft', 'Softly', 'Louder') are apparatus only when bracketed, italic, or alone.
sung_trap: 'f' and 'p' as lone letters can also be OCR debris, footnote letters, or the letter itself in a spelling or alphabet song ('P is for pie'). 'Piano' is sung in Tin Pan Alley ('Play that piano', 'He\'d have to get under... the piano'). 'Forte' is sung as 'his forte'. 'Full' and 'soft' are ordinary sung words ('Soft as the voice of an angel', 'Full fathom five'). 'Swell' is a sung verb and noun ('the swell of the sea', 'a regular swell' in music-hall slang). Treat a word as a mark only when it is bracketed, italic, or free-standing with no grammatical role.
traditions: all printings transcribed from notation: sheet music, hymnals, gospel and school songbooks, part-songs, operetta vocal scores

entries.term: Ad lib. / Colla voce / Cadenza (freedom marks)
label_when: Any free-standing or bracketed occurrence. 'Ossia' introduces an alternative reading (notes or words); keep any alternative WORDS as variant text, annotated.
sung_trap: 'freely' and 'optional' can be sung ('Freely, freely, ye have received'). A cadenza is sung on vocables ('Ah___', 'Ah! ah! ah!'). Those vocables count as sung text; only the label 'Cadenza' is apparatus. 'ad lib' in 1920s lyrics as slang ('he can ad-lib') is sung only inside syntax.
traditions: sheet music, art songs, operatic and parlour ballads, Tin Pan Alley, gospel songbooks

entries.term: Articulation and keyboard marks leaking into text (8va, Ped., loco, *)
label_when: Any occurrence of these tokens in a lyric line extracted by OCR or e-text from a piano-vocal or organ score is apparatus. They come from the accompaniment staff and land in the text stream at line start or end or between syllables.
sung_trap: 'loco' (crazy) is sung in some 1920s songs. 'Sw.', 'Gt.', 'Ch.' could be name abbreviations. 'sim.' and 'tr' are not words. A '*' may be a pedal release, a footnote, an omission mark or an entry sign; decide from position (a '*' under or after a bar in score OCR is pedal).
traditions: OCR'd sheet music and hymnals with organ registration, Tin Pan Alley piano-vocal copies

label_when: Any occurrence; often beside an Italian or English tempo word. OCR turns the note glyph into 'J', 'q', 'j', 'd' or '|'.
sung_trap: None. An OCR 'J = 80' might be read as text; treat any '=' followed by digits as apparatus in a lyric.
traditions: sheet music after c.1815, art songs, hymnals and gospel songbooks (late 19th c. on)

label_when: Alone on a line, or after a tempo or dance heading or tune name, in songbooks that give time signatures in text (school, community, camp and college songbooks; shape-note indexes). A lone 'C' at the top of a text transcribed from notation is a time signature, not a word.
sung_trap: 'common time' and 'triple time' can be sung in poems about music or dance. Fractions like '3/4' are sung only in comic patter. Prose 'Time' phrases such as 'To keep due Time and Hours' (D'Urfey title apparatus) are lyric or title text, not signatures. Moore's '(Time - the Ninth Century)' is a historical-setting header (editorial or stage domain), not a musical time; the corpus has it wrongly hoisted into [air:] (eng_celtic_thomas_moore.txt:3320).
traditions: school and community songbooks, college songbooks, shape-note and tonic sol-fa books, camp-meeting and gospel books

entries.term: Key labels and pitch/tonic sol-fa key statements
label_when: Alone on a line or in a tune header beside the tune name and meter, in tonic sol-fa books (Curwen), shape-note tunebooks ('Key of A minor'), community songbooks and sheet-music covers.
sung_trap: 'key' is a sung word ('the key of heaven', 'the key of the door', 'turn the key'), and 'doh' and 'lah' appear as sung solmization in songs like 'Do-Re-Mi'-type teaching songs. A label pairs 'Key'/'Doh'/'Lah' with a note letter and optional flat/sharp/minor, with no verb.
traditions: tonic sol-fa publications (Britain, 1850s on), shape-note tunebooks, school and community songbooks, sheet-music covers

entries.term: Tonic sol-fa and shape-note notation lines and syllables
variants: d r m f s l t d'
Fa sol la fa sol la mi fa
Do re mi fa sol la si
label_when: Lines made entirely of sol-fa letters, colons, bars, dashes and dots are notation, not lyric. In shape-note practice a 'singing the notes' pass is printed as syllables in a tunebook index or note; it is not lyric unless the edition sets it as a verse.
sung_trap: Nonsense refrains built on these syllables are SUNG and count: madrigal and ballett 'Fa la la' refrains (Morley, Weelkes: 'Fa la la la la'), 'Sol fa' lines in comic songs, and teaching songs whose text IS the syllables. 'Fa la' or 'fa-la-la' inside a stanza with real words, or as a refrain after rhymed lines, is sung. A line of single letters (d, r, m, s, l, t) with colons and bars is notation.
traditions: Curwen tonic sol-fa books, Welsh and Scottish sol-fa hymnals, shape-note tunebooks (Sacred Harp, Southern Harmony), Elizabethan madrigal and ballett texts (as the trap)

variants: Uke tuning: G C E A
Tune Uke A D F# B
label_when: A line consisting ENTIRELY of chord tokens (a capital letter A-G, optionally #, b, m, 7, 9, maj, dim, aug, +, °, sus) separated by spaces is a chord line, not lyric. Chord tokens inline above or between syllables in OCR are apparatus. Uke and guitar tuning headers ('Tune Uke A D F# B') are apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Uke' and 'Ukulele' are sung in 1920s songs ('Ukulele Lady', 'with my ukulele'). 'Tune Uke' must NOT be read as a 'Tune:' line (see the Tune entry). A single capital 'A' or 'I' alone on a line could be lyric fragment or OCR; only lines in which every token is a chord symbol and at least one token has a chord suffix or is in B-G count as chord lines. 'Guitar' and 'banjo' are sung nouns.
traditions: Tin Pan Alley sheets 1915-1929 (uke diagrams nearly universal from c.1922), cowboy and folio songbooks, early hillbilly songbooks

entries.term: Sheet-music underlay hyphenation and melisma extenders
variants: 2nd verse words stacked under notes: '1. Oh the... 2. And the...'
label_when: In texts transcribed from underlay, spaced hyphens inside a word and runs of underscores or dashes after a syllable are typographic extenders. Normalise them (rejoin the syllables, drop the extender) and do not delete the word. Interleaved numbered verse lines from stacked underlay must be de-interleaved (numbering domain).
sung_trap: The words and vocables themselves ('Ah', 'Amen', 'Glory') are sung and must count once. Real hyphenated compounds ('war-hawks', 'humble-bee') are not underlay; underlay hyphens are spaced (' - ') or split a word with no compound reading.
traditions: e-texts and OCR of sheet music, gospel songbooks, hymnals with interlined texts, school songbooks

entries.term: Music cues and sound-effect directions in descriptive and theatrical songs
label_when: Bracketed, italic or free-standing, between or inside lines. Descriptive songs ('The Village Blacksmith' style parlour pieces, battle-pieces, train songs) and burlesque, melodrama and music-hall texts print these as cues.
sung_trap: Imitative sung vocables count as sung text: 'Ding dong, ding dong', 'Rat-a-plan', 'Tara-ra-boom-de-ay', 'Toot, toot'. 'bells', 'drum', 'bugle' are common sung nouns ('Ring out, wild bells'). They are cues only when bracketed or italic and without syntax, in a noun-only or third-person form.
traditions: descriptive parlour songs, music-hall and burlesque, Civil War and battle songs, melodrama and operetta libretti
examples: "(Bells.) Ding dong! the bells are ringing"

variants: Emphasis marks in CAPS or italics (typographic)
label_when: Bracketed delivery and gesture instructions in reciters' anthologies (e.g. Bell's Standard Elocutionist, 'Speaker' and 'Reciter' collections, 'pieces for declamation'). Audience-reaction brackets ('(Laughter.)', '(Applause.)') in printed recitation transcripts are apparatus, not text.
sung_trap: The recited poem is counted text. Words like 'pointing', 'whisper', 'pause', 'louder' occur in the poem itself ('Pause, traveller!', 'whispering low'). They are apparatus only when enclosed in parentheses and in the participial or imperative stage form, with no metrical role.
traditions: recitation books and elocution manuals (1850-1920), temperance and Sunday-school reciters, printed music-hall monologues
examples: "(Pause. Very slowly.) And the stars were shining."

variants: Sung to the tune of X
To be sung to the tune of X
label_when: Line-initial 'Tune' followed by ':', '--', '.--', ',' or '-' plus a tune NAME (quoted, italic, or capitalised title), placed between title and stanza 1 or right after the title. Also any 'To the tune of ...' or 'Sung to ...' heading line. The corpus hoists these into the TITLE as [air: X] (eng_american_*.txt from Southern War Songs) but leaves some inline: 'Tune--“John Anderson, my jo.”' (eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt:21183). The tune NAME is apparatus even though it is often a singable line of another song.
sung_trap: 'tune' is a sung verb and noun: 'Tune your harps high, and spread the sound' (eng_hymn_watts.txt:5388), 'Tune my heart to sing thy grace', 'thy merry whistled tunes', 'his tempest tune', 'AN OLD TUNE' (a poem title, title domain), 'Tune Uke' (a ukulele tuning instruction, chord-diagram domain). It is sung when 'Tune' is a verb with an object or a noun with an article or possessive and the line is in the stanza's meter. The label form has 'Tune' bare, capitalised, followed by tune-delimiting punctuation and a proper title, outside the stanza block. Watts's 'To the tune of the 113th Psalm.' is apparatus, but the corpus currently stages it as a TITLE line (eng_hymn_watts.txt:13301-13303); flag that.
traditions: Scots and Irish song collections (Burns, Hogg, Tannahill), broadsides and garlands, songsters, political and Civil War song books, temperance and campaign songsters, hymnals (alternative tunes), college and union songbooks

entries.term: Numbered airs and songs in ballad operas, libretti and cantatas
variants: AIR XVI. Over the hills and far away.
Air IX -- O Polly, you might have toy'd and kist.
Air (as a section label after Recitativo)
label_when: Line-initial 'Air'/'Song'/'No.' plus a roman or arabic numeral, optionally followed by the tune name in italics (Beggar's Opera style), or alone as a section label alternating with 'Recitativo' (Burns's cantata: '# APPARATUS: Air', eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt:4200). In ballad operas the tune name printed after 'AIR XVI.' is the source tune and is apparatus, not the opening of the sung text. The corpus TITLE 'Air IX -- O _Polly_, you might have toy'd and kist.' [air: O Jenny, O Jenny...] shows the number in the title; there the title line is the first sung line, so check for duplication.
sung_trap: 'Song' and 'ballad' are sung words ('a song of the sea'). 'Finale' and 'Romance' are sung nouns. They are labels when they carry a numeral or 'No.', or stand alone as a heading with nothing but a performer or genre after them.
traditions: ballad operas (Gay's Beggar's Opera, Polly, Love in a Village), comic opera and Gilbert & Sullivan libretti, cantatas (Burns's 'Jolly Beggars'), oratorio wordbooks, operetta
examples: "AIR XXXI. Of all the girls that are so smart."

entries.term: Same tune / To the foregoing tune / Ditto
variants: The Second Part, To the same Tune.
To the foregoing Tune; In Imitation of ...
label_when: After a title, alone on a line, or in italics at the end of a title line. D'Urfey's Pills attaches it to titles ('QUAKER'S _Petticoats. To the foregoing Tune._', eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt:12882), and the corpus also has it as apparatus ('_The Second Part, To the same Tune._', '_The_ NEWS _Monger. To the same Tune._'). 'Do.' or 'Ditto' in the tune slot means 'same tune as above'.
sung_trap: 'Do.' is the English verb 'do' when it is a word in a sentence ('What shall we do.'). It is a ditto only in the tune or air slot ('Air--Do.'). 'same tune' can be sung ('they all sang the same tune'). It is apparatus only in a heading after a title or after Tune/Air.
traditions: Restoration and 18th-c. song collections (D'Urfey, Playford), broadside garlands, Scots and Irish collections, songsters, campaign songbooks

variants: To a tune of his own
To the tune of, Fortune my foe
To the tune of, Flying Fame
Or, X (alternative tune after 'To the tune of')
To a New Tune (title suffix, e.g. 'Gilderoys last Farewel. To a New Tune.')
label_when: In the broadside title block, after the main title and subtitle and before stanza 1, often in black-letter or italic. It is apparatus even when it trails the title on one line, as in the corpus 'Gilderoys last Farewel. To a New Tune.' (eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt:1157).
sung_trap: 'new tune' can be sung ('I'll sing you a new tune'). It is apparatus when introduced by 'To' plus an article plus 'tune', in a title or heading, or when followed by a comma and a tune name.
traditions: English and Scottish broadsides (Pepys, Roxburghe, Bagford, Euing ballads), garlands and chapbooks, Playford and D'Urfey
examples: "A Lamentable Ballad of the Tragical End of a Gallant Lord. To the tune of, Fortune my Foe."

entries.term: Hymn and psalm tune names as headings
label_when: A proper name, in caps or small caps, alone on a line above or beside a hymn, usually paired with a meter label and/or a composer line ('ST. ANNE. C.M.' 'William Croft, 1708'). In words-only hymnals it may appear only in an index line or a cross-reference ('Tune 245').
sung_trap: Tune names often coincide with words in a hymn ('Coronation': 'Bring forth the royal diadem'; 'Bethany', 'Olivet', 'Antioch', 'America', 'Italian'), and 'America' is a sung word. A tune-name line is a lone proper noun or short name in caps, paired with a meter label or composer or date line, and does not scan as a hymn line. A sung line has a verb and fits the meter.
traditions: hymnals with tunes (Hymns A&M 1861 on, Methodist, Presbyterian, Lutheran, Moravian), metrical psalters (Scottish Psalter, Tate & Brady with tunes), shape-note tunebooks, gospel songbooks

entries.term: Composer, arranger and source credit lines under tunes
label_when: Line-initial 'Music by' / 'Words by' / 'Arranged by' / 'Arr.' / 'Harm.' followed by a personal name, initials or 'the author'; or a composer-and-date line beside a tune name. Always apparatus in a lyric count.
sung_trap: 'Words by which the wretched are consoled?' (eng_british_matthew_arnold.txt:1151) is a sung line; there 'by' starts a relative clause, not a name. 'music by moonlight', 'written by the hand of God' and the like are sung. A credit line is followed by a capitalised personal name or initials and stands alone with no verb.
traditions: sheet music, music-hall and Tin Pan Alley, hymnals, gospel songbooks, parlour songs, school and community songbooks, Moore and Scots collections ('Air by X')
examples: "Words by Thomas Moore.  Music by Sir John Stevenson."

entries.term: Performer credit lines ('As sung by', 'Sung with great success by')
variants: Sung with great success by X
Sung with immense success by X
Sung with rapturous applause by X
Composed for and sung by X
The celebrated song sung by X
As sung at the X Theatre
Sung by Mr. X at Covent Garden
label_when: A heading or subtitle line (sheet-music cover, songster heading, 18th-c. song-sheet heading) that names a performer or venue. Always apparatus.
sung_trap: 'sung' is a sung past participle ('the song my mother sung', 'sung by the cradle'). It is a credit line when 'sung by' is followed by a title (Mr., Miss, Mrs., Madame) or a capitalised name or venue, in a heading position.
traditions: 18th-c. pleasure-garden songs (Vauxhall, Ranelagh), minstrel songsters, music-hall, vaudeville and Tin Pan Alley sheets, parlour ballads
examples: "Sung with immense success by The Great Vance"

variants: Words Written For A Melody By X (title)
Song For An Air By X (title)
label_when: Line-initial 'Melody' followed by ':' or '--' plus a name, or 'Melody by' plus a name, between title and text. Also inside TITLES of the form 'Written For A Melody By Felton' / 'Song For An Air By Hummel' (eng_british_felicia_hemans.txt:15715, 9456). Those are titles carrying tune information; keep them as titles (title domain) but note the tune reference.
sung_trap: 'Melody throughout the year.' (eng_hymn_cowper.txt:2079) is a sung line, as are 'the melody of birds', 'sweet melody'. It is a label only line-initial with tune punctuation or 'by' plus a name.
traditions: Moore's Irish Melodies, Byron's Hebrew Melodies (title-level), parlour songs, school songbooks, Hemans's song texts

entries.term: Page and number cross-references to tunes
label_when: Any page or number reference attached to a tune or music statement; always apparatus. The corpus has '_Tune of_ Oh! how happy's he. _Pag._ 104.' as apparatus (D'Urfey).
sung_trap: None sung.
traditions: D'Urfey's Pills and other 18th-c. collections, words-only hymnals, songsters with separate music sections, shape-note indexes

label_when: Alone on a line, or line-final after a hymn or psalm number, part label or tune name ('Hymn 3:27. 1st. C. M.', eng_hymn_watts.txt; 'Second Part. C. M.'), or as the last words of a title ('The Hosanna in Long Metre', 'in Common Metre').
sung_trap: 'C. M.' as initials: Herrick's 'The words found true, C. M., remember me.' (eng_british_robert_herrick.txt:650) is a SUNG line addressing a person. Meter labels are never mid-sentence and never followed by a verb. 'common measure' can be sung ('the common measure of mankind'), and 'measure' is sung often ('repeat his merry measure', van Dyke; 'Measure all you give', Procter; 'tread a measure'). The label is capitalised, standalone or after a hymn number, without an article.
traditions: Watts, Wesley, Doddridge, Newton and Cowper (Olney Hymns), Tate & Brady, metrical psalters, American hymnals and shape-note tunebooks, gospel hymnals

variants: Glory to the Father in Long Metre
label_when: Same as C.M.: standalone, or after hymn, part or tune number, or title-final 'in Long Metre'. Corpus: 'Hymn 3:26. 1st. L.M.', 'First Part. L. M.', 'Otherwise it must be sung to the usual tunes of the Long Metre.' (eng_hymn_watts.txt:23481, an editorial singing note, apparatus).
sung_trap: 'L. M.' as initials of a dedicatee or signatory (by-line). 'long measure' sung in drinking or satirical songs. The label has no syntax around it.
traditions: Watts, Wesley, Doddridge, metrical psalters, American and British hymnals, shape-note tunebooks

label_when: Same as C.M. Corpus: 'Hymn 3:28. 1st. S. M.', 'Hymn 3:31. 2d. S. M.', 'Short Metre.' standalone.
sung_trap: 'S. M.' as initials. 'short measure' sung in tavern or drinking songs about cheating publicans, and 'S. M.' can also abbreviate 'Sancta Maria' in Latin rubrics. The label has no syntax around it.
traditions: Watts, Wesley, metrical psalters, hymnals, shape-note tunebooks

label_when: Standalone or beside a tune name or hymn number.
sung_trap: 'D.C.M.' and 'D.S.M.' start with 'D.C.'/'D.S.' and must NOT be read as Da Capo or Dal Segno; check for the trailing 'M.'. 'Double' alone on a line in hymnals is a meter or tune instruction. 'double' is otherwise a sung word ('double, double toil and trouble').
traditions: Victorian and American hymnals, gospel hymnals, Methodist and Baptist hymnals, Sacred Harp

entries.term: Particular / Peculiar Metre (P.M.) and named particular meters
label_when: Standalone or beside a hymn number or tune name.
sung_trap: 'peculiar' is a sung word in Watts and Herrick: 'Peculiar honours to our King;' (eng_hymn_watts.txt:17224), 'Peculiar grace', 'To His Peculiar Friend' (Herrick titles). 'P. M.' is also 'post meridiem' ('at 3 P.M.') in songs and diaries, and initials. 'irregular' is sung in poems. The label is the bare meter phrase with no article or syntax, capitalised, in heading position.
traditions: Watts, Wesley (whose many 'peculiar' meters are labelled), 18th-19th c. hymnals, shape-note tunebooks, gospel hymnals ('Irregular')

label_when: Standalone or beside a hymn number or tune name ('Darwall's 148th. H.M.').
sung_trap: 'H. M.' in British songs is 'His/Her Majesty' ('H.M.S. Pinafore', 'H. M. the King', 'on board H. M. S. Victory'), which is sung or titular. The meter label is never followed by 'S.' or a name and stands alone. 'Hallelujah' itself is sung everywhere; only the phrase 'Hallelujah Metre/Meter/Measure' is a label.
traditions: Watts and Wesley hymnals, 18th-19th c. psalters and hymnals, shape-note tunebooks

label_when: Standalone, or beside a hymn number or tune name in hymnals from c.1780 on. A token of digits plus 's' (optionally with apostrophe), joined by '&', 'and' or ',', is a meter.
sung_trap: Price notations look similar but are print apparatus of another kind: '5s.' after 'price' means five shillings ('handsomely bound, roxburgh style, price 5s.,', eng_british_felicia_hemans.txt:16526). Spelled-out 'Sevens', 'Tens' and so on can be sung ('sixes and sevens', 'at sixes and sevens', 'in tens and twenties'). Treat spelled forms as meter only in heading position paired with another meter word or a tune name. Decades ('the 1890s') are not meters.
traditions: Wesleyan and later hymnals, American hymnals and gospel hymnals, Moravian hymnbooks, shape-note tunebooks

label_when: Standalone, or beside a tune name, in hymnals after c.1860 (Hymns A&M, later American hymnals): a group of 4-12 numbers between 4 and 14, joined by '.', ',' or spaces, optionally ending in 'D.' or 'with Refrain'. Validate against the hymn: the numbers should equal the syllable counts of the stanza lines.
sung_trap: Scripture citations look similar: 'The rich sinner dying, Psalm 49. 6 9. Eccl. 8. 8.' (eng_hymn_watts.txt:1258) and 'Psalm 73. 25' are scripture references (editorial or bibliographic apparatus, another domain). They follow a book name or abbreviation, and their numbers are verse numbers that do not match the stanza's syllable counts. Dates ('1.8.6.1.') and money are other confounders.
traditions: Victorian and Edwardian hymnals, American denominational hymnals, gospel songbooks, school hymnals

entries.term: Singing notes about tune fit (editorial musical instructions in prose)
variants: Otherwise it must be sung to the usual tunes of the Long Metre.
This hymn may be sung to any tune of the same metre.
To be sung as a duet.
This psalm may be sung in four parts.
The last line of each verse to be sung twice.
Sing the first two verses before the sermon.
Repeat the first stanza to complete the tune.
N.B.--The chorus is to be sung after every verse.
Note.--The words in italics are to be sung by the leader.
If sung to X, repeat the last line.
label_when: A prose sentence (often 'N.B.', 'Note.' or italic) addressed to the singer about tune, meter, repeats or parts, placed before or after a hymn or song.
sung_trap: None, provided the sentence is prose and the meter does not fit. A rare danger: a hymn line that happens to contain 'sung' and 'tune' ('His praise be sung in every tune'). Sung lines rhyme and scan with the stanza.
traditions: Watts, Wesley, metrical psalters, songsters, school songbooks, gospel songbooks
examples: "Otherwise it must be sung to the usual tunes of the Long Metre." (eng_hymn_watts.txt:23481)

entries.term: Anglican and Gregorian chant labels and psalter pointing
variants: Glory be to the Father (chant gloria)
label_when: Tone, chant or mode headings standalone above canticles or psalms are apparatus. A single '*' mid-verse dividing two half-verses, '|' between words, and '†' at a flex are pointing marks: strip them and keep every word.
sung_trap: The psalm or canticle words are sung and count. 'Chant' is a sung verb and noun ('Dance to her chant', 'chant the praises'). It is a label only alone or with Single/Double/Anglican/Gregorian or a tone number. A mid-verse '*' can also be a footnote anchor; inside a pointed psalter, though, a '*' near the midpoint of every verse is pointing.
traditions: Anglican pointed psalters (Cathedral Psalter 1875, Oxford Psalter), Prayer Book canticle books, Catholic and Anglo-Catholic hymnals, Victorian hymnals with chant appendices
examples: "O come, let us sing unto the Lord: * let us heartily rejoice in the strength of our salvation."

entries.term: Shape-note tunebook headers and form labels (Fuguing tune, Anthem, Set piece)
label_when: A line that bundles tune name, meter, key, composer and date, or a part label (Treble/Counter/Tenor/Bass) before a staff in transcription. All apparatus. Shape-note 'Repeat' and 'Fine' follow the general repeat/navigation rules.
sung_trap: 'Anthem' is sung ('Sing the nation\'s anthem') and 'Ode' appears in titles (title domain). 'Treble', 'Tenor' and 'Bass' are sung nouns in poems. They are labels when alone or line-initial with '.' before a staff transcription, or in a tune header.
traditions: American shape-note tunebooks (Sacred Harp, Southern Harmony, Missouri Harmony, Christian Harmony), New England tunebooks (Billings), camp-meeting songsters
examples: "WONDROUS LOVE. P.M. Key of A minor."

entries.term: [Music] placeholders and music-underlay blocks in e-texts
variants: [Music: The King is gone to _Oxon_ Town,
label_when: Any bracketed transcriber placeholder for engraved music. The corpus has D'Urfey blocks '[Music:' (eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt:598, 7213, 7256, 10745-10751, 11553, 12993, 13743).
sung_trap: Inside '[Music: ...]' Gutenberg transcribers often reproduce the words underlaid on the staff ('[Music: The King is gone to _Oxon_ Town,'). Those words DUPLICATE stanza 1 or carry part labels ('_First Nose._', '_CHO. of all._', '_1 N._, _2d._'). Exclude them from the count so that stanza 1 is not counted twice, and keep the printed stanza as the counted text. If a song's only text is inside the [Music:] block, extract it once.
traditions: Project Gutenberg and other e-texts of song collections with music (D'Urfey's Pills, Playford, Child-ballad tune appendices, Scots and Irish collections, hymnals)

entries.term: Tune-type designations in Scots, Irish and Welsh collections
label_when: After 'Tune--', 'Air--' or 'Alaw--', or alone in parentheses after a tune name, in Scots, Irish and Welsh song collections. The corpus has pibroch section labels [URLAR], [SIUBHAL], [CRUNLUATH] as structure headings (section domain) in some eng_celtic files.
sung_trap: These are sung nouns when inside verse ('M\'Pherson\'s Rant' as a title, 'The Ruffian\'s Rant' as a tune name, 'dance a reel', 'a lilt of the pipes'). They are tune designations only in tune-line position. Welsh 'Alaw' and 'Tôn' appear in bilingual Welsh hymnals and song books (cym_ files).
traditions: Scots Musical Museum, Thomson's Select Collection, Burns and Hogg editions, Irish collections (Moore, Petrie, Bunting), Welsh bilingual songbooks and hymnals

label_when: In a footnote, source line or epigraph credit, usually followed by a page/line reference or closing a citation. Never in sung text.
sung_trap: None in English song; 'ib' does not occur as a sung word. Watch for OCR splitting 'Ibid.' off a note onto its own line.
traditions: Scholarly editions (Byron, Coleridge, Percy, Ritson, Child), annotated anthologies, Burns editions

label_when: Alone on a line after a poem, or in a by-line slot, meaning 'same author as the previous item'; or in a note citation. 'By the Same.' / 'The Same.' standing under a title is attribution.
sung_trap: 'the same' is common sung text ('Burns the same, where'er it goes'); it is attribution only when it is the whole line (optionally 'By the same.') in by-line or end position with a period and no verb. 'Idem' can be sung in a Latin macaronic student/drinking song only when it sits inside a metrical Latin line.
traditions: Elizabethan/Jacobean miscellanies, Greek Anthology translations, 18th-c. collections, anthologies

label_when: Inside a footnote or bracketed note, followed by a work, line or page reference ('cf. Gray').
sung_trap: 'Compare' is a sung verb ('Shall I compare thee'); it is apparatus only when capitalised at the head of a note and followed by a citation, not a clause.
traditions: Scholarly and annotated editions

label_when: In notes, headnotes, glosses and title subtitles ('A New Song, viz. The Lover's Complaint').
sung_trap: Essentially never sung; 'namely' is sung only inside a metrical line. In 17th-c. broadside titles 'viz.' belongs to the long title, not the lyric.
traditions: Broadside long titles, Pepys/Roxburghe ballads, scholarly notes

label_when: In a gloss or bracket: '[sc. the king]' supplies an understood word.
sung_trap: 'Sc.' also abbreviates SCENE ('Act iv. sc. 1', a source citation) and SCOTS/Scottish in glossaries ('Sc. bairn'); none of these is sung. Disambiguate by what follows: numeral = scene, a noun phrase = scilicet, a dialect headword = language label.
traditions: Scholarly editions, Shakespeare song editions, Scots glossaries

label_when: In a note or parenthesis followed by a page, number, note, appendix or work; or a standalone cross-reference line under a song in a songster/hymnal ('For music see No. 112').
sung_trap: 'See' is extremely common sung text ('See, the conquering hero comes', 'See, see, &c.'). It is apparatus only when followed by a locator (p., No., Note, Appendix, a numeral, an italic title) and nothing verbal; 'v.' alone is also verse/versus and roman V (stanza 5).
traditions: Annotated editions, songsters, hymnals, Pills to Purge Melancholy

label_when: Introduces a paraphrase/gloss of a word in a note, sidenote or bracket ('TAKES YOU, i.e. captivates'); in parentheses or brackets inside or after a lyric line, the gloss is apparatus while the surrounding line is lyric.
sung_trap: 'that is' is common sung text; apparatus only with a preceding quoted/CAPITALISED headword and inside a note or bracket. Never treat 'i.e.' forms as sung.
traditions: Scholarly editions, Scots and dialect songbooks, Elizabethan anthologies (Bullen, Arber)
examples: i.e. quartered.  CANTON, in heraldry, is a square space

label_when: Only in notes and prefatory prose.
sung_trap: 'for instance' can be sung (comic songs: 'For instance, take my uncle'); abbreviated forms never.
traditions: Annotated editions, prefaces

label_when: Inside notes or glossary entries after a headword.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Scholarly editions, glossaries

label_when: Line-initial, starting a prose instruction or remark (often to the singer or reader: 'N.B. The last two lines of each verse are repeated'). Whole line/paragraph is apparatus.
sung_trap: A letter-song or comic patter song may voice 'N.B.' as part of the joke; sung only when inside a metrical, rhyming line of the lyric.
traditions: 18th-c. songsters, Pills to Purge Melancholy, broadsides, hymnals ('N.B. This hymn may be sung to ...')
examples: N.B. The Chorus to be sung after each Verse.

label_when: After a verse epistle or a poem printed as a letter, introducing prose or verse added by the author/editor outside the poem proper; or after a song in a songster introducing a remark.

Followed by a page number in a note, citation or cross-reference line; a line consisting only of 'p.71.' or 'Pag. 104' is apparatus. In Pills to Purge Melancholy, 'Vol. 4. Pag. 330.' under a song points to the tune and is apparatus.
sung_trap: Verse epistles (Burns, Swift) may have a postscript IN VERSE that is part of the poem: count it as lyric if it is metrical and rhymes with the poem's scheme, but drop the 'P.S.'/'Postscript' label itself. Comic letter songs may sing 'P.S.'.

In sheet music 'p', 'pp', 'ppp' WITHOUT a following number are dynamics (piano/pianissimo - performance-direction domain), not pages. 'page' is sung ('a little page', the boy servant); apparatus only before a number.
traditions: Burns epistles, 18th-c. verse letters, comic songs
All annotated editions, Pills to Purge Melancholy, Memoir-citing editions (Hemans), songster cross-references

label_when: In credit lines and notes.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Anthology notes, hymnal credits
examples: Words by H. Smith et al.

entries.term: op. cit. / loc. cit. / ut supra / supra / infra / ante / post / above / below
label_when: Inside notes or citation lines. 'As above' / 'Same as above' alone under a song in a songster or hymnal means 'same tune/chorus as previous' (apparatus).
sung_trap: 'above', 'below', 'ante', 'post' are sung words ('the stars above'); apparatus only inside a note or as a one-line pointer like 'Chorus as above.' (which also tells you the chorus is repeated).
traditions: Scholarly editions, songsters, hymnals

label_when: After a page or line reference in a note.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Scholarly editions
examples: Herd, vol. ii. p. 56 et seq.

label_when: In notes/glossary citations of a dictionary entry.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Scholarly editions, glossaries

label_when: Bracketed or parenthesised, often italic, immediately after a single odd word or spelling, signalling the oddity is in the source. Remove the bracket and its contents; keep the preceding word.
sung_trap: SCOTS 'sic' = such is sung and common ('On sic a day!', 'sic a husband', 'sic like trashtrie', 'Sic' ribbons, sic' ringlets'): unbracketed, adjectival, before a noun or 'a'. Latin 'sic' inside a metrical Latin line ('sic transit gloria mundi', 'Sic semper tyrannis' in a Confederate song) is sung. Only [sic]/(sic) in brackets after a word is editorial.
traditions: Scholarly editions, anthologies, transcribed broadsides; Scots songs for the sung trap
examples: the god of day had slowly sank [sic] beneath

label_when: Inside an author credit or date bracket ('John Wilbye, fl. 1598-1614').
sung_trap: 'flourished' is a sung verb; apparatus only directly before a year. 'Fl.' also abbreviates flute in instrumental lines (performance domain).
traditions: Elizabethan anthologies, Home Book of Verse, hymnal indexes

label_when: Immediately before a year or date range, in a credit, source line or date bracket.
