sung_trap: 'about' is sung; apparatus only before a bare year. 'c.' also = chapter, cents (price), and 'C' = chorus label in some hymnals; disambiguate by following token (year vs number vs nothing).
traditions: Anthologies (Bullen's Lyrics from Song-Books 'circ. 1613'), scholarly editions, hymnals
examples: From THOMAS CAMPION's _Third Book of Airs_ (circ. 1613).

entries.term: b. / d. / ob. / obiit / aet. / natus (life dates)
label_when: Inside an author credit, bracketed date span, footnote or headnote ('Esq. ob. 1610', 'aet. 23'). Whole credit line is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'd.' also = pence in prices ('6d.') and appears in bowdlerised sung oaths ('d--d', 'D--n') which ARE sung; 'born/died/aged' are sung in elegies and ballads when inside a metrical line.
traditions: Hymnals, Home Book of Verse ('Robert Burns [1759-1796]'), scholarly editions, memorial verses, broadside elegies
examples: York, ob. 1588.   Co. Kent, Esq. ob. 1610.

label_when: In headnotes, footnotes, source lines and collation ('[MS. M. First published, _Childe Harold_, 1812 (4to).]'). Any line or bracket whose subject is a manuscript is apparatus.
sung_trap: None as an abbreviation; 'manuscript' is very rarely sung. Do not confuse with 'Mrs.' or OCR 'Ms' of a sung 'M's'.
traditions: Byron/Coleridge/Wordsworth scholarly editions, Percy's Reliques, Child, Ritson, Herd, Burns editions

label_when: In notes, source lines, title pages, collations and signatures of notes ('--Ed.'). Any note signed Ed. is wholly apparatus.
sung_trap: None as abbreviation. 'Ed'/'Ned' as a name in comic songs is sung ('Poor Ed was a sailor'); a sung name is inside a metrical line, not followed by a numeral or closing a bracket.
traditions: Scholarly editions, anthologies, Burns editions, broadside reprints
examples: ed. 1662, p. 214, under the title of "On his Mistresse,

label_when: Credit line under/over a title or after the poem; bracketed translator's note; hymnal credit ('Tr. J. M. Neale, 1851'). Whole line is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Tr.' or 'tr' alone over notes is TRILL (performance domain). 'Englished' was used as a TITLE in the corpus ('--- TITLE: Englished') because a printing headed a translation that way; it is a heading, not lyric. 'translated' is sung only inside a metrical line ('translated to the skies').
traditions: Hymnals (Neale, Winkworth, Caswall), Greek Anthology and classical translations, Moore's Anacreon, German Lieder translations, opera libretti

label_when: Source or permission line, usually at foot of poem or in a note.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Anthologies (Home Book of Verse, Oxford Book), newspaper verse, hymnals

entries.term: vol. / vols. / tom. / pt. / bk. (volume and part citations)
label_when: Followed by a numeral (arabic or roman) inside a citation, source line, footnote or cross-reference.
sung_trap: 'Part', 'Book' and 'Volume' are part-name headings (other domain) or sung nouns; an abbreviated form + numeral inside a citation is never sung.
traditions: Pills to Purge Melancholy cross-references, Johnson's Museum citations, scholarly editions, Burney's History of Music
examples: see Burney's HISTORY OF MUSIC, vol. iii. pp. 399-400,

entries.term: fol. / ff. / f. / r. / v. / sig. / col. (folio, leaf, column)
label_when: Followed by a leaf/column number or recto/verso sigil, or as a format designation (4to, 8vo) in a source note.
sung_trap: 'fol' and 'fal' are sung nonsense-refrain syllables ('Fol de rol', 'fol lol de riddle', 'With a Fal, &c.'): sung when hyphenated or repeated with vowels and without a numeral; apparatus 'fol.' always has a period plus number. 'ff' alone over a line is fortissimo (performance). 'Col.' capitalised can be Colonel, sung in war songs ('Col. Ellsworth').
traditions: Percy Folio editions, Child, Bodleian/Harleian MS citations, sung-trap in comic and folk refrains

entries.term: l. / ll. / line references and margin line numbers
label_when: 'l.'/'ll.' + numeral inside notes or collations. Isolated numbers 5, 10, 15... at the right margin (or appended after wide whitespace) every fifth line are line counters, not lyric.
sung_trap: 'l.' + number after a currency amount is POUNDS sterling ('5l. a year' in a comic song is sung 'five pound'); a number at line end after whitespace could also be a rhyming sung numeral ('in eighteen-sixty-one'), but sung numbers are almost always spelled out or fit the meter, while margin counters advance by 5 and break the meter.
traditions: Scholarly editions (Oxford, Aldine), school anthologies, sung-trap in comic songs

label_when: With a numeral in a note, scripture citation, or hymnal credit ('Vs. 1-3, Watts; vs. 4, anon.').
sung_trap: 'V.' alone on a line is roman stanza 5 (numbering domain) or versus/vide. 'Verse' is also a part label (other domain) and a sung noun.
traditions: Hymnals, scripture references, scholarly notes

label_when: With a numeral in notes, collations and hymnal credit lines ('Sts. 1, 2, Latin, 1544').
sung_trap: 'St.' = SAINT is sung ('St. Patrick's Day', 'the bells of St. Clement's') and = Street in imprint addresses ('6 Great St. Andrew Street', apparatus). Saint is followed by a proper name; stanza by a numeral.
traditions: Hymnals, scholarly editions; saint-trap in Irish, Catholic and nursery songs
examples: Sts. 1, 2, John Mason Neale; st. 3, anon.

label_when: With a numeral in a cross-reference or index.
sung_trap: 'note' is a sung noun ('a note of music', 'a five-pound note'); apparatus only before a numeral or in 'See note'.
traditions: Scholarly editions

entries.term: cap. / ch. / chap. / sec. / § / art. / para. (division citations)
label_when: Followed by a numeral (often roman) inside a citation of a prose source, statute or scripture commentary.
sung_trap: 'cap' (nightcap, cap and bells) and 'art' (thou art, art of love) are very common sung words; apparatus only with a period and a following numeral. 'Ch.' is also an abbreviated Chorus label in hymnals (part-name domain).
traditions: Scholarly notes, legal-copyright notices, theological headnotes in hymnals

label_when: Alone on a line in the by-line slot or at the end of a poem, often right-aligned, dashed or bracketed; or inside a hymnal credit.
sung_trap: Archaic 'anon' = soon/presently is sung ('With sweaty speed. Anon shot by', 'I come anon'): it sits inside a sentence and is usually lower-case mid-line. Apparatus 'Anon.' stands alone (or with a date) and closes the item.
traditions: Anthologies (Oxford Book, Home Book of Verse, Bullen), hymnals, broadside reprints

label_when: In the by-line or signature slot, or in brackets glossing a signature.
sung_trap: A pseudonym can coincide with a character name sung in the song; it is a signature only when it stands alone in by-line or end position with no verb and the song does not address that name.
traditions: Newspaper and magazine verse, Civil War songbooks, music-hall sheets, annuals and keepsakes

label_when: Credit line, headnote or bracketed tag on a poem. Whole line is apparatus.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Burns editions (Doubtful section), Elizabethan anthologies, hymnals, Jacobite song collections

label_when: In a footnote, sidenote, bracket or collation giving an alternative wording; a whole 'Variants'/'Various readings' section after a poem is apparatus even though it quotes verse.
sung_trap: 'or' is a constant sung word; it introduces a variant only inside a note or a bracket like '[or, "darling"]'. Quoted variant lines are verse-shaped but are not the sung text: do not count them unless the corpus deliberately chose the variant.
traditions: Scholarly editions, Burns and Percy editions, hymnals giving alternative words

entries.term: collation verbs: om. / add. / del. / corr. / conj. / emend. / read / for ... read
label_when: Inside a collation note or footnote after a lemma or a source siglum.
sung_trap: 'add', 'read' and 'for' are sung words; apparatus only in a note whose subject is a text witness.
traditions: Scholarly editions (Byron, Coleridge, Wordsworth, Child, Percy), errata lists

label_when: A line made of a line number, a word followed by a closing square bracket ']', then a variant and a siglum (year, MS., edition letter). Always apparatus; often in smaller type below the poem.
sung_trap: A closing ']' in lyric text can also end a bracketed editorial insertion inside a real line ('[be]'); the lemma form has NO opening '[' and is followed by a siglum.
traditions: Oxford/Clarendon and Aldine scholarly editions, Coleridge (E. H. Coleridge), Byron (E. H. Coleridge), Wordsworth (Knight/Hutchinson)

entries.term: orig. / original reads / the original has / so in original
label_when: Footnote or bracketed note reporting the source's wording; any line beginning with these phrases is apparatus, along with the quoted reading it introduces.
sung_trap: 'original' is a sung word in comic songs ('the original Dixie'); apparatus only line-initial with a reading/citation following, or in a note.
traditions: Bullen's Elizabethan anthologies, Percy, Ritson, Bodleian editions, PG transcriptions

label_when: In a gloss, sidenote or translator's note introducing a literal rendering.
sung_trap: 'lit' (past of light) is sung ('lit the candle'); abbreviated 'lit.' with period inside a gloss or note is apparatus. 'literally' sung only inside a metrical line of a comic song.
traditions: Translations (Gaelic, Welsh, German, Greek Anthology), Scots songbooks

entries.term: language and register labels in glosses
label_when: Inside glossary entries, footnotes and sidenote glosses.
sung_trap: 'Fr.' can be Friar in a ballad's speaker credit; 'Sc.' scene/scilicet (see those entries). None is ever sung.
traditions: Burns glossaries, Scots and Irish songbooks, Child and Percy glossaries, translated hymns

entries.term: witness / version sigla (A, B, Q, F, Child letters)
label_when: A single capital letter (or letter+number) alone on a line or in brackets before a ballad text, or inside collation notes. Marks which version follows; not lyric.
sung_trap: 'A' is a sung word but never alone on a line with a period; a lone 'A.' / 'B.' heading a ballad is a siglum. Distinguish from lettered footnote markers (inline after a word) and from hymnal meter abbreviations (C.M., L.M.: meter domain).
traditions: Child's English and Scottish Popular Ballads, Shakespeare song editions, Percy collated texts, Motherwell/Kinloch versions

label_when: In tune/air lines, credit columns, tables of contents and songster headers meaning 'same as above'; ditto marks (") repeated in a column.
In tune, credit or heading lines of songsters: 'Air--Do.' or 'To the same Tune.' means the same tune as the previous song.
sung_trap: 'ditto' is sung in comic songs ('and ditto for me'); sung only inside a metrical line. 'Do.' can also be a solmisation syllable ('Do, re, mi') sung in singing-school songs; that 'Do' has no period-plus-tune context.
'_Heads I win--ditto tails?_' (Lowell) is sung. 'Do' is a sung verb, so 'Do.' is a label only when it follows an 'Air--' or 'Tune' cue.
traditions: Songsters, Burns and Moore tune lines, broadside collections, music-hall songbooks
Lowell 1 sung row. Durfey apparatus '_The Second Part, To the same Tune._' 2. Expected in songsters.
examples: _The Second Part, To the same Tune._  (apparatus, eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt)

label_when: Inline, immediately after a word or punctuation with no space (or bracketed), inside or at the end of a lyric line: 'Thy looks are wan, thine eyes are wet.[ll][293]'. Strip the marker, keep the line.
sung_trap: A bracketed number alone on a line before a stanza is stanza numbering (numbering domain). A digit that is part of a sung year or quantity ('in '61', '42nd Street', '5l.') is sung; footnote digits break the word ('wet.293') or sit in brackets after punctuation.
traditions: PG transcriptions of scholarly editions (Byron, Moore, Hemans), Southern War Songs, Burns editions, songsters with notes
examples: Thy looks are wan, thine eyes are wet.[ll][293]

label_when: Bracketed letter(s) immediately after a word or line-end punctuation: 'Yet cling to Being's severing link.[lh]'. Strip it; also find and drop the matching note body ('[F] Orig. ed., _warty_.').
sung_trap: A bracketed letter or word supplied INTO a line by an editor ('[be]', 'burst[s]', 'F[oe]minae') is an editorial insertion of sung text, not a marker: keep the enclosed word(s) (drop brackets) when they complete grammar or a ligature; markers come after the word/punctuation and are not words.
traditions: Byron (Coleridge ed., two-letter markers), Bullen anthologies (capital letters), Percy
examples: When neither fell, though both were loved.[bx]

entries.term: symbol footnote markers (asterisk, dagger, double dagger, section, parallels, pilcrow)
label_when: Attached to a word in a lyric line ('all we † call pith') or opening a note body at the foot of a song ('* The author was then ...'). Strip inline marker; drop note body.
sung_trap: Rows of asterisks ('*   *   *   *   *') are omission/section breaks (print domain), not footnotes. Asterisks replacing letters of a sung word ('d---d', 'the ****') mark a bowdlerised SUNG word: the word is sung, the stars are censorship. In hymnals '*' may mark a stanza to omit (performance direction).
traditions: All annotated printings, songsters, hymnals, PG texts
examples: Which extract, all we † call pith

entries.term: footnote bodies and PG footnote blocks
label_when: A prose sentence (often starting with the marker or '[Footnote') placed after a stanza or at the end of a song; spans until its closing bracket or blank line. Whole block is apparatus, even if it quotes verse.
sung_trap: A note may quote a lyric line; quoted lines inside the note are not additional sung text.
traditions: All PG transcriptions with notes; scholarly editions
examples: [3] Collins's Ode on the death of Thomson, the last written, I

label_when: Line-initial heading or bracket opener introducing prose; everything until the next song or stanza is apparatus.

A section heading plus everything under it until the next song/book division. Entries begin with a line or page reference ('19 ff.', 'l. 23', 'Page 33') or a headword, then comma or period and a gloss.
Line-initial 'NOTE' or 'Note' followed by ':' or '.--' or a period. The prose that follows, up to the next item or stanza, is also apparatus.
sung_trap: 'note' is a sung noun; the label is capitalised, line-initial, followed by '.', '.--' or ':' and then prose, not verse.

Glossary headwords are dialect lyric words ('bairn', 'gang', 'wee'), and notes quote lyric. The headword-comma-gloss shape and line references mark apparatus. An 'ADDENDUM' that contains actual verses is verse; check whether stanzas follow.
'Notes of victory,' (Hemans), 'Notes sweetly changing:' (Durfey) and 'my daily note' are sung: 'note' 202 and 'notes' 227 mid-line rows. A label needs ':' or '.--' right after the word at line start.
traditions: Scholarly editions, Burns, Moore's Irish Melodies (Moore's own notes), Scott's Minstrelsy, songsters
Burns/Scots editions, school-text editions, Percy, Child, Herrick (Hazlitt), Lovelace (Hazlitt), Watts
15 rows / 5 files (Shelley 9, C. Rossetti, Lear, Watts 'Transcriber's Note.', Lovelace). The prose bodies are larger.
examples: 19 ff. =thirds=, =sixths=, etc. For the musical terms see an unabridged dictionary.
Note.--I retain this little poem, not as historically accurate, but as  (eng_british_christina_rossetti.txt)

entries.term: Another version / later editions read / continuation in other copies
variants: The second stanza in the MS. runs
label_when: Heading or bracketed lead-in before an alternate text of the same song. The heading is apparatus; the text that follows is a variant witness and must be flagged so it is not counted as a second sung pass of the same song (decide per corpus policy whether the variant is kept as its own item).
sung_trap: 'Another' was staged as a TITLE in the corpus ('--- TITLE: Another'), where an Elizabethan/Herrick printing heads a second epigram 'Another'; that is a title, not lyric. Inside verse 'another' is sung.
traditions: Herrick, Burns, Percy, Child, Scott's Minstrelsy, Byron (Coleridge ed.)

entries.term: First published / Printed in / Originally appeared in
label_when: Bracketed or italic line after a title or a poem, or inside a headnote: '[MS. M. First published, _Morning Chronicle_, March 7, 1812'.
sung_trap: None realistic.
traditions: Scholarly editions, anthologies, newspaper verse

entries.term: Text of / Text from / From the MS. / Collated with
variants: The text is given from the folio MS., with corrections
From a copy in the British Museum
From a broadside in the Roxburghe Collection
Taken down from the singing of
label_when: Headnote or source line before or after a song stating its witness.
sung_trap: 'From the' begins many sung lines ('From the halls of Montezuma', 'From the deep and troubled waters', 'From the festal floor.'): apparatus only when followed by a source object (MS., copy, collection, singing of, recitation, broadside) and not by a verb-bearing clause; check also position (heading/end slot) and typography (italic, bracketed, smaller).
traditions: Percy, Ritson, Child, Scott, Motherwell, Christie, folk-song collections (Sharp, Baring-Gould, Kidson), Southern War Songs
examples: From the singing of Mr. H. Burstow, Horsham, 1893.

variants: right-margin bracketed word after wide spacing ('[ye')
margin word without bracket after 10+ spaces
label_when: Text separated from the lyric by a long run of spaces, often bracketed or opening with '[' but not closing, glossing a dialect word or summarising the stanza: '_Yea_ tower her up, as Danae was,   [ye'. Strip the margin text; keep the lyric line. Ancient-Mariner-type prose glosses (narrative summaries printed beside stanzas) are wholly apparatus.
sung_trap: Wide internal spacing also occurs in indented verse and in two-column sung layouts (e.g. call/response printed side by side); a gloss is a single word or short phrase that translates or summarises, often bracketed, not rhyming with the stanza.
traditions: Bullen/Arber Elizabethan editions, Early English Text Society texts, Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1817 gloss), Scots songbooks with margin glosses
examples: _Yea_ tower her up, as Danae was,                            [ye

label_when: A run of alphabetised lines in the form 'Headword(,|-|:) short English gloss.' usually after a song or at the back of a book. Every line is apparatus.
sung_trap: A gloss entry ('Bairn, child.') looks like a two-word verse fragment; tell by alphabetical sequence, one dialect headword + one English synonym, no meter, no rhyme with neighbours.
traditions: Burns (Kilmarnock and later), Scots songbooks, Irish and dialect songbooks, Barnes's Dorset poems, Child, Percy
examples: Fou, drunk.  Gang, go.  Gloamin', twilight.

label_when: A parenthesis or bracket immediately after a dialect or foreign word, containing an English equivalent, 'i.e.', '=' or a pronunciation hint. Remove the parenthetical; keep the sung word.
sung_trap: Parentheses also enclose SUNG asides and echoes ('(Oh, my darling!)', '(Hurrah!)', '(He did, he did!)' in music-hall and Tin Pan Alley songs): sung parentheses are metrical, often repeated, and in the singer's voice; glosses translate a single preceding word.
traditions: Scots, Irish, Welsh and dialect songs; translated hymns; minstrel songs with dialect glosses

entries.term: bracketed editorial insertions and supplied text
label_when: Square/angle brackets INSIDE a lyric line enclosing letters or words the editor supplied or a ligature expansion. The brackets are apparatus; the enclosed text is normally sung and kept. A bare '[?]' or '[word?]' expresses doubt: drop '[?]'.
sung_trap: The enclosed word IS lyric ('Whether the roses be your lips or your lips [be] the roses.'). Contrast stage directions in brackets ('[Exit.]', '[Aside]', other domain) and footnote markers ('[lh]', after the word).
traditions: Scholarly and anthology editions (Bullen, Percy, Child), PG transcriptions of Latin/ligatures
examples: Then burst[s] she forth in passion

label_when: Bracketed or Latin phrase marking missing text; alone on a line or replacing a line. Apparatus; it also tells you a stanza is incomplete (do not flag the short stanza as a lyric defect).
sung_trap: An ellipsis '...' inside a sung line can be the poet's own (trailing off); editorial ellipses are bracketed or stand alone as a line.
traditions: Percy Folio texts, Child, Burns fragments, Byron/Coleridge MSS., Elizabethan song-books
examples: or an HIATUS in the MS.  The latter reads:--

label_when: Bracketed or footnoted prose by a translator; signed Tr./Trans.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Hymnals (Latin, German, Greek translations), Gaelic/Welsh/Irish song translations, Lieder and opera translations, Greek Anthology
examples: [The Welsh word _hiraeth_ has no English equivalent.--Tr.]

label_when: A quotation printed above the poem (often italic, indented, in quotation marks) followed by a dash and an author/work name alone on the next line or right-aligned. Both the quotation and its credit are apparatus (the quote is not the poem's lyric).
sung_trap: Dash-initial lines occur INSIDE verse ('--Far in my own bright land!', '--Bird of the midnight's purple sky!' in the corpus): a sung dash line is a full clause or exclamation continuing the stanza's meter; a credit is a bare name or title + period, no verb, usually after a quotation and before the poem's first stanza.
traditions: Scott (invented 'Old Play' mottoes), Byron, Moore, Hemans, Victorian annuals, hymnal texts headed by scripture

label_when: Book abbreviation + chapter (arabic or roman) + verse, alone on a line above/below a hymn or after the first-line heading; may follow a scripture quotation epigraph.
A line made up of book abbreviations plus chapter and verse numbers, or 'Ver. N.' alone between stanzas of a psalm paraphrase, or a topic line ending in a reference.
sung_trap: 'Rev.' is also Reverend (credit apparatus) and 'Psalm' is sung inside lines ('sing a psalm'). A metrical psalm's TITLE ('Psalm 100') is a title (title domain). Book names (Isaiah, John) are sung inside hymn lines; references are recognisable by numerals and colons/roman numerals.
'John', 'Mark' and 'Job' are sung names and words. '_Matt._' is a Beggar's Opera speaker. 'Rev.' can be 'Reverend'. A reference needs digits after the book name.
traditions: Hymnals (Watts, Wesley, Sankey, Methodist, Episcopal), metrical psalters, gospel songbooks
137 rows / 1 file (eng_hymn_watts.txt). Expected in all scripture-indexed hymnals.

entries.term: cross-reference and index lines (contents, index of first lines)
label_when: Any line ending in a leader (dots/spaces) + page or hymn number, or a heading 'Contents'/'Index'. Index-of-first-lines entries reproduce REAL sung first lines but are duplicates and not lyric occurrences.
sung_trap: An index entry has identical words to a sung first line; tell by trailing page number/leader dots and alphabetical ordering among unrelated songs.
traditions: Hymnals, songsters, collected poems, anthologies, PG front/back matter
examples: Ae fond kiss, and then we sever .......... 112

label_when: Heading plus 'for ... read' lines with page/line references.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Early printed songbooks, scholarly editions

label_when: Bracketed caption line or caption under a plate; may quote a lyric line as caption text.
sung_trap: A caption quoting a lyric line duplicates sung text; drop it so the line is not counted twice.
traditions: Illustrated song books, Christmas carol books, children's song books, PG texts

label_when: Alone on a line directly below or above a title (or at the end), 'By' + a personal name, description or initials, no verb. Whole line apparatus. 'By Permission / By Desire / By Request' under a title are performance/publication notes, also apparatus.
sung_trap: 'By' begins countless sung lines ('By Goddes fay, by Goddes fay!', 'By the light of the silvery moon', 'By yon bonnie banks', 'By this, &c.'). Tell: a sung By-line continues into a clause or oath with meter and is inside a stanza; a credit By-line is followed only by a name/description, is set apart (blank lines, centring, caps), and occurs once per item.
traditions: All: anthologies, Southern War Songs, newspaper verse, sheet music covers, songsters

entries.term: Words by / Lyric by / Poetry by / Verses by / Book by / Libretto by
variants: Words by X; Music by Y
label_when: Credit line on sheet-music first page/cover or under a songster title. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Words by which the wretched are consoled?' (corpus) and 'Words from me are vainer still' are sung lines beginning with 'Words': credit lines have 'Words by' + PROPER NAME and nothing else (or '; Music by').
traditions: Victorian/Edwardian sheet music, Tin Pan Alley, music-hall, minstrel sheets, songsters, G&S libretti
examples: Words by Andrew B. Sterling.  Music by Harry Von Tilzer.

entries.term: Music by / Composed by / Melody by / Air by / Set to music by
label_when: Credit line on sheet music, libretto title page, songster heading or hymn credit; may include an opus number. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Composed by conventions and Counsellor Grey.' is a SUNG line in the corpus (a satirical political song): it is metrical, part of a stanza, and the 'by' object is not the song's composer. Check that the line sits inside a stanza and rhymes before excluding.
traditions: Sheet music, Tin Pan Alley, music hall, G&S, parlour ballads, hymnals ('Music by Lowell Mason')

entries.term: Written by / Writ by / Wrote by / Written and composed by
variants: Written by X. Composed by Y
label_when: Credit line under a title or at the head of a sheet/songster song ('Written by W. H. Archbold and Monroe H. Rosenfeld. Composed by Felix'). Apparatus, including any wrapped continuation line.
sung_trap: 'Written by' can open sung lines in hymns and ballads ('Written by the finger of God'); credit has a personal name object and no rhyme/meter.
traditions: Music hall, Tin Pan Alley, American songsters, broadsides ('Writ by a Prisoner')
examples: Written by W. H. Archbold and Monroe H. Rosenfeld. Composed by Felix

entries.term: Arranged by / Arr. / Harmonized by / accompaniment by
label_when: Credit line on sheet music or hymn tune credit. Apparatus.
sung_trap: None realistic; 'arranged' inside a sung line is a verb.
traditions: Sheet music, Tin Pan Alley 1920s ukulele editions, Moore's Irish Melodies ('symphonies and accompaniments by Sir John Stevenson'), hymnals, folk-song arrangements

entries.term: Adapted / Altered / Alt. / Imitated / Paraphrased / Founded on / After / Suggested by
label_when: Credit or source line under/over a title or after a poem ('Altered from an old English song.'). Apparatus. 'Parody on X' and 'Answer to X' lines are attribution/subtitle, not lyric.
sung_trap: 'After' and 'Altered' begin sung lines ('After the ball is over'); credit has a name/source object only, with no subject+verb clause.
traditions: Hymnals ('alt.' on almost every text), Burns (Altered from an old song), broadsides (answers and parodies), songsters, anthologies
examples: Altered from an old English song.

entries.term: Sung by / As sung by / Sung with great applause by / Introduced by / Featured by
variants: Sung by Mr. X at the Y Theatre
As sung by Mr. X at the Y
As sung by the Christy Minstrels
Sung by her with great éclat
As sung at the Theatres Royal
label_when: Credit line under a title (often across several lines naming a performer and venue). Entire block apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Sung by the angels', 'sung by the cherubim' can be sung in hymns; credit lines name a mortal performer/venue (Mr., Miss, Madame, theatre names) and are outside the stanza.
traditions: Music-hall sheets and songsters, American minstrel and variety songsters, Vauxhall and pleasure-garden songs (18th c.), Tin Pan Alley, Civil War songsters
examples: As sung by Mr. Sam Cowell at the Canterbury Hall.

entries.term: Written expressly for / Composed for / Written for the occasion
variants: Written at the request of the committee for
label_when: Line under the title or prefacing the song stating its commission/occasion. Apparatus (may wrap onto several lines).
sung_trap: 'For the Fourth of July' could be sung inside a patriotic stanza; occasion lines are outside the stanza and lack rhyme.
traditions: American patriotic and temperance songs, Masonic songs, Burns occasional verse, odes for anniversaries, hymn dedications
examples: Written at the request of the committee for the Constitutional

entries.term: Dedicated to / Inscribed to / Respectfully dedicated to
label_when: Line under the title on sheet music/poems, in smaller or italic type, followed by a name with honorific. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Dedication' can be a poem's TITLE (title domain), and a dedicatory POEM is verse to be counted if the corpus includes it. 'In memory of' begins sung elegy lines; the label is followed only by a name.
traditions: Sheet music, parlour ballads, Victorian collected poems, hymn tunes, Civil War memorial songs
examples: Respectfully dedicated to Miss Annie Lee.

entries.term: To X, Esq. (dedicatee line) and honorifics
label_when: A 'To ...' line under a title whose object is a real person with honorific or degree letters; honorific-laden name lines in credits ('son of Anthony Aucher, Esq., of'). Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'To X' is also a TITLE form ('To Anthea', 'To Electra' in the corpus; title domain) and 'To' opens sung lines. 'Esquire', 'Mister', 'the Colonel' are sung in comic and military songs ('Mr. Brown, Esquire'); sung forms are inside a metrical line and usually spelled out.
traditions: Elizabethan and Cavalier verse, Burns epistles, sheet music, 18th-c. songbooks

entries.term: signatures and initials at the end of a poem or note
label_when: Alone on the last line of a poem or note, usually right-aligned, often after a dash; initials or a full name ending in a period. Apparatus (corpus has 'R.B.' and 5x 'Robert Burns.').
sung_trap: (1) Speaker labels ('MARIA.', 'KARL.', 'SHE.', 'HE.', 'BOTH.') are character names in caps that PRECEDE speech and recur (speaker domain); signatures come once, after the text. (2) Hymnal meter tags 'C. M.', 'L. M.', 'S. M.', 'P. M.', 'H. M.', 'C. P. M.', '8s & 7s' look like initials but are meters (meter domain). (3) 'D. C.', 'D. S.' are da capo/dal segno. (4) Roman numerals 'I.', 'V.', 'X.' alone are stanza numbers. (5) A name line inside a stanza ('Robert Burns' addressed in a tribute song, 'Burns the same, where'er it goes') is sung.
traditions: Burns editions, newspaper and magazine verse, Victorian annuals, epistles, Southern War Songs

entries.term: bare author-name credit and bracketed name-with-dates
label_when: A personal name (often caps or small caps, often right-aligned) alone on a line after the poem (anthology convention, e.g. Stevenson's Home Book of Verse) or before it, with or without a date bracket.
sung_trap: Speaker labels and addressed names (see signatures entry). A personal name inside a stanza is sung.
traditions: Home Book of Verse, Oxford Book of English Verse, Golden Treasury, school anthologies, hymnals

label_when: Inside a by-line or credit bracket, or alone after a name. Apparatus.
sung_trap: Years are sung when spelled out in meter ('In eighteen hundred and forty-one'); digits in a credit bracket are not.
traditions: Anthologies, hymnals, Elizabethan song anthologies

label_when: Alone in the by-line or end slot, or in a credit line with 'arr.'. Apparatus (melody-origin forms overlap the tune/air domain).
sung_trap: 'unknown' is sung ('the unknown land', 'unknown to fame'); credit 'Unknown' is the entire line, capitalised, often bracketed with a century. 'Traditional' is rarely sung.
traditions: Home Book of Verse, Oxford Book, folk-song collections, spiritual and plantation-song books, hymnals

entries.term: Old Song / Old Ballad / old copy / from an old
label_when: Credit or source tag in the by-line/end slot or brackets; in Scots collections 'Old Song' at the end marks a non-Burns text. Apparatus. 'Old Song' can also be a TITLE (title domain) when it heads the item.
sung_trap: 'Old' opens many sung lines ('Old Dog Tray's ever faithful', 'Old Abe has got into a trap', 'Old Books are best' in the corpus): credit tags are 2-3 words, no verb, standalone or bracketed.
traditions: Scots songbooks (Herd, Johnson's Museum, Jacobite Relics), Percy, Ritson, Scott, songsters

variants: From THOMAS CAMPION's _Third Book of Airs_
label_when: A line naming a source book, play, opera, show or language, alone in the heading/credit slot or in parentheses after the title. Apparatus (the corpus already hoists these into '--- FROM:').
sung_trap: Same 'From the' trap as above: 'From the halls of Montezuma', 'From the morn to the evening he strays' are sung; source lines contain a work title (often italic/quoted), a language name, or a show name, and no clause verb.
traditions: Elizabethan song-book anthologies, Victorian poems from longer works, opera/operetta extracts, Tin Pan Alley show songs, translations
examples: From JOHN WILBYE's _Second Set of Madrigals_, 1609.

label_when: Classical author name or abbreviated work citation, usually caps or small caps, right-aligned or alone after a translated epigram/ode.
sung_trap: These names may appear inside a poem's verse as subjects; tag form is a lone name + period at the end.
traditions: Greek Anthology translations, Horatian imitations, 17th-18th c. epigram collections, Victorian classical anthologies

entries.term: hymnal credit block (author, date, translator, alteration)
label_when: One or two credit lines above or below a hymn text, usually split left (text author) and right (tune composer). Apparatus; scripture refs and meters nearby are separate entries/domains.
sung_trap: Hymn texts can name saints and authors ('St. Bernard', 'Wesley's hymns') inside lines; credits have date/abbrev structure.
traditions: Protestant hymnals, Catholic hymnals, Sunday-school and gospel songbooks (Sankey), Shape-note books (composer credits on tunes)

variants: Author of 'Silver Threads Among the Gold'
label_when: Appended to a by-line on sheet music/songsters/title pages. Apparatus.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Victorian sheet music, Tin Pan Alley, music hall, Victorian poetry title pages

entries.term: collection / source sigla and named collections
label_when: In headnotes, footnotes, source tags and credit lines; often followed by vol./p./No. Apparatus.
sung_trap: Very rare; 'museum', 'miscellany' are not sung in these contexts.
traditions: Burns editions, Scots collections, Percy/Child, Restoration drolleries, Bullen anthologies
examples: WITS INTERPRETER, 1662, p. 236.  But here "naked Besse,"

entries.term: Entered according to Act of Congress
variants: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1863, by X, in the Clerk's Office of the District Court of the United States for the Southern District of New York
Entered according to act of Congress A.D. 1862
Ent'd according to Act of Congress
Entered according to Act of Congress in the year 1852 by X in the Clerk's Office of the Dist. Court of the Eastern Dist. of Pa.
Entered according to Act of Congress, in the Office of the Librarian of Congress, at Washington
Entered, according to Act of Congress
Entered at the Library of Congress
label_when: Small-type notice at the foot of the first page of American sheet music or the verso of a songster title page; may wrap over 2-4 lines. Entire block apparatus.
sung_trap: None (a song about Congress would not use this formula).
traditions: American sheet music and songsters 1790-1870s; minstrel, Civil War, Confederate (Confederate imprints say 'Entered according to Act of Congress of the Confederate States')
examples: Entered according to Act of Congress, A.D. 1861, by A. E. Blackmar & Bro.

variants: Copyright MCMI by Francis, Day & Hunter
Copyright 1919 by Jerome H. Remick & Co., New York & Detroit
label_when: Foot of first page of sheet music, verso of title page, or under a song in a songster/anthology. Apparatus. Roman-numeral years (MCMV) belong to it.
sung_trap: Roman-numeral years (MDCCCXCIV, MCMV) must not be mistaken for stanza numerals; they start with M/MD/MC and follow 'Copyright' or a publisher.
traditions: Victorian/Edwardian sheet music, Tin Pan Alley, music hall, post-1870 songsters and anthologies, G&S vocal scores
examples: Copyright MCMVI by Jerome H. Remick & Co.

variants: The right of public performance is reserved
This song may be sung in public without fee or licence, except at Theatres and Music Halls, which rights are reserved
This song may be sung in public without fee or license
label_when: Small-type notice on sheet music, libretto title pages or under anthology poems. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'By permission' can be a sung phrase in a comic song; the notice is boilerplate in small type with publisher names.
traditions: British music-hall sheets (Francis, Day & Hunter, Reynolds), G&S (Chappell), Tin Pan Alley, Home Book of Verse credits
examples: This song may be sung in public without fee or licence, except at Theatres and Music Halls.

entries.term: Entered at Stationers' Hall / Licensed according to order / Imprimatur
variants: This may be printed, R. P.
label_when: Foot of a broadside/song sheet or below a title on engraved 18th-19th c. British songs. Apparatus.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: 17th-c. black-letter broadsides (Roxburghe, Pepys), 18th-c. engraved single songs ('Published as the Act directs'), Victorian British sheet music, G&S

label_when: Price + currency amount on a cover, title page, head/foot of a sheet or in a catalogue line. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'price' is sung ('the price of a pint', 'beyond price'), and amounts are sung in comic songs ('Only a penny a bunch', 'two-and-six'); an apparatus price line begins with 'Price'/'Pr.' and gives an amount in figures with s./d./cts./$, alone on its line.
traditions: Sheet music (US and UK), dime songsters, penny song books, chapbooks, broadsides

variants: Boston: Oliver Ditson & Co., 277 Washington St.
London: Francis, Day & Hunter, 142 Charing Cross Road
London: Chappell & Co., 50 New Bond St.
Jerome H. Remick & Co., New York-Detroit
Leo Feist, Inc., Feist Building, New York
label_when: Foot of cover/first page, title page, or a line after a songster song: a publisher name with address, city, or '&' and 'Co.'. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Published' is rarely sung; place names (Boston, New Orleans, Richmond) are sung inside stanzas, but in imprints they precede a colon and a firm name or street address.
traditions: American and British sheet music, Confederate imprints (Southern War Songs), songsters, hymnals, G&S libretti
examples: New York: Published by Firth, Pond & Co., No. 1 Franklin Square.

entries.term: Printed by / Printed for / Sold by (broadside and chapbook imprints)
variants: Printed and sold by J. Pitts, 6, Great St. Andrew Street, Seven Dials
H. Such, Printer & Publisher, 177, Union Street, Boro', S.E.
London, Printed for F. Coles, T. Vere, and J. Wright
Printed for P. Brooksby, at the Golden Ball in Pye-corner
label_when: Last line(s) of a broadside, slip song, garland or chapbook naming printer/seller and address. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Sold' is sung ('sold by auction', 'sold for a song', 'I sold my cow'); imprint lines have 'Printer'/'Printed'/'Sold by' + firm name + street address, typically after 'Finis' or a rule.
traditions: 17th-c. black-letter ballads, 18th-19th c. broadsides and slip songs (Seven Dials), Scottish chapbooks and garlands, American broadside publishers (De Marsan, Wrigley)
examples: J. Pitts, Printer, Wholesale Toy and Marble Warehouse, 6, Great St. Andrew Street, Seven Dials.

entries.term: plate numbers, engraver's and edition marks
label_when: Alphanumeric publisher initials + number at the foot of each page of sheet music or engraved songs; 'Made in U.S.A.' lines. Apparatus.
sung_trap: A lone number at page foot is a page/plate number, not a sung numeral.
traditions: Engraved sheet music 1800-1929, G&S vocal scores, Tin Pan Alley

label_when: On covers, title pages and running heads of serial songsters and penny song series, or as opus numbers on sheet music. Apparatus.
sung_trap: 'No.' + numeral above a song inside a hymnal or songster is the item number (numbering domain). 'Number' is sung ('Number one, number two' counting songs).
traditions: American dime songsters, Delaney's song books, Musical Bouquet, Victorian penny series, art-song sheet music

variants: Also published for Band and Orchestra
Sent post-paid on receipt of price
For sale by all music dealers
Music of this song can be had of
The music of this song is published by X, price 30 cents
On all phonograph records and player rolls
label_when: Back covers, inside covers, foot of songster songs, end of libretti; also a line directly after a songster song pointing to where its music can be bought. Apparatus.
sung_trap: Titles of other songs listed in adverts look like lyric fragments; they are lists of titles with prices or composer names.
traditions: Tin Pan Alley sheet music back pages, American songsters (music-available footnotes), music-hall sheets, hymnal back matter
examples: The music of this song is published by Wm. A. Pond & Co., price 40 cents.

variants: To the Tune of X, Pag. 104
label_when: Short line under a title or song in D'Urfey/Wit and Mirth or similar multi-volume collections, pointing to another volume and page (usually the tune). Apparatus.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Pills to Purge Melancholy, Wit and Mirth, Watts' Musical Miscellany, 18th-c. multi-volume songbooks

entries.term: datelines (place and/or date at end of poem)
label_when: Alone on the last line (or first line under the title) of a poem, often right-aligned or italic: place, comma, date; or bare year/month-year with a period. Apparatus (corpus: 'March, 1787', '1846.', '1628.').
sung_trap: Sung dates are spelled out and metrical ('In eighteen hundred and sixty-one', 'On the first of May'); sung place names sit in a clause ('Ayr, gently murmuring, sweetly flow'). A dateline is a noun phrase only, with digits, ending a poem.
traditions: Burns, Byron, Wordsworth, Hemans, Civil War and prison songs, newspaper verse, Victorian collected poems

label_when: A line consisting only of a year (arabic, roman, or with A.D./Anno), optionally parenthesised/bracketed, before or after a poem, or after an attribution.
sung_trap: Roman-numeral year vs stanza number: years start with M (MDCC...) and are long; stanza numerals are short (I-XXX, sometimes LXXXIII, CXV in long sequences). 'Anno Domini' can be sung inside a Latin carol line.
traditions: Collected poems, anthologies, broadsides ('Anno 1650'), Victorian sonnet sequences

entries.term: Written at / Composed in / Written on / Lines written (circumstance lines)
variants: Written on the blank leaf of
label_when: A subtitle or headnote under/over the title, or a line after the poem, stating where/when/why it was written. Apparatus. (When it IS the title, e.g. 'Lines Written in Early Spring', the title domain handles it.)
sung_trap: 'Written in' can begin a sung line ('Written in the stars', 'written in my heart'); circumstance lines name a place/date/object, have no rhyme, and stand outside the stanza.
traditions: Burns, Wordsworth, Byron, Romantic and Victorian poets, Civil War prison songs, hymn writers
examples: Written in a wrapper, enclosing a letter to Captain Grose.

entries.term: First produced at / first performed / original cast (libretti and show songs)
variants: First produced at the Savoy Theatre, March 14th, 1885
First produced at the Opera Comique
Performed at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden
As it is acted at the Theatre-Royal in Drury-Lane
label_when: Title-page or front-matter lines of libretti, ballad operas and show-song sheets. Apparatus (dramatis personae lists are speaker/cast apparatus).
sung_trap: None in lyric position; character names from the cast list reappear as speaker labels (speaker domain).
traditions: Gilbert & Sullivan libretti, ballad operas (Beggar's Opera), Victorian burlesques, Broadway/Tin Pan Alley show songs
examples: First produced at the Savoy Theatre, London, March 14th, 1885.

label_when: A line made only of digits or a lower-case roman numeral, with optional dashes, brackets or a trailing period, sitting between lines that otherwise run on (it often breaks a sentence or even a stanza). Also 'Page N'/'p. N' alone on a line.
sung_trap: Digits sung inside a line ('In eighteen hundred and 61', 'Number 9', "the spirit of '76", counting songs '1, 2, 3') always share the line with words. A digit-only line is never sung. A year alone on a line ('1846.') is a date of composition, not a page, but it is still not sung.
traditions: All OCR'd books, songsters, hymnals, IA/HathiTrust plain-text dumps; PG texts where proofers did not remove them
examples:
And the silver moon was gliding
                34
Above the milky way.

label_when: Bracketed or braced page number, either alone on a line or glued to the start or end of a line or mid-line (a PG HTML-to-text page anchor). Delete the token and keep the rest of the line.
sung_trap: None. A bracketed number is never sung. Do not mistake it for a footnote ref (see footnote entry): a page anchor is usually 'Pg' or a brace, or it has a space before it, or it starts the line, while a footnote ref is glued to the end of a word or to punctuation.
traditions: Project Gutenberg / Distributed Proofreaders HTML-derived texts, GITenberg
examples: {37}Sons of the South awake to glory,

label_when: A short line in caps or small caps, sometimes with a page number at either end, that repeats the book, section or current-song title at intervals of a page (roughly every 25 to 50 lines), whatever the stanza structure. It often sits mid-stanza or mid-sentence. Verso and recto heads alternate.
sung_trap: A refrain also recurs, but it recurs at stanza ends, it is part of the syntax or rhyme, and it does not carry a page number. A running head copies the book or section title and recurs at page-length intervals. If the repeated line equals the work's own title and falls inside a stanza, it is a head.
traditions: Songsters, collected poems, hymnals, IA OCR, unproofed PG/GITenberg

variants: Copyright, 1887, by J. J. Hood. Used by per.
Copyright MCMXII by Jerome H. Remick & Co.
label_when: A credit, copyright or permission line under a hymn or song that sheet music and gospel hymnals print at the foot of each page. It is alone on a line and usually starts 'Copyright', 'Used by', 'By per.', 'Printed in' or 'Made in'.
sung_trap: None. These lines are never sung.
traditions: Gospel hymnals 1870-1920 (Biglow & Main, Hope, Hood), Tin Pan Alley sheet music, music-hall songs, school songbooks
examples: Copyright, 1891, by Wm. J. Kirkpatrick. Used by per.

variants: single word at page foot repeating the next page's first word
label_when: A single word (or word fragment) alone on a line, often deeply indented or right-aligned, that is identical to the first word of the line after it. Mostly pre-1820 printings.
sung_trap: One-word sung lines ('Hark!', 'Alas!', 'Farewell!', 'O!') do not duplicate the next line's first word and usually carry exclamation punctuation. Catchword plus next line = duplicate; drop the catchword only.
traditions: Pre-1820 books: Herrick 1648, Lovelace, Percy's Reliques, Watts, 18th-c. songsters, chapbooks
examples:
And
And now the storm-blast came

label_when: At a page foot, alone on a line (sometimes beside a catchword): one or two capital letters (sometimes doubled, sometimes an asterisk) with an optional digit, or a volume prefix followed by a letter.
sung_trap: 'O', 'A' and 'I' alone on a line can be sung (interjection, article, pronoun), but they come with punctuation or syntax ('O!', 'I,'). A letter with a digit (A2) is never sung. When it is a bare capital, check whether it falls at a page boundary and whether the text before and after runs on without it.
traditions: Hand-press and 19th-c. books, broadsides with sheet signatures, chapbooks
examples:
Who would not be a soldier?
                    B2
Who would not be

label_when: In editions taken from manuscripts (Percy Folio, Child ballads, Bannatyne, Harleian), as a bracketed or alone-on-line leaf number in the text or beside the title.
sung_trap: The vocable 'fol' is sung: 'fol de rol', 'fol-lol-de-ra', 'fol de riddle'. 'fol' followed by a period and a number is a folio; 'fol' followed by vocables (de, lol, ral, la) is sung.
traditions: Percy Folio editions (Hales & Furnivall), Child, Ritson, early-ballad anthologies

label_when: An integer at the end of a lyric line after a run of 3 or more spaces or a tab, usually a multiple of 5 or 10, rising monotonically through the poem. Also line-initial '_185' or a number in brackets. Strip the number and keep the line.
sung_trap: Lines that genuinely end in a numeral ('in the year of '98', 'Engine 9') have it after a normal single space with punctuation agreement, and the number does not keep rising by 5 or 10 every 5 or 10 lines. Check the spacing gap and the arithmetic sequence.
traditions: Annotated school editions (Riverside, Golden Treasury), long poems, Whittier/Lowell anthologies, Swinburne/Rossetti editions, Browning, Coleridge
examples: In the gain or loss of one race all the rest have equal claim.     20

label_when: Alone on a line, or at the start of a line followed by period or space and a capitalised first word, at the head of each stanza. Hymnals print '1 When I survey...' with no period. Strip the number and keep the words.
sung_trap: Counting songs are mostly printed in words ('One man went to mow'); when digits are sung ('1 2 3 4 5, once I caught a fish alive') they run inside a line with commas and are not sequential stanza heads. A numbered line inside a NOTES block ('3. Seven sheets, Canto I...') is a note, not a stanza.
traditions: Hymnals, gospel songbooks, school songbooks, songsters, sheet-music verse 1/verse 2, broadsides
examples: 2 Were the whole realm of nature mine,

entries.term: Roman numeral on a line (stanza/section number)
label_when: A line made only of a valid roman numeral (regex ^\s*[MDCLXVI]+\.?\s*$, or the lower-case form), optionally centred, that falls between stanzas and increments through the file. Section headings with a word ('Part II.', 'Canto III.', 'Book I', 'Fytte the First', 'Sonnet XII', 'Pause I.') belong to the section-name domain but are labelled the same way.
sung_trap: 'I' alone on a line can be the pronoun in dialogue ('Who killed Cock Robin? / I, said the Sparrow'), but then it has a comma or other text. 'MI'/'Mi' (a valid roman 1001) is a solmization syllable, and 'MIX', 'DIX', 'LI' and 'DI' parse as roman numerals but are words or syllables. Treat as numeral only when it is bare (optional period) and belongs to an incrementing I, II, III... series.
traditions: Odes, sonnet sequences, long ballads, collected poems (Swinburne, Tennyson, Rossetti), Child ballad fyttes, Watts/Wesley hymn books
examples:
XXIV
And I had done a hellish thing,

label_when: A line with no letters (only asterisks, dashes, underscores, tildes, equals, plus or arrows) or only a dingbat, or a bracketed ornament word. It marks the end of a section or of a song, a page break, or omitted text.
sung_trap: Censored oaths keep letters attached ('D—n', 'G-d', 'd----d', 'the d---l', 'what the ****') and are sung as the word. Dashes inside a line ('O--', 'Fears-', 'resolved--') are sung pauses or punctuation. Only a line with no word characters (or only an ornament word in brackets) is a separator.
traditions: Everywhere: PG thought-break convention, songsters, hymnals, collected poems; corpus already annotates '<-------------------->' and '*       *       *'

entries.term: Omission marks (dotted line / stars standing for omitted verses)
label_when: A line made only of dots, spaced dots or asterisks inside a song, or a bracketed or parenthesised statement that lines were left out.
sung_trap: An ellipsis attached to words is a sung hesitation or trailing-off and stays lyric ('. . . So he wove her wailing', 'Is . . . my Love for you.', "I love the winter dearly too, . . . but then"). Only a dots-only line (nothing to sing) is apparatus.
traditions: Anthologies, Ingelow/Rossetti/Barrett Browning editions, excerpted hymns, school readers, newspaper reprints

label_when: 'etc.' or '&c.' at the end of a line that repeats the opening words of a chorus or of an earlier line. The printer is telling the singer to carry on with text already given. Strip the 'etc.' token; the remaining incipit is only a cue, not a newly sung line, so it should not count as new lyric.
sung_trap: '&' alone is 'and', and is sung. In a lyric, 'etc.' or '&c.' is never sung except as comic patter that says the word aloud ('and so on, et cetera'), and then it is spelled out.
traditions: Songsters, war songbooks, campaign songsters, hymnals with refrain cues, broadsides
examples: They have gone from us forever, etc.

label_when: 'Do.' (capital D, period) or 'Ditto' alone on a line or at the end of a line, or a row of ditto ticks, standing for the line or words above.
sung_trap: 'Do' is a sung verb ('Do not forsake me') and a sol-fa syllable. The printer's 'Do.' is alone on its line or follows 'Chorus—', has a period, and does not fit the grammar.
traditions: Songsters, broadsides, campaign songbooks, music-hall song sheets

variants: 1. A General Song of Praise to God.
label_when: A 'Contents'/'The Table' heading and the list that follows it: titles in print order, each ending in a page number (with dot leaders or a comma) or each starting with an item number, unrhymed, no stanza shape. 'The End of the Table.' closes an 18th-c. contents list.
sung_trap: The entries are titles of songs elsewhere in the book, so they match title words. A real song never ends a line with a dot leader and a page number. When numbered entries have no page numbers (Watts' 'The TABLE.'), the cue is position: after 'The End.' or before the first song, plus a run of title-like lines.
traditions: All books; songsters print contents on the back cover; Watts' Divine Songs 'The TABLE.' leaks in eng_hymn_watts.txt
examples:
The TABLE.
1. A General Song of Praise to God.

entries.term: Index of first lines / titles / tunes / authors / subjects / texts
variants: Index of First Lines and Titles
A mighty fortress is our God . . . 266
label_when: A back-matter list under an INDEX heading: alphabetised lines, each ending in a hymn or page number, often with dot leaders, sometimes with a meter abbreviation.
sung_trap: A first-line index entry IS a verbatim lyric line, but it is a duplicate of a line counted in the body. It is apparatus because of position (after the last song, alphabetical order, a trailing number). Never count it as sung.
traditions: Hymnals (always), gospel songbooks, collected poems, Golden Treasury, songsters

label_when: A front-matter heading and its entries, each giving a picture caption and a page or position word ('Frontispiece', 'To face p. 24').
sung_trap: 'Vignette' and 'frontispiece' do occur in verse ('In bright vignettes, and each complete', 'On frontispiece or title-page'), but inside a rhymed line with syntax. Apparatus entries end in a page number or 'Frontispiece' and sit under the list heading.
traditions: Illustrated gift-book editions (Longfellow, Whittier, Tennyson), illustrated songbooks, nursery-rhyme collections

label_when: Square brackets starting with Illustration, Picture, Image, Graphic, Engraving, Portrait or Photograph. They can span several lines until the closing bracket. Remove all of it.
sung_trap: Captions often quote a lyric line ('[Illustration: "Under the spreading chestnut tree"]'). The quote is a duplicate of the body text; never count it. A sung line never begins with '[Illustration'.
traditions: Project Gutenberg / DP texts, GITenberg

variants: Drawn by F. O. C. Darley
label_when: A short line, often a quoted lyric line, followed by '--Page N' or 'p. N', or a line naming an artist with 'Engraved by', 'Drawn by', 'del.', 'sculp.' or 'pinx.'. It is not part of any stanza.
sung_trap: The quoted line is lyric text, but it occurs again in the body. The page reference or artist credit marks this copy as a caption. 'Drawn by' inside a rhymed line ('Drawn by a rat-tailed, ewe-necked bay') is sung.
traditions: Illustrated poetry editions, gift books, illustrated songsters and sheet-music covers

label_when: The first word of a poem or stanza broken by a large decorative capital: a single capital alone on a line or detached by a space, or a bracketed letter, or a first word missing its first letter. Rejoin it; do not count the lone letter as a line.
sung_trap: 'O' or 'A' alone can be sung ('O / say can you see' never happens in print, but 'O!' does). Check whether letter plus next word makes a dictionary word ('T' + 'HE' = 'THE'). If it does, it is a drop cap.
traditions: Illustrated editions, Kelmscott/Arts-and-Crafts printings, 18th-c. books, PG texts that kept the separated initial
examples:
W
HEN the hounds of spring are on winter's traces

label_when: Not a label in itself. Caps on the first word or words of a poem or stanza, followed by lower case, are small caps rendered as capitals: normalise the case and keep the words as sung. Capitals on a whole short line that ends in a period ('CHORUS.', 'FANNY.') are a heading or speaker label (other domains).
sung_trap: The capitalised opening words ARE sung. Do not strip them as a heading. Test: the caps run continues straight into lower-case words on the same line, with no period after the caps.
traditions: PG plain-text renderings of nearly all 19th-c. books; hymnals; libretti (speaker names)
examples: THE curfew tolls the knell of parting day,

label_when: Text wrapped in '=' (or '+', '~' or '#' in some DP outputs). This is a typeface marker: strip the delimiters. Its usual position, as a bold headword at the start of a note ('=Sir Olaf=. A conventional name...'), shows the line is in a NOTES or GLOSSARY section and is therefore apparatus.
sung_trap: The words inside can be sung if the marked span sits inside a lyric line. The markup itself is never sung. A line that starts with a =headword= followed by period and prose is a note; in the corpus such notes have been staged as TITLE records.
traditions: PG school editions with notes (Riverside Literature Series, Macmillan Pocket Classics), DP texts
examples: =clavichord=. An instrument of the type of the piano

label_when: Underscores (or slashes, asterisks or <i> tags) around words. Strip the markers. Whole-line italic in parentheses or after a dash is usually a direction, tune name or source credit (other domains decide by the words).
sung_trap: Italics also mark sung emphasis, refrains, foreign phrases and quoted speech ('_once_ more', '_Right about wheel!_'), all of which are sung. Markup alone never decides: judge by content.
traditions: Every PG text, GITenberg markdown, war songbooks, Herrick/Lovelace editions with italic names
examples: Then rise, ye sons of free-born sires, _once_ more! and freedom's won,

label_when: A '{' or '}' at line end, or in a column across 2 to 3 lines, renders a printed brace. It groups lines for a repeat, a triplet or simultaneous voices. Strip the brace. Any words after it ('Twice', 'bis', 'Repeat') are a repeat cue (other domain).
sung_trap: None. Braces are never sung. 'bis' after a brace is a repeat cue; 'bis' in OCR is often a misread 'his' (see OCR entry).
traditions: Songsters, glee and catch books, Augustan poetry editions, hymnals, libretti (ensemble numbers)
examples:
Hurrah! hurrah! for Southern rights, hurrah! }
Hurrah! for the Bonnie Blue Flag            } Twice.

label_when: A bracketed or superscript number or letter, or a reference symbol, glued to the end of a word, title or punctuation mark. Strip the token and keep the line.
sung_trap: A bracketed lower-case WORD that fits the grammar ('Then [he] rode on') is an editor supplying missing lyric. Keep the word and drop only the brackets. An asterisk standing for a censored word ('D*** him') is a sung word.
traditions: PG texts of annotated editions (Hemans, Moore, Scott, Burns, Poe), anthologies; corpus: 'darksome death?[8]', 'Dark Isle's[160]', 'ISRAFEL. [1]'
examples: From the Dark Isle's[160] mystic bowers,

label_when: A '[Footnote' bracket (it can span many lines until ']'), or a line starting with a number, letter or symbol and period followed by prose glossing a word or giving a source ('--_Memoir_, p. 197'), usually after the stanza or in an end section.
sung_trap: Footnotes often quote lyric lines or variant readings. These are not sung occurrences. Prose without metre, citations ('p. 84', 'ed. 1669'), and a matching reference mark upstream are the tests.
traditions: Annotated editions, PG, war songbooks, Percy/Child ballad editions, Burns editions
examples: [Footnote 3: Written at the request of a friend.--_Memoir_, p. 84.]

variants: multi-line sidenote ending with ']' several lines later
label_when: Square brackets beginning 'Sidenote', 'Margin' or 'Gloss', running until the closing bracket, perhaps several lines on. Remove the whole span, including continuation lines.
sung_trap: Coleridge's Ancient Mariner glosses are authorial, but they are prose and were not recited with the verse. Sidenote dates in war songbooks are dates of events. Neither is lyric. The continuation lines have no brackets of their own, so track the open bracket.
traditions: Ancient Mariner (1817 gloss), historical ballad collections, war-song anthologies with event dates; present in the corpus
examples:
[Sidenote: The ancient Mariner beholdeth a sign in the element afar
off.]

variants: LONDON: / PRINTED FOR J. JOHNSON, IN ST. PAUL'S CHURCH-YARD. / 1798.
label_when: Short centred lines in capitals before the first song: book title broken over several lines, editor and illustrator credits, edition statement, and a place: publisher, year imprint (the year is often a roman numeral). A half-title is the bare book or division title again, alone on a line (e.g. 'Hymns.' after 'End of the First Book.' in Watts).
sung_trap: Title fragments ('OF THE', 'SONGS') look like lyric fragments. Tell them apart by capitals, centring, absence of rhyme or metre, the place:publisher line, and position before the first song or at a division. A real dedicatory poem (e.g. Stevenson's 'From Her Boy') is verse and is kept.
traditions: Every printed book; GITenberg front matter; corpus annotations already include Clough, Kemble, E. B. Browning title pages
examples:
LYRICAL BALLADS,
WITH A FEW OTHER POEMS.
LONDON:
PRINTED FOR J. & A. ARCH, GRACECHURCH-STREET.
1798.

variants: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1863, by ..., in the Clerk's Office of the District Court of ...
This song may be sung in public without fee or license, except at theatres and moving picture houses.
Published by permission of the proprietors.
label_when: Prose legal formulas, alone on a line or a short paragraph, on the verso of the title page, at the foot of sheet music, or under a hymn.
sung_trap: None. These are never sung.
traditions: US 19th-c. books and sheet music, British music-hall sheets, Tin Pan Alley, gospel hymnals, G&S libretti ('Entered at Stationers' Hall')
examples: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1862, by A. E. Blackmar & Bro.

variants: Printed by Ballantyne, Hanson & Co. Edinburgh & London
Chiswick Press: Printed by Charles Whittingham
Printed and sold by J. Pitts, 6, Great St. Andrew Street, Seven Dials
H. De Marsan, Publisher, 54 Chatham St., N. Y.
Johnson, Song Publisher, 7 N. Tenth St., Phila.
label_when: A line naming a printer or publisher with an address or a 'Printed by/for' or 'Sold by' formula. It sits at the foot of a broadside (often in a border box), after 'THE END', or on the last page.
sung_trap: Broadside ballads sometimes name places and tradesmen in the lyric ('in Seven Dials there lived a maid'). An imprint has a street number and 'Printer'/'Publisher'/'Sold by' and no metre.
traditions: Broadsides (Catnach, Pitts, De Marsan, Wrigley, Such), chapbooks, songsters, Victorian books
examples: J. Wrigley, Publisher of Songs, Ballads, and Toy Books, 27 Chatham St., N.Y.

variants: Sent post-paid on receipt of price.
De Witt's Song and Joke Book
Containing all the latest and most popular songs
Copies of this song, and 600 others, can be had at
Also published for Band and Orchestra
label_when: Commercial prose on covers, flyleaves, back pages or song headings: prices, series titles, performer credits ('Sung by', 'Introduced by'), catalogue lists.
sung_trap: Back-cover 'thematic' catalogues in sheet music and songsters print the opening verse or chorus of OTHER songs. Those are real lyric lines, but of a different item, shown as an advertisement. Exclude them from the current song and do not stage them as songs. 'As sung by' and 'dedicated to' credits are never sung.
traditions: Tin Pan Alley and music-hall sheet music, dime songsters, Beadle/De Witt/Wehman series, Victorian ballad sheets, hymnal back pages
examples: Price 10 Cents. Sent post-paid on receipt of price.

label_when: An alphanumeric code at the foot of every sheet-music page: publisher initials plus plate number, and often '-N' for the page within the song.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Tin Pan Alley, music-hall and parlour sheet music, G&S vocal scores (Chappell), hymn octavos

entries.term: End marker (FINIS / The End / End of Vol.)
variants: Fine (sheet-music end of a D.C. repeat)
label_when: Alone on a line (often centred and in caps, with a period) after the last stanza of a song, section, volume or book. Libretto 'CURTAIN' and 'END OF ACT' alone on a line.
Alone, at the end of an item, book or file. In sheet music 'Fine' over the staff marks the D.C. end point.
sung_trap: 'Fine' is common in lyrics as an adjective ('Fine weather on his brow', 'Fine Apples and Pears to sell', 'Fine knacks for ladies') and is only the musical end mark when it stands alone ('Fine.', '_Fine._'), often after 'D.C. al'. 'The end' can be sung ('The end is easily foretold', 'The end of joy and all prosperitee'). In Holmes's 'One-Hoss Shay' the line 'End of the wonderful one-hoss shay.' is the poem's own penultimate line (it rhymes with 'say'). Apparatus end markers have no rhyme partner, no metre and nothing after them in the same song. 'Thus endeth the first fytte' in minstrel ballads is sometimes printed by the editor and sometimes rhymes inside the stanza: keep it only if it completes the stanza's rhyme scheme.

'fine' is sung in 282 mid-line rows / 120 files and line-initially in 'Fine Apples and Pears to sell:' (Durfey). 'End in a large reward.' (Watts) and 'End this murderous holocaust' are sung. Herrick's '_End._' is a SPEAKER (Endymion).
traditions: Every printed book; Watts (corpus: 'End of the First Book.', 'The End.'); Percy/Child (fytte ends); 17th-c. books (FINIS); libretti (CURTAIN); sheet music (Fine)
5 rows / 2 files (Watts 4, Holmes 1).
examples:
End of the Second Book.
Hymns.
Book 3.

label_when: Alone on a line, usually parenthesised or italic, at page or column ends in serials, songsters and sheet music. 'V.S.' marks a fast page turn in sheet music.
sung_trap: 'Over' and 'turn' are common sung words ('Over the hills', 'Turn, turn, turn'). They are apparatus only when alone on a line, parenthesised or abbreviated (P.T.O., V.S.) and not part of the syntax.
traditions: Newspaper and magazine poetry, songsters, sheet music, serialised long poems

variants: line repeated before and after a page break
stanza from a facing column interleaved
stanza out of order after a plate
label_when: There is no label word. It shows as an exact duplicate line next to a page-break artifact (page number, running head), or as two unrelated rhyme schemes alternating line by line, or as a wide internal gap splitting a line into two independent halves. Flag rather than count.
sung_trap: Sung refrains and incremental repetition duplicate lines legitimately ('Lord Randal, my son' / 'Mother, make my bed soon'). A page-break duplicate is a single adjacent repeat with no structural place and usually sits next to a page number or head. Two-column songster OCR alternates lines of two different songs, which breaks both rhyme chains.
traditions: IA/HathiTrust OCR of songsters and newspapers printed in 2 to 3 columns, hymnals with words set between staves
examples:
The stars were shining brightly, and the sky was calm and blue,
The stars were shining brightly, and the sky was calm and blue,

variants:
1. Come, thou Fount of ev-'ry bless-ing,
2. Here I raise mine Eb-en-e-zer,
3. O to grace how great a debt-or
syllable hyphens: 'bless - ing', 'Hal - le - lu - jah', 'ev - 'ry'
label_when: Lines transcribed from music where all stanzas run under the notes: consecutive lines start with 1., 2., 3. and belong to different stanzas, and words are split into syllables with spaced hyphens and underscores. Rejoin the syllables, strip the extender underscores and dashes, and regroup the lines by stanza number.
sung_trap: The syllables ARE sung, so the words are lyric; only the hyphens, underscores and interleaving are artifacts. 'Ah', 'O' and 'la' on melismas are real sung vocables; strip only the trailing underscores or dashes.
traditions: Hymnals and gospel songbooks with music, sheet music (verse 1/verse 2 under the staff), G&S vocal scores, school songbooks
examples: Glo - - - - - ri - a in ex - cel - sis De - o

variants:
harvest-seed--as fathers bled, their sons must
    bleed,
Fears- (single hyphen standing for an em dash)
label_when: (a) A printer's hyphen at a line end with the remainder starting the next line (often lower case). Join the word; these are rare in verse, common in notes and prose. (b) A turnover (runover): an over-long verse line whose last word or words are carried to the next line, deeply indented, right-aligned or preceded by '['. Rejoin it to the line above; it is not a separate sung line.
sung_trap: Comic split rhymes are deliberate and sung exactly as broken ('I'm sure you couldn't do it, e-', 'Yet I wish that I could modi-'). Gilbert, Calverley and music-hall patter break words at the rhyme position, and the fragment rhymes with its partner line. Compounds ('TO-DAY', 'over-') and a single hyphen used for a dash ('Fears-', 'anguish-') are sung punctuation. A turnover is detectable because the stanza's other lines are short, the carried piece is deeply indented, and the rhyme or metre only works when it is rejoined.
traditions: All printings; turnovers are common in long-line poems (Whittier, Lowell, Swinburne, Southern war songs); comic splits occur in G&S, Calverley, music hall
examples:
What tho' they count as harvest-seed--as fathers bled, their sons must
    bleed,

variants: stray single letters: i, l, j, ' , ~, |, •, ■
label_when: There is no label word, but these tokens damage the lyric count: digits inside words, non-words that become real words under the standard swaps, or lone punctuation or speck characters on a line. Repair or flag; a speck-only line is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'O' the interjection is sung, and OCR often renders it as the digit '0' ('0 say can you see'), so restore the O. 'bis' is both an OCR misread of 'his' and the Latin repeat cue: as a repeat cue it follows a brace or stands alone ('bis.'), while 'bis' before a noun ('bis heart') is 'his'. 'l' alone can be the end of a broken word. Never count punctuation-only lines.
traditions: IA/HathiTrust/Google OCR, unproofed GITenberg, early PG (pre-2000) texts
examples: 0 Tlie stars were sbining brightly in l862,

entries.term: Long s (ſ) and its OCR f-substitution
label_when: There is no label word; it is a spelling artifact in pre-1800 printings or their facsimile transcriptions. Normalise ſ to s, and an OCR 'f' to 's' where the f-reading is a non-word.
sung_trap: Real f-words exist and pair with s-words: fame/same, fold/sold, fell/sell, fat/sat, fit/sit, fin/sin, feat/seat, fore/sore, fought/sought, foul/soul, fold/sold, fang/sang, find/sind. Settle these by the rhyme partner and context; never by blanket substitution. ſ never appears word-finally, so an 'f' at the end of a word is a real f.
traditions: 17th-18th-c. books and broadsides (Herrick 1648, Lovelace, Watts first editions, ballad operas, Percy 1765), facsimile transcriptions, ECCO/EEBO-derived text
examples: Fair daffadills, we weep to fee

label_when: There is no label word; these are character-level. Decompose typographic ligatures (ﬁ to fi), turn PG bracket notation ([ae], [oe]) into letters, and repair dropped-ligature gaps.
sung_trap: æ and œ in Cæsar, pæan, æonian, Mænad are genuine period spellings of sung words. Keep them as text and fold them to ae/oe for tokenising and pronunciation; they are not apparatus.
traditions: PG texts (Unicode and bracket notations), OCR of 19th-c. books, classical-diction poetry (Swinburne, Tennyson, Bryant)

label_when: Square-bracket codes from DP proofing or transliteration conventions, inline or alone on a line. '/*' and '*/' alone on a line delimit poetry blocks in raw DP or GITenberg sources. Strip the codes; if a transliterated word stood in the lyric, keep its sound only when it can be recovered.
sung_trap: A bracketed editorial word that completes the grammar ('[and]') is supplied lyric: keep the word. '[sic]' is never sung.
traditions: Project Gutenberg, Distributed Proofreaders, GITenberg raw files

variants: Obvious typographical errors have been corrected.
label_when: A line or block starting 'Transcriber', 'Errata' or 'Corrigenda', or a list of 'p. N, X changed to Y' or 'for X read Y' entries. It may sit at the start or end of a text, or be inlined in parentheses inside a TITLE or lyric line (as in the corpus).
sung_trap: Errata and change lists quote lyric words; the 'for X read Y' and 'changed to' syntax marks them as apparatus. A corrected word should go into the lyric, not the note.
traditions: Project Gutenberg, DP, GITenberg; old books with errata slips; corpus: eng_hymn_watts.txt 'Transcriber's Note.' and the TITLE 'Christ the King at his table, Cant. (Transcriber's Note'
examples:
Transcriber's Note.
Obvious printer's errors have been silently corrected.

entries.term: Project Gutenberg header / footer / licence boilerplate
variants: The Project Gutenberg EBook of Southern War Songs, by W. L. Fagan
This eBook is for the use of anyone anywhere at no cost and with almost no restrictions whatsoever.
This eBook is for the use of anyone anywhere in the United States and most other parts of the world
Title: / Author: / Editor: / Release Date: / Posting Date: / Last Updated: / Language: English / Character set encoding: ISO-8859-1
*** START OF THIS PROJECT GUTENBERG EBOOK SOUTHERN WAR SONGS ***
*** START OF THE PROJECT GUTENBERG EBOOK ...
*** END OF THIS PROJECT GUTENBERG EBOOK ... ***
End of the Project Gutenberg EBook of ...
Updated editions will replace the previous one--the old editions will be renamed.
Section 1. General Terms of Use and Redistributing Project Gutenberg-tm electronic works
*END*THE SMALL PRINT! FOR PUBLIC DOMAIN ETEXTS*
label_when: Any line containing 'Project Gutenberg', 'Gutenberg-tm', 'EBook #', or the START/END triple-asterisk banners, plus everything outside those banners. Field-label lines (Title:, Author:, Release Date:) above the START banner.
sung_trap: 'start' and 'end' are sung words. The PG banners always say 'PROJECT GUTENBERG' and sit inside '***'. Nothing outside the START/END pair is lyric.
traditions: Project Gutenberg, GITenberg (identical text files)
examples: *** END OF THIS PROJECT GUTENBERG EBOOK SOUTHERN WAR SONGS ***

variants: Produced by Charles Aldarondo and the Online Distributed Proofreading Team at http://www.pgdp.net
(This file was produced from images generously made available by The Internet Archive/American Libraries.)
Produced from page images provided by the Internet Archive
This book was produced from scanned images of public domain material
label_when: A line starting 'Produced by', 'E-text prepared', 'Transcribed from' or 'HTML version', or a parenthesised 'This file was produced from images' notice, near the top of a PG text.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Project Gutenberg, DP, GITenberg
examples: Produced by David Garcia and the Online Distributed Proofreading Team

variants: This book is part of the GITenberg project
label_when: Lines from repository metadata, Markdown or HTML markup, HTML entities, file paths and URLs that appear when a GITenberg repo or a PG HTML file is staged instead of the .txt. Strip tags and entities (decoding & to '&', — to an em dash) and drop metadata lines.
sung_trap: A decoded entity ('&') is sung as 'and'. Markup itself is never sung.
traditions: GITenberg repos, PG HTML editions, web-scraped songbook pages
examples: Sons of the South awake to glory,

variants: Digitized by the Internet Archive in 2008 with funding from Microsoft Corporation
Generated for ... on 2023-01-01 GMT / Public Domain, Google-digitized / http://www.hathitrust.org/access_use#pd-google
label_when: A digitizer or library line, often repeated on every page in IA/HathiTrust/Google plain-text OCR, or an isolated bookplate or stamp text. Drop it wherever it appears.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Internet Archive, HathiTrust, Google Books OCR; library copies of songsters and hymnals

label_when: A bracketed note, alone on a line, that a page was blank.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: PG/DP, IA

label_when: Bracketed statements, or star rows inside a ballad, recording physical loss in a manuscript or broadside. They are not sung, and they mean the stanza count and rhyme chain have a hole.
sung_trap: Not sung. Do not repair rhyme across the gap or count the marker as a line.
traditions: Percy Folio, Child ballads, Bannatyne/Maitland editions, broadside facsimiles

variants: To ..., this volume is respectfully inscribed
label_when: A heading followed by prose paragraphs: long unbroken lines, no stanza shape, no rhyme.
sung_trap: 'TO THE READER', 'DEDICATION' and 'PROEM' often head a poem (Herrick, Lovelace, Longfellow 'Proem'), and the corpus has 'TO THE READER.' as a heading. If verse lines (lineated, metrical, rhymed) follow, it is a poem title and the poem is lyric. Only the prose version is apparatus.
traditions: Every book; Lyrical Ballads 'Advertisement'; Herrick/Lovelace; Watts 'Preface'; songster introductions
examples:
ADVERTISEMENT.
The majority of the following poems are to be considered as experiments.

entries.term: Printed date / place line at foot of a poem
label_when: Alone on a line, usually italic or right-aligned, directly after the last stanza (sometimes before the first). It is a date or a place-and-date. Corpus examples: '1846.', '1628.'.
sung_trap: Years are sung inside lines ('In eighteen hundred and sixty-one', "in the year of '98"). A date line has no verb, sits alone at the poem's edge, and is often italic.
traditions: Collected poems (Whittier, Longfellow, Wordsworth), war songbooks, hymn collections

variants: | C C | G G | A A | G - |
label_when: Bracketed music placeholders, PG audio or score links, ABC-notation header lines (single letter + colon) and tune lines, bar lines, time signatures, or note-letter sequences with bars, apostrophes and commas for octaves. Delete them; they contain no lyric.
sung_trap: Single note letters can collide with the article 'A' and the pronoun 'I' only in a bare letter line. A notation line is made of letters A to G (or a to g) with |, :, numbers, apostrophes or commas, and has no words. Meter abbreviations (C.M., L.M., 8.7.8.7.) and key lines are a different domain (meter-or-tune) but are also non-lyric.
