traditions: PG music-bearing ebooks (hymns, folk-song collections, nursery songs with scores), ABC-transcribed folk tunes, school songbooks

variants: Tune Uke: A D F# B
label_when: A line made only of chord tokens (regex [A-G][#b]?(m|maj|min|dim|aug|sus|add)?[0-9]*(/[A-G][#b]?)?) separated by spaces, two or more of them, no other words, placed above a lyric line. Also inline bracketed chords inside a lyric line (strip the brackets and contents). Ukulele tuning and 'vamp' lines from 1920s sheet music.
sung_trap: 'Am' is sung in 'Am I blue?' and 'A' and 'I' are words, but a sung line contains other words. Treat a line as chords only when every token parses as a chord. 'Vamp till ready' is never sung.
traditions: 1920s Tin Pan Alley sheet music (ukulele arrangements), later songbooks, folk-song collections with guitar chords
examples:
G              D7             G
In the shade of the old apple tree

variants: d' (high octave), s, (low octave), r1, t1
Doh Ray Me Fah Soh Lah Te
do re mi fa sol la si
do re mi fa so la ti
ut re mi fa sol la
label_when: Lines of single or double-letter sol-fa initials separated by colons, bar strokes, dots and dashes, with octave marks; Curwen key lines ('Key G', 'Doh is G', 'M. 72'). Also a scale run of syllables printed as a reference row above or below the words.
sung_trap: Solmization syllables are sometimes the lyric: rounds and catches that sing 'Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la', singing-school songs ('Do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si, do, sing the scale'), and comic songs that sing the scale. 'Fa la la' (madrigal refrain), 'fal lal la', 'fol de rol', 'tol de rol', 'la la la', 'derry down', 'hey nonny' are sung vocables (the corpus has about 71 such lines) and are NEVER notation. Notation uses single-letter initials (d r m f s l t) with colons or bars, or a bare scale row with no rhyme and no repetition in parallel stanzas. Sung syllables are full syllables in a lineated, rhymed or refrain position and recur in every stanza.
traditions: Curwen tonic sol-fa hymnals and school songbooks (Britain, 1850-1920), American singing-school tunebooks, Elizabethan madrigal and catch collections (sung 'fa la')

label_when: Never a label. Listed here so separator or omission rules do not swallow them: dashes or asterisks attached to letters inside a lyric line stand for a sung word.
sung_trap: These ARE sung (as the word, or as a blank the singer fills). Only treat a dash or asterisk run as apparatus when it fills the whole line with no letters.
traditions: Broadsides, songsters, music-hall songs, Burns, 18th-c. satire

entries.term: Early-modern spelling conventions (not apparatus, but normalise)
variants: ye with superscript e / y^e (= the)
label_when: Never a label. Character conventions that should be normalised for tokens and pronunciation and kept as lyric.
sung_trap: 'ye' as a pronoun (you) is sung 'ye'. 'ye' as a thorn-article before a noun ('ye olde', 'y^e King') is sung 'the'. Decide by grammar: article before noun or adjective versus subject or object pronoun.
traditions: 17th-c. books (Lovelace 1649, Herrick 1648), broadside facsimiles, EEBO-derived text, Hazlitt/Grosart old-spelling editions

variants: Chappell & Co., 50, New Bond Street, W.
label_when: Cover, title and foot-of-page text of opera, operetta and musical-comedy libretti and vocal scores: authorship credits, publisher address, price, rights notice, number headings.
sung_trap: The credit words appear in sung patter ('I am the very model...'), but the credits are formulaic ('Words by', 'Music by', 'arranged by') and sit outside any number. Speaker names, act and scene headings and stage directions belong to other domains but must also be excluded.
traditions: Gilbert & Sullivan (Chappell libretti and vocal scores), Victorian burlesque and comic opera, Edwardian musical comedy, ballad operas
examples: Words by W. S. GILBERT. Music by ARTHUR SULLIVAN.

entries.term: Centring, right-alignment and indentation as layout
label_when: Never a label by itself, but a strong cue: whitespace that centres a short caps line (heading, number, running head) or pushes a fragment to the right margin (turnover, catchword, attribution, line number) marks the line as non-lyric or as a continuation of the line above.
sung_trap: Stanza indentation that alternates with rhyme (indented short lines, indented refrains) is prosodic layout of sung lines. Keep those lines. Only centring of an isolated non-verse token, or right-push of a fragment, is evidence of apparatus.
traditions: All plain-text stagings
examples:
Arise! ye sons of free-born sires; arise! your country save;
                                                    —_Charleston Mercury._

variants: ? or � replacing curly quotes or dashes
label_when: There is no label word; character damage from a wrong charset (ISO-8859-1, cp1252, UTF-8). Decode or repair. The corpus has "`Tis" (backtick for apostrophe) in eng_hymn_watts.txt.
sung_trap: These are the sung word's punctuation or letters. Repair rather than strip, or tokens such as "’Tis" will mis-count.
traditions: Older PG texts (ISO-8859-1), GITenberg conversions, web-scraped songbooks
examples: Iâ€™m sure you couldnâ€™t do it

label_when: Line-final, after the last sung word of a verse, set off by '--', ':--' or '—'. Strip the suffix. It means the chorus repeats here.
sung_trap: The text before the dash is sung, so drop only the cue. A line that consists only of the cue, such as 'glee:--CHORUS.', may be the tail of a wrapped verse line: the word 'glee' is sung and the cue is not.
traditions: 6 rows / 2 files (parlour_monroe_h_rosenfeld 5, parlour_charles_graham 1). Expected to be very common in sheet-music and songster texts from the 1880s to the 1920s.
examples: This bunch of shamrock from my mother dear.--CHORUS.  (eng_parlour_monroe_h_rosenfeld.txt)

entries.term: Pibroch movement names (NOT in seed list)
label_when: Alone on a line, in bracketed or CAPS form, between stanzas of a Gaelic song built on the pibroch form (e.g. Moladh Beinn Dobhrain).
sung_trap: These are never sung in the English translations. 'Ground' and 'Variation' can occur as sung English words, so treat them as labels only when they stand alone in a pibroch-form item.
traditions: About 14 bracket marks / 3 files (celtic_msm_duncan_macintyre, celtic_msm_alexander_macdonald, celtic_msm_robert_mackay_rob_donn). Already classed as apparatus.

label_when: Alone on a line, before the closing short stanza of a ballade, chant royal or similar.
sung_trap: There are no sung uses in the corpus. 'envoy' (an ambassador) could be sung mid-line, so treat it as a label only when alone.
traditions: 8 rows / 5 files (Andrew Lang 4, Austin Dobson, Henley, Swinburne 'ENVOI', Kilmer 'L'ENVOI').

label_when: Alone, in caps, before the closing stanza of a fable-song or comic ballad. The text that follows is verse.
sung_trap: 'moral' is sung in 37 rows across 22 files ('In moral mercy, truth, and justice!'). Browning sings 'That's the tale: its application?'. Strip only the bare heading.
traditions: 2 rows / 2 files (Thackeray, John Godfrey Saxe). Expected in comic-song books and children's song books.

label_when: Line-initial, followed by ':' or '.--' (strip the prefix; any verse after it is kept), or alone.
sung_trap: In verse epistles the postscript text is itself verse: 'POSTCRIPTUM.--And you, whom we all so adore,' (Dobson). Remove only the label. Do not read 'Ps.' (Psalm) as P.S.
traditions: 2 rows / 2 files (Leigh, Dobson).
examples: POSTCRIPTUM.--And you, whom we all so adore,  (eng_british_austin_dobson.txt)

label_when: Alone, as an ode-section heading, often numbered.
sung_trap: 'Turn' and 'Stand' are common line-initial sung verbs: 82 rows / 43 files and 82 rows / 47 files ('Turn out! turn out!', 'Stand undaunted.'). Treat them as labels only when alone, capitalised, without an object, inside a Pindaric item.
traditions: 0 in the corpus. Expected in anthology printings of Gray, Cowley, Jonson and Collins, and in odes set to music (Dryden's St Cecilia odes).
examples: (expected) THE TURN. / THE COUNTER-TURN. / THE STAND.  (Jonson's Cary-Morison ode)

label_when: Alone (often italic or indented), between the two halves of a madrigal or over a voice-part copy.
sung_trap: 'Tenor' and 'Treble' can be sung nouns ('the tenor of his ways'). 'Risposta' is never sung.
traditions: 1 row (Wilbye '_Risposta._'). Expected in Fellowes-style madrigal and lutenist reprints.

entries.term: Sheet-music section names (Tin Pan Alley and music hall; expected)
label_when: Alone, in caps or bold-as-caps, or line-initial with ':' or '.'. In sheet music they usually sit above the staff.
sung_trap: 'Vamp' is a sung slang verb in 1910s-20s songs ('She's a vamp'). 'Break', 'Trio' and 'Tag' are ordinary sung nouns or verbs. Treat them as labels only when alone and capitalised.
traditions: 0 in the corpus. Due with the Tin Pan Alley and music-hall sheet-song loads.

label_when: Alone, possibly followed by a numeral, a dash and performer names, or the tune name. In G&S: 'SONG—KO-KO.', 'TRIO.', 'RECITATIVE.'.
sung_trap: Sung forms are frequent: 'air' 1,011 rows / 333 files; 'round' 1,331 / 345; 'glee' 205 / 106; 'catch' 155 / 73. At line start: 'Air, quoth he, thy cheeks may blow' (Shakespeare), 'Song and the mandolin!' (Palmer), 'A Song of hey down derry,' (Durfey). Treat these as labels only when alone or followed by a numeral or a performer name, with no verb.
traditions: Lovelace 'SONG.' 2 rows; Rosenfeld 'glee:' (sung). Apparatus: Burns Jolly Beggars 'Recitativo' 8, 'Air' 8; '_A_ SONG.' 8. Gay's 'Air I --' was hoisted into TITLE (69 airs). Expected massively in PG 808 (G&S, about 349 numbers).

entries.term: ALL / Both / Ambo / Omnes / Tutti / Together
label_when: Alone, in caps or italics with a period, between parts in a dialogue song. Or as a CAPS prefix plus period followed by verse ('ALL. So it really doesn't matter...'): strip the prefix only.
sung_trap: Line-initial 'All' is sung in 1,603 rows / 412 files ('All alone,') and 'Both' in 122 rows / 58 files ('Both cold and hot,'). A label needs CAPS or italic with a period and no comma. Durfey's 'Omnes abhinc profugiunt_,' is a sung Latin line.
traditions: Gilbert ALL. 3 rows plus BOTH. alone (with SHE.) about 15; Herrick '_Ambo._' 3; Lovelace 'BOTH.'; Coleridge and Shelley 'BOTH.'; apparatus '_All Sing._' 5. Expected throughout G&S.
examples: ALL. So it really doesn't matter, matter, matter, matter, matter!  (eng_hall_ws_gilbert.txt)

label_when: Alone, or line-initial with '--' or '.'. In hymnals and glee books often in small caps above the staff.
sung_trap: 'His giga solo.' is sung. 'bass', 'treble' and 'tenor' can be sung nouns. Treat them as labels only when they head a line alone with a period or dash.
traditions: 1 row (George Pope Morris, The Maid of Saxony). Expected in hymnals, glee books and G&S.

entries.term: Numbered speaker prefixes (NOT in seed list)
label_when: A digit in parentheses, or a digit plus period, at line start, alternating 1/2/3 within one dialogue item, followed by verse. Also mid-line: '(2) He wull. (1) He woon't.' Strip each prefix.
sung_trap: Do not confuse with stanza numbers, contents numbers ('1. A General Song of Praise') or sung numerals. The test is alternation of the same small set of digits inside one item and the item being a dialogue or eclogue.
traditions: 109 rows / 4 files (William Barnes eclogues 71, Herrick 'The Kiss. A Dialogue' 27, Byrd 6, Watts 5). Apparatus 'FIRST VOICE.' and 'FIRST ANGEL'.
examples: (2) Do goo, George, no.  The pleace we can't get drough.  (eng_hall_william_barnes.txt)

label_when: A whole line of one to four CAPS words, ending in ':' or '.' (or nothing), that names a character before that character's lines.
sung_trap: ALL-CAPS SUNG lines exist. Emphasis: 'THE SIGNAL IS WAVING!--Till morn we'll remain' (Morris), 'FOR EVER: men have grown at length' (Procter). Whole caps stanzas: 'SO, HONOR UNTO THOSE THAT STOOD!' (Buena Vista). Caps refrain words. Require: short, a known character name or 'HE/SHE/BOTH', no verb, and ending in ':' or '.'.
traditions: About 140 genuine rows / 15 files (Shelley translations of Faust, Calderón and Cyclops, about 119; Gilbert SHE./BOTH. 15; Coleridge 'FOSTER-MOTHER.'; Morris 'KARL.'). Apparatus holds about 400 more (JOHN. 56, HATHORNE 45, MARTHA 30, THOMAS. 16 ...).

entries.term: Speaker abbreviation prefix, italic (dialogue and ballad opera)
label_when: Line-initial italic name or abbreviation with a period (inside or just outside the underscores), followed by verse. It can also recur mid-line ('_Ambo._ Let's cheer him up. _Sil._ Behold him weeping-ripe.'). Strip each one.
sung_trap: Several traps. '_End._' is Endymion, not an end marker. '_Matt._' is Matt of the Mint, not Matthew. '_Her._' is Herrick or Hernandez, not the pronoun. '_V_.' is the Vicar, not a versicle. Durfey's '_Item._ Poor folks brown Bread I give' is a SUNG word in a mock will. Durfey italicises sung names, as in '_Peggy_ to the Mill is gone' with no period after the name. A label requires the period.
traditions: 302 rows / 14 files. Gay (Beggar's Opera) 68, Herrick 117, Hemans 67 (dramas), Jean Ingelow 17, Clough 11, Landor 9, Samuel Daniel 9, Durfey, Herbert, Davenant.
examples: _End._  Ah! Lycidas, come tell me why  (eng_british_robert_herrick.txt)

label_when: Line-initial CAPS abbreviation plus a period, then spaces and verse. Strip the prefix. It is often followed by heavy indentation in echo lines ('DES.                So it really doesn't matter--').
sung_trap: 'MAR.' and 'DES.' clash with the month abbreviations Mar. and Dec. in dates. 'ALL.' clashes with sung 'All'. 'W.' is a single initial. Lovelace's 'GERARDINE.', 'LUCASTA.' and 'HONEY.' rows are editorial-note headwords, not speakers, so check context.
traditions: 25 rows / 4 files (Gilbert 12, Lovelace 8, Watts-Dunton 'CHORUS.' 4, Cowper 1). This becomes the dominant leak in the incoming G&S load (PG 808).
examples: ROB. My eyes are fully open to my awful situation--  (eng_hall_ws_gilbert.txt)

variants: (The GIRLS attempt to waltz to the music; but, overcome by their feelings, they resume / their tasks.)
label_when: A whole line, or a trailing or embedded clause, in ( ) or [ ] or italics, describing action in the third-person present tense, often naming a character in CAPS. Directions can wrap over two lines.
sung_trap: MOST wholly parenthesised lines are SUNG. Of 360 such lyric rows / 93 files, the great majority are sung asides, echoes and refrains: '(Said I to myself--said I)' Gilbert x13, '(Hey, but she sickens as the days go by!)', '(Hark to the thrush's trilling)', '(Butter and eggs and a pound of cheese)', and Manson's '(_Sing hey down ho, the bleak winds blow._)'. A direction has no rhyme function, uses third-person action verbs (attempt, gives, slaps, rising, falling) or CAPS character names, and breaks the metre.
traditions: About 10 genuine rows / 6 files (Morris 2, Ingelow, Hemans, Barnes, Longfellow). Bracketed directions are already apparatus (Barnes '[_weeping._]').
examples: (The GIRLS attempt to waltz to the music; but, overcome by their feelings, they resume  (eng_american_george_pope_morris.txt)

label_when: Line-initial 'SCENE' or 'ACT' with a numeral or '.--', followed by italic setting prose. 'Curtain' or 'Tableau' alone at the end of an act.
sung_trap: 'scene' is sung in 186 rows across 94 files ('The scene seems a desert'). 'Curtain'd with cloudy red,' (Milton) and 'Act when Thou wilt,' (Herrick) are sung. A label requires CAPS or a numeral and a trailing setting description.
traditions: 3 rows / 3 files (Longfellow, Matthew Arnold, George Houghton). Expected throughout G&S and any libretto.
examples: SCENE II.--_Noon. A Glen on the highest skirts of the woody region of  (eng_british_matthew_arnold.txt)

variants: heard gradually dying away at a distance_
label_when: Bracketed or italic, alone or next to a speaker name.
sung_trap: 'Without Hood or Scarff' and 'Within the glen' are sung. Treat these as labels only when bracketed or italic and next to a speaker or at item start.
traditions: Shelley 'FAUST [FROM A DISTANCE]: Here!' (TITLE); Christina Rossetti '[Outside.]' (TITLE); apparatus prose 'heard gradually dying away at a distance_'.

entries.term: Music, dance and business cues inside the music staff
label_when: Bracketed '[Music: ...]' block remnants, or a cue word alone between verses.
sung_trap: 'Dance and sing,' (Gay), 'Dance, Red Flamingo Feather!' and 'Dance by fu' light.' are sung (24 line-initial 'Dance' rows / 14 files). A cue is alone, capitalised, without a comma or object.
traditions: Durfey 9 '[Music:' fragments (already apparatus). Expected in music-hall and minstrel songsters ('Dance.', 'Symphony').

variants: Repeat the first stanza to complete the tune.
Where the tune includes two stanzas.
label_when: Parenthesised or italic instruction, or a trailing (bis)/(twice) after a sung line. Strip the instruction. The repeat may need expanding if sung-line counts matter.
sung_trap: 'Repeat the exulting strain.' (Griswold, a sung refrain line x5), 'Repeat the joyful sound,' and 'Repeat the sounding joy.' (Watts) are SUNG: 61 mid-line and 12 line-initial 'repeat' rows. 'twice' is sung in 88 rows ('Chorus--Ance crowdie, twice crowdie'). An instruction is imperative to the performer and refers to 'line/stanza/chorus/tune'.
traditions: 4 rows / 3 files (Ina M. Porter, Carrie Bell Sinclair, Watts 2). 0 rows of (bis), D.C. or :||. Expected in songsters and sheet music.

label_when: Line ends in &c./etc. after a truncated incipit of an earlier chorus or burden line. The line stands for the whole refrain, so annotate it as a cue: the incipit words are sung but the line is not new lyric. The corpus already uses '[CHORUS: abbreviated return, printed "&c." in the source]' (21 marks).
sung_trap: Compare the incipit with an earlier refrain line. '&' inside a line is often sung 'and' (Durfey '_Sat & knotted, & knotted_'). Comic songs may sing 'et cetera' as words. Stage 'etc.' inside editorial prose is apparatus of a different kind.
traditions: 1,095 rows / 69 files. Durfey 461, Burns 288, John Skinner 35, Lady Nairne 25, Gay, Foster, Emmett 'Dixie', Hanby, Bayly, Moore, Root, Payne, Holmes, Franklin.

label_when: Alone at item or section start, or bracketed above a verse. Dynamics are lowercase single letters standing alone.
sung_trap: All 80 corpus hits are sung ('Slowly drifted out of the battle's storm', 'Slow to argue, but quick to act'). Byron's '[mf]' is a FOOTNOTE LETTER ANCHOR, not mezzo-forte. Treat these as marks only when alone, in Italian, or as a dynamic letter.
traditions: 0 genuine rows. Expected in Tin Pan Alley, music-hall and hymnal sheet music.

entries.term: Tune line (Air / Tune / To the tune of)
variants: Air, "To ladies eyes a round, boy."
Sung to the air of X
label_when: Line-initial 'Tune--', 'AIR--', 'Air,' or 'Air:' followed by a QUOTED or italic tune name, or '(X air.)'. Standard staging hoists these into the TITLE as [air: X].
sung_trap: Line-initial 'Air' and 'Tune' are often sung. 'Tune my heart to sing thy grace' (Robinson), 'Tune your harps high' (Watts), 'Air, quoth he, thy cheeks may blow' (Shakespeare), 'Air coin'd to words my Julia could not hear' (Herrick), Riley's dialect 'Air you go' to keep a fine store'. 'tune' is sung in 142 mid-line rows / 79 files. A tune line needs a quoted or italic proper title, or 'air/tune of'.
traditions: 10 lyric rows / 4 files (Watts 5, Burns 3, Halleck 1, Morris 1); 477 hoisted [air:] marks; 245 files whose 'italic music/air credit lines' were stripped. Expected in every songster.

variants: To the tune of the 113th Psalm.
As the new tune of the 50th Psalm.
label_when: After a hymn number or alone. It names the metrical-psalm tune or metre to sing to.
sung_trap: 'Psalm' is sung in hymns ('in psalm and hymn'). A reference needs an ordinal plus 'Psalm' with 'As the' or 'tune of'.
traditions: About 8 rows / 1 file (Watts).
examples: To the tune of the 113th Psalm.  (eng_hymn_watts.txt)

label_when: Alone, or trailing a hymn number. Digit-comma or digit-period sequences standing alone are syllable-count metres.
sung_trap: 'And common-metre rhymes.' (Cable) and 'Love hath his meter too' are sung. Herrick's 'The words found true, C. M., remember me.' is SUNG: 'C. M.' there are initials. Treat metre names and codes as labels only when the line is otherwise empty or is a hymn heading.
traditions: About 36 rows / 1 file (Watts: 30 metre names plus 6 '8,7,8,7'-type rows). Otterbein headers note 'metre heading not staged'. Expected in every hymnal.

label_when: A CAPS or small-caps proper name alone above a hymn, usually with a metre code or composer name.
sung_trap: Tune names can be ordinary words ('REST', 'HOPE', 'ZION'). Treat them as labels only when alone in caps above the first stanza.
traditions: 0 in lyric rows (Otterbein says 'tune name not staged'). Expected in the incoming hymnals.

label_when: Only 'Selah' standing alone, or line-final in a psalm paraphrase, is a musical or liturgical mark (not sung in English metrical psalmody). Hallelujah, Alleluia and Hosanna are sung.
sung_trap: Hallelujah is sung in 4 line-initial and 11 mid-line rows ('_Chorus_--Glory! Glory Hallelujah!'). Hosanna is sung. Some anthems sing 'Selah', so check whether it is part of the rhyme or metre.
traditions: 0 Selah in the corpus. Expected in psalters and anthem books.

variants: Glory to the Father in Long Metre.
label_when: Alone, as a heading over a doxology stanza.
sung_trap: Latin liturgical phrases are SUNG when they are the burden: 'Miserere Domine.' (Procter, a burden x6) and 'Gloria tibi Domine!' (Procter). 'The Christian Doxology.' is a heading.
traditions: 4 rows / 1 file (Watts).

label_when: A short line after the hymn's topic line saying when or where it is used.
sung_trap: 'Morning' and 'evening' are sung words. Treat these as labels only when the line is a complete short phrase in heading position before stanza 1.
traditions: 4 rows / 1 file (Watts).

entries.term: Hymn topic or argument line echoing the title (NOT in seed list)
variants: The blessedness of saints, and misery of sinners.
Sincerity and hypocrisy; or, Formality in worship,
label_when: The first lyric row of an item repeats the TITLE (a subject title, not a first line), often ending in '.' and followed by a number, metre or 'Ver.' line.
sung_trap: In most hymnals and song books the title IS the first line and is sung. 1,464 items / 364 files have first row equal to title, overwhelmingly sung first lines (Cowper 69, Moore 56, Wesley 53, Burns 44, Campion 39). It is apparatus only when the title is a topic phrase with no verse shape, as in Watts.
traditions: About 291 items in eng_hymn_watts.txt. Also the 'italic topic line' in Otterbein (not staged).

entries.term: Roman or arabic numeral alone (section or poem number)
label_when: A line that is only a numeral with optional period or brackets, at item start or between stanzas (In Memoriam sections, sonnet-sequence numbers, numbered parts).
sung_trap: 'I' alone could be the pronoun in a dialogue answer, so check the stanza position. 'I, I,' is sung. 'X' is a letter. 'For C is so very particular' (Gilbert) is sung. A label has no other word on the line.
traditions: 67 lyric rows / 9 files (Browning 19, Paul H. Hayne 10, D. G. Rossetti 9, Spenser 9, Tennyson, Willson). About 150 more as apparatus (II 23, III 21, IV 16 ...).

entries.term: Arabic item or stanza number prefix
variants: 181. A DIALOGUE BETWIXT HORACE AND LYDIA, ...
223. THE FAIRY TEMPLE; OR, OBERON'S CHAPEL
label_when: Digit plus period at line start before a CAPS title (poem number in a collected edition), or before stanza 1 in hymnals that number stanzas.
sung_trap: Numbered speakers (see the numbered speaker prefix entry) and sung numbers ('Three cheers, etc.') are not this. Herrick's '1. Has it a speaking virtue? 2. Yes.' is dialogue.
traditions: 112 digit-led rows / 6 files (Herrick 50, Watts 41, Barnes 10, Byrd 7, Byron 2, Browning 2).
examples: 223. THE FAIRY TEMPLE; OR, OBERON'S CHAPEL  (eng_british_robert_herrick.txt)

entries.term: Back-of-book index entry (NOT in seed list)
label_when: Lines of volume roman numeral plus page-number lists, or 'Surname, Forename,' headwords. A whole index has been staged as an item.
sung_trap: None: index lines are never sung. Note that the headword lines ('Crew, Lady,') look like verse fragments.
traditions: 14 lyric rows plus the TITLE 'Carlisle, Countess of, I. 78' (eng_british_robert_herrick.txt, lines 9606-9640). Expected at the end of every hymnal.

variants: 1. A General Song of Praise to God.
A slight Specimen of Moral Songs, viz.
label_when: A run of numbered title lines, or a 'TABLE/CONTENTS' heading, typically after 'The End.'.
sung_trap: None, but the numbered lines look like short end-stopped verse lines.
traditions: About 35 rows / 1 file (eng_hymn_watts.txt, lines 24614-24656).

entries.term: Editorial prose paragraphs staged as lyric
variants: These lines refer to the prohibition published by the
as it is printed in LUCASTA.
The first stanza of this song was the composition of a
written and published before I heard the supposed facts of its first
Mab" (8 204-206). See editor's note on this passage.
label_when: Long lines with prose syntax and bibliographic vocabulary (edition, printed, published, poem, stanza, MS., p./vol., see), usually in runs, often between items or after a NOTE label.
sung_trap: Imperative 'See' opens many sung lines ('See the rivers flowing', 'See yon far heathy hills'), and verse uses 'printed' and 'reads' ('such as thou art printed in the heart'). Require prose length plus at least two bibliographic terms, or adjacency to a note label.
traditions: About 440 candidate rows (the bibliographic-vocabulary filter also catches some sung lines). Lovelace 48, Watts 41, Burns 32, Herrick 22, Browning 16, Durfey 16, Shelley 14, Procter 11, Holmes 7, Stevenson 7.
examples: These lines refer to the prohibition published by the  (eng_british_richard_lovelace.txt)

variants: written by the poet.  Lucasta, <N>N, erroneously has THIS.
label_when: A line starting with or containing MS./orig. ed./om./var. plus a quoted or italic word.
sung_trap: None in the corpus, but MS. and Ms. could be sung titles ('Ms. Jones'), and 'reads' is sung ('Whilst all the house my passion reads').
traditions: Lovelace 1 lyric row plus apparatus; Herrick footnote '[E] Orig. ed.'; Byron bracket notes.
examples: MS. reads:--"Youre phansie, madam," omitting "that's to  (eng_british_richard_lovelace.txt)

variants: [Sidenote: The angelic spirits leave the dead bodies,]
label_when: A bracketed '[Sidenote: ...]' (Gutenberg convention for margin glosses), or an 'Argument' prose summary heading.
sung_trap: 'argument' is sung in 8 mid-line rows ('So deep in tangled argument'). The Ancient Mariner glosses are authorial prose but not verse.
traditions: 35 [Sidenote] rows / 2 files (Coleridge, Lovelace), all already apparatus.

label_when: An italic headword followed by a comma and a gloss, or 'i.e.' plus a gloss, alone on a line.
sung_trap: The dialect headwords are sung inside the poems, so strip only the gloss lines, never in-verse dialect words.
traditions: About 240 glossary-pattern apparatus rows; 685 files declare 'glossary lines' stripped.

variants: Extempore Reply to Verses addressed to the Author by a Lady, under the
On reading, in the public papers, the Laureate's Ode, with the other
On hearing the bells ring on the passage of the constitutional
Written at the request of the committee for the Constitutional
Addressed to the Young Gentlemen leaving the Academy at Lenox,
label_when: Opening prose sentence (often wrapped, often italic or CAPS) before stanza 1, starting with On/Written/Addressed/Extempore/Inscribed/Occasioned and a gerund or participle.
sung_trap: 'On seeing her waddling form so fair,' (Lear) and 'On hearing this, the Sultan smiled' (Aldrich) are sung. 'On her sons to meet the foe!' is a sung refrain. A headnote has no rhyme and continues as a prose clause onto the next line.
traditions: 6 rows / 4 files (Burns 3, Whittier, Fanny Kemble, Holmes), plus ALL-CAPS headnotes in Pike and Lovelace.
examples: Extempore Reply to Verses addressed to the Author by a Lady, under the  (eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt)

variants: “They learn in suffering what they teach in song.”--Shelley.
“And send the godly in a pet to pray.”--Pope.
label_when: A quoted line or foreign-language phrase at item start, ending in '--Author.' or followed by an attribution line.
sung_trap: Dashes followed by a capitalised word are common in sung lines: 202 rows / 80 files match '--Name.' at line end, almost all sung ('Half in smiles, half in tears--Theodosia Prevost.', 'SOLO--SOPHIA.' is a label). An epigraph is in quotation marks AND precedes the first stanza.
traditions: Mostly already apparatus (Hemans, Burns, Wordsworth). Lovelace 'VANITAS VANITATUM.' 1 lyric row.
examples: # APPARATUS: “They learn in suffering what they teach in song.”--Shelley.  (eng_british_felicia_hemans.txt)

variants: DEDICATED TO MR. JOHN MERRIFIELD, COUNSELLOR-AT-LAW.
TO THE HONOURABLE MY COUSIN ANNE LOVELACE.
TO MY TRUELY VALIANT, LEARNED FRIEND; WHO IN HIS BOOKE
label_when: A CAPS or italic 'TO <person>' / 'DEDICATED TO' line, often wrapped over 2-3 lines, before the first stanza.
sung_trap: Sung lines open with 'To' constantly. A dedication is in CAPS, contains honorifics (MR., ESQ., LADY) and precedes stanza 1.
traditions: About 20 rows / 2 files (Lovelace, Herrick). Expected on every sheet-music cover ('Respectfully dedicated to Miss ...').
examples: TO THE HONOURABLE MY COUSIN ANNE LOVELACE.  (eng_british_richard_lovelace.txt)

variants: _Writ by the Famous Mr._ NAT. LEE.
Written by W. H. Archbold and Monroe H. Rosenfeld. Composed by Felix
label_when: Line-initial 'Set by', 'Composed by', 'Words/Music by' or 'Written by', or a CAPS 'BY MR. X', containing a personal name with honorific or initials. Often wrapped onto a second line.
sung_trap: Line-initial 'By' is overwhelmingly sung. 'By Chickamauga River.' (refrain x3), 'By Pocumtuck Side.', 'By the women of Marblehead!'. 'Sung by thee!' (Nairne), 'Sung by flaming tongues above' (Robinson) and 'Words by which the wretched are consoled?' (Arnold) are sung. A credit needs a person's name with Mr./Mrs./Dr./initials and no verse continuation.
traditions: 9 rows / 4 files (Lovelace 5, Herrick 2, Holmes 1, Rosenfeld 1); 245 files had 'italic music/air credit lines' stripped. Expected on every sheet-music and songster item.

variants: The celebrated comic song, as sung by
label_when: 'Sung by' or a similar phrase plus a performer name (often CAPS) under a title or at the end of a credit line.
sung_trap: 'Sung by thee!' and 'Sung to the bees stealing out and in.' are sung. A credit names a stage performer with an honorific or a CAPS surname.
traditions: 1 lyric row (Durfey). Expected in nearly every music-hall and minstrel songster item.

label_when: An author's name alone at the end of a verse epistle or hymn, usually followed by a place-date line.
sung_trap: The signature can be IN THE RHYME. Burns: 'Then know all ye whom it concerns, / Subscripsi huic, / Robert Burns.', where concerns/Burns rhyme, so it is part of the poem. 'Yours and mine--' and 'Yours are Hampden's ...' are sung. Check whether the name completes a rhyme before stripping it.
traditions: 9 rows / 1 file (Burns), plus 'Yours,' and 'Subscripsi huic,' 5. The Otterbein hymnal signature line is already quoted into '--- AUTHOR:'.

label_when: Alone, at item start or end, with a language name or translator name.
sung_trap: 'From the ...' opens 458 sung lines / 182 files ('From the sword,'). A credit names a language or source and has no verb.
traditions: Bracket mark 1 (Lovelace '[From The French.]'); apparatus 3 '_The same in_ LATIN.'; titles carry 'Taken from Anacreon'.

variants: [Published by Forman, "Poetical Works of P. B. S.", 1876; dated 1820.]
label_when: Bracketed or trailing note naming the edition, date and format (4to, 8vo).
sung_trap: None.
traditions: About 30 bracket rows (Byron 13, Shelley 16), already apparatus.

entries.term: Printer's imprint, price and publisher's advertisement (NOT in seed list)
variants: OR $3 FOR THE SET, ENCLOSED IN NEAT BOX.
of this song will be sent by mail for 25 cents. Address, FRANK
‘A more _wholesome_ book for young readers we have seldom seen.’--_The
label_when: CAPS city or printer lines, price lines with cents, $ or s./d., 'sent by mail' offers, and press-review blurbs, usually at the end of a file or between items.
sung_trap: Comic songs sing prices ('one shilling the box--' is sung patent-medicine patter). An imprint has a city plus a colon, PRINTERS, or a price with no verse context.
traditions: 5 lyric rows / 2 files (Waugh 3, Browning 2), plus apparatus (MACMILLAN, LONDON:, review blurbs, sheet-music mail-order ad). Expected heavily in songsters and sheet music.

variants: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1862, by ... in the Clerk's Office of the District Court of ...
This song may be sung in public without fee or licence
label_when: Any line starting 'Copyright' or 'Entered according to', or containing 'rights reserved' or 'Secured', usually at the foot of the first sheet-music page.
sung_trap: None realistic.
traditions: 0 in the corpus (Gilbert header notes a Berne-Convention notice in a rejected edition). Expected on every post-1870 US sheet song and Tin Pan Alley item.
examples: (expected) Copyright, 1905, by Jerome H. Remick & Co.

label_when: A place name plus date, or a year alone, at the very end (or start) of an item, often after a signature.
sung_trap: Narrative ballads sing dates ('In seventeen hundred and seventy-five') and places. Refrain-final place names are sung: 'At Manassas.', 'For Baltimore.', 'At Lindenore.', 'Through Lexington.'. A date line has digits or 'Anno' and no verb.
traditions: 13 lyric rows / 6 files (Burns 7, C. Rossetti 2, Whittier, Herrick, Lovelace, Rankin); more as apparatus (Venice, Tampa, March 1820).

entries.term: Embedded CAPS title / sub-heading inside an item
variants: EPITAPH ON THE TOMB OF SIR EDWARD GILES ...
label_when: A CAPS line (often wrapped across 2-3 lines) without verse rhythm, between items that were merged, or a sonnet-sequence member title.
sung_trap: ALL-CAPS SUNG lines: Boker's 'AND EVERLASTING GLORY UNTO BUENA VISTA'S DEAD!', Morris's 'THE PILOT'S ON BOARD!--thank heaven', Poe's 'By the name of ANNABEL LEE;' (mixed). Lovelace's 'THOSE HONOURS COME TOO LATE, / THAT ON OUR ASHES WAITE.' is a CAPS sung couplet. A heading has no end rhyme with its neighbours and no exclamation.
traditions: 378 ALL-CAPS lyric rows / 47 files in total, of which about 150 are headings (D. G. Rossetti House of Life titles, Lovelace, Herrick, Coleridge, Pike, Boker).

label_when: Alone, with a period, a genre word optionally preceded by A/Another/The.
sung_trap: 'Song whose burden sigheth,' (Christina Rossetti) and 'A Song of hey down derry,' (Durfey) are sung. 'Answer' is sung in 320 rows, and Herrick's '_Ans._' is a speaker. A heading has a capitalised genre word plus a period and nothing else.
traditions: Lovelace 'SONG.' 2 and 'ODE.' 1; apparatus '_A_ SONG.' 8. Expected in anthologies and songsters ('Another.', 'The Answer to the above').

variants: Sincerity and hypocrisy; or, Formality in worship,
The FOUR-LEGG'D ELDER: Or a Horrible Relation of ...
label_when: Heading-position line containing '; or,' or ': Or' joining two title phrases, sometimes wrapped.
sung_trap: 'or' joins sung clauses everywhere. A heading has this in a title position with no verse rhythm.
traditions: Watts topic lines (part of the topic-line entry), Herrick numbered titles, Durfey TITLE lines.

label_when: Bracketed volume number at the start of a TITLE (Pills to Purge Melancholy volume).
sung_trap: None.
traditions: 361 [v.N] marks (Durfey, Lovelace TITLE lines).
examples: --- TITLE: [v.5] Plain Proof Ruin'd: Or, a Grand CHEAT Discover'd.  (eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt)

entries.term: Trailing line number (NOT in seed list)
label_when: Four or more spaces, then an optional underscore and a 1-4 digit number at line end (critical-edition line numbering). Strip the number and keep the verse.
sung_trap: Sung lines can end in numbers ('Of eighty and five', 'calibre fifty-four'), but those are words, not digits after a wide gap.
traditions: 468 lyric rows / 6 files (Shelley 273, Coleridge 79, Christina Rossetti 78, Keats 22, Lowell 8, and one more).
examples: My way, and lost my servants and my comrades.                        _70  (eng_british_percy_bysshe_shelley.txt)

label_when: Bracketed digits or 1-2 lowercase letters glued to the end of a word or line, or dagger and asterisk marks after a word. Strip the anchor and keep the word.
sung_trap: Editorial SUPPLY brackets look identical and hold SUNG text: 'measure[s]', 'burst[s]', 'queen[s]' ([s] in Dowland, Wilbye, Byron, Lovelace), 'Come [Harriet]! sweet is the hour' (Shelley), 'Ph[oe]bus' ([oe] ligature, 13 rows) and Barnes 'dr[=e]ve' ([=e] macron, 12 rows). Keep bracket contents that complete a word or name.
traditions: 14 lyric rows / 3 files (Matthew Arnold 9, Wordsworth 3, E. B. Browning 2). Byron has about 60 one-off letter anchors; Herrick and Barnes have [A]/[E]. 913 files declare footnote markers stripped. A further 72 '(N)' digit rows in Barnes are speaker numbers, not footnotes.
examples: Recalls the obscure opposer he outweighed.[9]  (eng_british_matthew_arnold.txt)

label_when: A line made only of asterisks, dots or dashes (section break or omission), or asterisks replacing suppressed words inside a line.
sung_trap: Barnes's echo lines '--_my dears_;' and '--_bad chaps_.' are SUNG echo words. Grenfell's '... Here, in the hills of ages' and Browning's ellipsis-led lines are sung. Burns's '* * * Crochallan came,' contains sung words after a suppression mark. Only rows with no letters are pure ornament.
traditions: About 100 apparatus rows ('*  *  *' 19+18+9+7..., '<---->' 33); 21 lyric rows / 10 files are mostly sung.

label_when: Gutenberg-convention bracket at line end or alone.
sung_trap: None, except the Greek transliteration a poet quotes as verse ('{skênê pas ho bios, kai paignion.}', Campion), which is quoted text and should be flagged for review rather than counted as English lyric.
traditions: [Gothic: Eclogue.] 13 (Barnes), [Image] 1 inline in a Moore lyric row; 228 files had illustration captions stripped.
examples: Who, smiling will blend her bright welcome with mine.  [Image]  (eng_celtic_thomas_moore.txt)

label_when: An entity or angle-bracket tag inside a lyric row. Normalise it (— becomes a dash) and keep the sung words.
sung_trap: Lovelace's '<thee>' is an editorial supply of a SUNG word.
traditions: 7 rows / 3 files (Austin Dobson oxford 4, Lovelace 2, Campion 1).

entries.term: Drop-cap / small-caps opening word (SUNG; false positive for CAPS detectors)
variants: THE sky is ruddy in the east,
BY the hope within us springing,
IT was late in mild October
label_when: Never a label. The first word of a stanza is set in caps by printing convention. Normalise case only.
sung_trap: This is the trap itself. Any 'CAPS word at line start' rule, or a 'BY ... credit' rule, will misfire. Moore's 'BY that Lake, whose gloomy shore' looks like a byline.
traditions: 577 rows / 84 files with a CAPS first word followed by lowercase (Barnes and Burns contractions O'/A' account for about 400; Moore 80, Whittier, Pike).
examples: BY the hope within us springing,  (eng_celtic_thomas_moore.txt)

entries.term: Deliberate word-split hyphen at line end (SUNG)
label_when: Not a label. Only true line-wrap hyphenation from page width (a long prose or hymn line broken mid-word) is an artifact to rejoin.
sung_trap: Comic and Elizabethan verse splits words across lines on purpose for rhyme ('Yet I wish that I could modi-/fy', Lear; 'Can get, and look for no im-', Carroll; Campion 'them-'). Keep these as sung.
traditions: 18 rows / 13 files (Lear 2, Carroll 2, FitzGerald 2, Durfey 2, Beers 2, Campion, Herrick, Brontë).
examples: Yet I wish that I could modi-  (eng_british_edward_lear.txt)

entries.term: Italic whole line (SUNG burden; false positive for 'italic = apparatus')
variants: _'Tis o'er the Hills, and far away,_
_Thy thorn without, my thorn my heart invadeth._
label_when: Not a label. Italics mark the burden in broadside and Pills printings. Only italic lines with stage-direction verbs, credits (Set by, Sung by, Tune of) or topic headings are apparatus.
sung_trap: This is the trap: 476 italic-whole-line lyric rows / 39 files (Durfey 238, Dunbar 31, Herrick 25, Sidney 20) are overwhelmingly sung burdens and refrains.
traditions: Durfey, Dunbar, Herrick, Sidney, Gray, Melville ('_Sing and pray_.').
examples: _Which no Body can deny._  (eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt, x16, sung)

entries.term: Parenthesised sung aside / echo (SUNG; false positive for 'parentheses = direction')
variants: (Hey, but his face is a sight for to see!)
(Butter and eggs and a pound of cheese)
label_when: Not a label. These are sung interjections, echo lines and internal refrains.
sung_trap: This is the trap. Of 360 wholly-parenthesised lyric rows / 93 files, only about 10 are directions. Gilbert's 13 '(Said I to myself--said I)' lines are sung.
traditions: Gilbert, Morris, Morley, Allingham-type refrain songs, Barnes.

label_when: Inside a line, they mark that line (and usually its run) as editorial prose or a note.
sung_trap: 'sic' is Scots for 'such' and is SUNG constantly ('Sic a wife as Willie had', 'On sic a day!'): Burns about 55 rows plus many Scots files. Only the bracketed or italic [_sic_] is apparatus. 'Item.' (Durfey mock will) is sung. 'viz.' is apparatus in the Watts table. Burns's 'Subscripsi huic' is in the rhyme. 'Ps.' is Psalm, not P.S.
traditions: Lovelace page refs 15 rows; 'i.e.' glosses (about 15 apparatus); [_sic_] 1; Burns 'Anno Mundi' 2; Watts 'viz.'. 120 'latin_word' hits / 39 files, mostly Scots 'sic' (sung).

label_when: Italic or capitalised, at line start with a period or alone (speaker or stage function).
sung_trap: Durfey's 'Omnes abhinc profugiunt_,' is a SUNG macaronic Latin line, and Lovelace and Herrick quote Latin verse as text ('At lepus: in me omnis terrae ...'). Treat these as labels only when they function as a speaker or direction.
traditions: Herrick '_Ambo._' 3; Durfey (sung Latin); apparatus '_Exeunt_'.
examples: _Ambo._ Poor pitied youth! _Mir._ And here the breath of kine  (eng_british_robert_herrick.txt)

entries.term: Transcriber / digitisation notes and Gutenberg boilerplate
variants: End of the Project Gutenberg EBook
label_when: Any line naming the transcriber, a URL, the e-text project or an editorial status remark.
sung_trap: None.
traditions: Watts 'Transcriber's Note.' plus a paragraph with a URL (lyric rows 24658-24664); Dobson '(No author's name is stated)'; 5 files declare PG header/footer stripped.

label_when: Line-initial 'No.' plus a number above a song, or an index number alone.
sung_trap: 'No.' is the sung word 'No' plus a period ('No: beware of lovers' crying.', Corkine; 'Never.'). A label needs a digit after 'No.'.
traditions: 0 in the corpus. Expected in Beadle and De Witt songsters and gospel hymnals.

entries.term: Bare name alone line (ambiguous: speaker label, signature, or sung refrain)
label_when: Label (speaker) when a dialogue follows and the name recurs before speeches. Attribution when it ends an epigraph or is an author name after a quotation. Otherwise sung.
sung_trap: E. B. Browning's 'Sleep.' (x11) and 'My Kate.' (x7) are SUNG refrain endings, and 'At Manassas.' and 'For Baltimore.' are sung refrain tails. Hemans's 'Wordsworth.', 'Shelley.' and 'Akenside.' are epigraph attributions; Stedman's '_Coriolanus._' and '_Nursery Rhyme._' are epigraph source labels.
traditions: 64 mixed-case 'Name.'-alone rows / 25 files: E. B. Browning 11, Durfey 6, Hemans 5, Burns 5, Watts 4. Needs per-item review.

entries.term: Staging-format structural markers (pipeline markup, not printed text)
label_when: Always, when the marker is line-initial in the exact staging syntax: '--- KEY:' header, '# key:' header, or a bracketed ALL-CAPS section tag alone on its line. The corpus counts these as 46,151 [VERSE, 1,580 [BURDEN, 673 [REFRAIN, 255 [CHORUS, 8,725 '--- TITLE:' and 4,295 '# APPARATUS:'. They are structure for the reader to consume, never lyric. The text after '# APPARATUS:' is already flagged apparatus, so do not re-score it as a TITLE.
sung_trap: A sung line that genuinely begins with '#' or '---' does not occur in printed sources. '[' is only a trap when it opens a sung bracketed aside (rare). The staging tags are ALL CAPS with an optional number and close on the same line, so mixed-case bracketed prose is not a tag (see the bracketed-headnote entry).
traditions: Every staged file (GITenberg/PG anthologies, Kalliope XML, hymnals, songsters)
examples: [BURDEN]  /  --- TITLE: SONG OF THE TEXAS RANGERS  [air: The Yellow Rose of Texas]

entries.term: Bracketed multi-line editorial prose paragraph (headnote or explanatory note in square brackets)
variants: [This song is said to have been composed by ...
[These lines were given to Sir Walter Scott ...
[This piece is founded on a tale related by ...
[There is nothing in this sentimental song that ...
[These spirited and graceful stanzas appeared in the ...
[Those who only know the neighbourhood of ...
[Through the window December is seen ... (masque direction)
label_when: A line opens with '[' followed by a capitalised prose word such as This, These, The, Those, There, Published, First, MS, Read or Written, and the bracket closes on the same line or several lines later. Everything up to the matching ']' is apparatus. The corpus has 21 lines opening '[This/These/The ' alone.
sung_trap: Bracketed sung asides are short and metrical, and they rhyme with neighbouring lines. A bracketed paragraph is prose: it runs past a verse line's length with no rhyme, uses past-tense narration about the song ('was written', 'is said to'), or names the poet in the third person.
traditions: Modern Scottish Minstrel (Rogers), Whittier and Shelley collected works, Home Book of Verse, Oxford Book of English Verse
examples: [This song is said to have been composed by Schiller in answer to the

entries.term: Broadside long-title descriptive subtitle (Being / Shewing / Giving an account / Wherein)
label_when: In the block between a ballad's title and its first stanza, a prose clause begins with a participle (Being, Shewing, Showing, Giving, Declaring, Relating, Containing) or 'Wherein'. The clause often runs several lines and ends with a tune line or a licence line.
sung_trap: The same participles open sung lines. The corpus has 'Showing how, when young and sprightly, with a footstep falling lightly,' (T. D. English) and 'Showing how wise it is to cast away' (Moody), both sung. Label only before stanza 1, in unmetered prose, usually in a smaller font or in italics, and never rhyming with the next line.
traditions: 17th-18th c. black-letter broadsides (Roxburghe, Pepys, Bagford), Pepys/Euing ballads, garlands, Catnach/Pitts slip songs
examples: The Unfortunate Lover; Being a true Relation of a young Man who ... To the Tune of, Fortune my Foe.

entries.term: Broadside and chapbook genre-formula headings (A New Song / A Copy of Verses / An Excellent Ballad / A Lamentation)
variants: Excellent New Copy of Verses upon ...
A Copy of Verses on the Execution of ...
label_when: As a title line or title-prefix. The formula plus 'upon/on/of ...' is a heading. The corpus has '--- TITLE: A NEW SONG' (Stansbury), 'A New SONG in the Play call'd ...' and 'Excellent New Copy of Verses upon raising Recruits.' (D'Urfey).
sung_trap: 'A new song I'll sing' and 'Come listen to my new song' are sung. A heading stands alone, often in caps or italics, before the first stanza and ends in a full stop with no rhyme partner. A sung use sits inside a metrical line with a verb.
traditions: Broadsides, slip songs, garlands, Pills to Purge Melancholy, Revolutionary-era American broadsides
examples: A NEW SONG.  To the Tune of, Hosier's Ghost.

entries.term: Garland and chapbook packaging (garland title, contents of songs, chapbook licence)
variants: The Royal Garland of Love and Delight
Composed of several excellent new songs
Composed of four excellent new songs
Song I. / Song II. (inside a garland)
Licensed and entered according to Order
Newcastle: Printed by J. Marshall in the Old Flesh-Market
label_when: A title page or the first page of a 4-, 8- or 24-page garland or chapbook. 'Garland' sits in a title followed by 'Composed of / Containing ... songs', and a roman-numbered list of song titles comes before the first song. The printing year uses the 'Printed in the Year' formula.
sung_trap: 'Garland' as a sung noun ('Garland and airy cap adorn', Trowbridge, in the corpus) and in song titles ('The Willow Garland', Herrick) is lyric or title. A label needs the 'Garland, composed of / containing' frame or the contents list.
traditions: English, Scottish and Irish chapbooks and garlands (Dicey, Marshall, Randall, Johnston), American 18th c. songsters
examples: The Sailor's Garland, Composed of several excellent new Songs. I. The Sailor's Return. II. ...

entries.term: Execution and gallows broadside prose (trial account, confession, last dying speech)
variants: The Trial, Sentence, and Execution of ...
Who was executed at ... on Monday last
Copy of Verses (heading before the verse block)
label_when: On a gallows or murder broadside, the prose columns before 'Copy of Verses' (account, trial, confession) are non-lyric. Only the block after 'Copy of Verses' or 'Lines on ...' is verse.
sung_trap: The 'Copy of Verses' itself is often a first-person sung lament ('Come all you tender Christians'). Keep the metrical, rhymed block and drop the justified prose paragraphs. Prose lines are long, unrhymed, and full of dates, names and courtroom terms.
traditions: Catnach, Pitts, Such, Disley and Fortey broadsides (London), Scottish and Irish execution sheets, American murder ballad broadsides
examples: Trial, Sentence and Execution of William Corder, for the Murder of Maria Marten ... COPY OF VERSES.

entries.term: Broadside and miscellany subscription formulas (Finis + Quoth, initials, Ignoto)
label_when: Initials or a pseudonym stand alone on the line after the last stanza, after 'Finis.' or 'quoth', or in the margin beside a psalm number in the Old Version (Sternhold & Hopkins) psalter. England's Helicon and Davison's Poetical Rhapsody sign items 'Ignoto'.
sung_trap: Only 'quoth' inside a metrical line ('quoth he') is sung. The bare initials could be mistaken for a sung exclamation or an OCR fragment. Label them when they are the whole line, end in a full stop and follow the final stanza.
traditions: Black-letter broadsides, England's Helicon (1600), Tottel's Miscellany, Old Version metrical psalter (1562 onward)

entries.term: Songster miscellany prose (toasts, sentiments, jokes, conundrums, stump speeches, burlesque lectures)
label_when: These are songster section headings and the prose filler under them, placed between songs to fill out a page. Label the heading and every unmetered prose line under it until the next song title.
sung_trap: 'Toast' is sung inside drinking songs. The corpus has 'Instead of a Song, boy's, I'll give you a Toast;' (Burns) and ''Tis surely your Duty, to Toast a young Beauty' (D'Urfey). A one-line toast starting 'Here's to' can also open a sung stanza. Label it only under a TOASTS/SENTIMENTS heading or when it is a lone prose line with no rhyme partner. A conundrum has the 'Why ...? Because ...' or 'When is ...?' question-and-answer shape.
traditions: Beadle's Dime Song Books, De Witt, De Marsan, Wehman, Delaney, minstrel songsters, Barnum circus songster, 18th c. British jest-and-song books
examples: TOASTS AND SENTIMENTS. -- May the friends of our youth be the companions of our old age.

entries.term: Collection and songster category section headings (Comic Songs, Sentimental Songs, Poems of Nature ...)
label_when: A section heading alone on a line, usually plural and in CAPS or Title Case, often at a page head or between items, with no stanza following directly under it as its own text. Home Book of Verse and Oxford-type anthologies print 'POEMS OF ...' division headings.
sung_trap: A plural genre noun inside a sung line ('Sing me the songs of the Irish') is lyric. A heading is plural, stands alone, ends without punctuation or with a full stop, and is followed by an item TITLE rather than a verse.
traditions: Songsters, Home Book of Verse, Golden Treasury, Victorian anthologies, collected works (Wordsworth's classes, Byron's Hours of Idleness), children's anthologies

variants: To conclude with the laughable farce of ...
label_when: In minstrel programmes and songsters that print the show order: the part names, the act-order headings and the performer assignments on lines of their own, often with 'by Mr. X' and leader dots.
sung_trap: 'First part' and 'end song' do not occur as sung phrases. 'Plantation' and 'Essence' are sung nouns inside metrical lines. A label needs a performer's name or programme position.
traditions: Christy's, Bryant's and Haverly's minstrels, Wood's Minstrel Songster, Beadle's dime songsters, British Moore and Burgess Minstrels
examples: PART SECOND. -- OLIO. -- Banjo Solo .......... Mr. Hank Mason

entries.term: Concert, music-hall and theatre programmes and books of words
variants: Words of the Songs and Choruses
God Save the Queen (as closing programme item)
The audience is requested to join in the chorus
label_when: The heading of a programme or book of words, or the list of numbered items with performer names, leader dots and times. In a book of words, the frame text around each song (item number, performer, 'Interval') is apparatus.
sung_trap: 'God Save the Queen' and similar anthem titles are sung when their text follows. Here the title is only a listed programme item, so label it unless verse follows under it. 'Join in the chorus' inside a song ('Come, boys, join in the chorus') is sung.
traditions: Victorian and Edwardian music-hall bills, glee-club and choral-society concerts, oratorio and festival books of words, Savoy books of words
examples: INTERVAL. -- Part II. 7. Song ... 'The Holy City' ... Mr. Edward Lloyd.

entries.term: Libretto spoken dialogue (prose between musical numbers)
label_when: In libretti, ballad operas and burlettas, a speaker prefix followed by unmetered prose that runs to the right margin, before the next AIR/SONG/No. heading. The whole speech is non-lyric (spoken drama, not song or recited verse). Number headings mark where the lyric resumes.
sung_trap: Recitative and sung dialogue also carry speaker prefixes, but they are lineated verse that rhymes. Gilbert's sung dialogue such as 'KO-KO. ...' inside a numbered duet is lyric. Prose is detected by justified lines that run on, no rhyme, and sentence-length speeches, and by its place outside a number.
traditions: G&S libretti, Beggar's Opera and other ballad operas, Bickerstaffe and Dibdin comic operas, Victorian burlesques and pantomimes, musical-comedy libretti
examples: PEACHUM. Through all the employments of life ... (prose) -- AIR II. The bonny grey-ey'd morn.

entries.term: Stage positions, discovery and lighting directions
label_when: Inside a parenthesis or bracket, or after Enter/Exit, as a stage-position abbreviation (R., L., C., R.U.E.). 'Discovered' is a label in the opening scene-direction formula 'X discovered ...' set in italics or parentheses.
sung_trap: 'Discovered' is sung in the corpus: Gilbert's 'He was a great Inventor, and discovered, all alone,' and 'Who could give me good advice when he discovered I was'. Label only in 'is/are discovered' scene openings in italics or parentheses. A single-letter 'R.', 'L.' or 'C.' is a label only next to a stage verb or inside a direction.
traditions: G&S and other libretti, acting editions (French's, Lacy's, Dicks'), burlesques, pantomime books
examples: SCENE. -- Quarter-deck of H.M.S. Pinafore. SAILORS, led by BOATSWAIN, discovered cleaning brasswork. (Crosses R.)

entries.term: Music cues and lead-ins in libretti, acting editions and sheet songs
label_when: The word 'Cue' or 'Warn' ends in a colon or sits in a bracket, often followed by a quoted fragment of the preceding dialogue. Play-on and play-off cues sit on lines of their own between dialogue and the next number.
sung_trap: The quoted fragment after 'Cue:' repeats spoken words, so it must not be counted as lyric either. 'Play on' sung inside a lyric ('Play on, minstrel') is lyric.
traditions: Acting editions, melodrama prompt books, music-hall band parts, musical-comedy vocal scores
examples: Cue: '... and the old house fell.' -- Melo. No. 4.

variants: Slide 4: Mother waiting at the gate
label_when: Numbered slide or tableau cues in sheet music and slide-set booklets for 'illustrated songs' (c. 1894-1913), set in the margin or between lines, with a description of the picture.
sung_trap: 'Picture' and 'slide' are sung nouns ('Just a picture of you'). Label only with a number or colon, or when the word sits at a line edge in a bracket or parenthesis.
traditions: American and British illustrated-song sheet music and slide-set booklets, magic-lantern song readings
examples: Slide 6: The old homestead in moonlight.

entries.term: Restoration and 18th c. theatre-song headings (A Song in the Play call'd ...)
variants: A SONG in the Comedy call'd ...
A New SONG in the Play call'd ...
A Song in the Second Act of ...
A Song in the Tragedy of ...
A SONG Sung by Mrs. CAMPION, in the Comedy call'd ...
Set and Sung by Mr. Ramondon
Sung at the Theatre in Dorset-Garden
label_when: A title line combining 'in the Comedy/Play/Tragedy/Opera call'd' with 'Set by', 'Sung by' or 'The Words by'. In the corpus this is the dominant D'Urfey Pills heading shape, e.g. '[v.5] A SONG in the Comedy call'd Justice Buisy ... Set by Mr. John Eccles, Sung by Mrs. Bracegirdle.'
sung_trap: These headings are never sung. The trap is the reverse: 'Scotch Song' is a Restoration genre label for English songs in mock-Scots dialect, so the heading should not mark the lyric itself as foreign or as apparatus.
traditions: Pills to Purge Melancholy, Playford's Choice Ayres and Theater of Music, Orpheus Britannicus, single-sheet engraved songs (c.1690-1740)
examples: A SONG in the Comedy call'd, The Old Batchelour, Set by Mr. HENRY PURCELL.

entries.term: Instrument, staff and accompaniment labels (lute-song, continuo, obbligato, vocal-score staves)
variants: For the Lute and Bass Viol
label_when: A staff name at the left margin of a score transcribed as text, a line of figured-bass digits, or a scoring note under a title ('with Violin obbligato'). Elizabethan lute books print 'To the Lute' or 'Basso' at part heads.
sung_trap: 'Harp', 'lute' and 'organ' are common sung nouns ('Tune thy lute', 'The harp that once'). Label only when the word stands alone at the start of a staff line, follows 'for' or 'with' in a subtitle, or is paired with 'obbligato' or 'solo'. Lines of figured-bass digits are never lyric.
traditions: Dowland, Campion and Rosseter lute-song books, Playford/Purcell songs with thorough-bass, Victorian parlour songs with obbligato, octavo part-songs, vocal scores
examples: Voice } ... Piano } ... (with Violin obbligato ad lib.)

entries.term: Latin motet-division labels (supplementary to 'Prima parte / Seconda parte')
variants: The first part / The second part (Byrd, Morley)
The second part of the former
label_when: Alone on a line between sections of a madrigal, motet or anthem text, or as a heading suffix ('... Secunda pars').
sung_trap: These are never sung. In Latin motet texts that sit inside English songbooks, keep the Latin lyric lines and drop only the 'pars' line.
traditions: Byrd's Psalmes, Sonets and Songs and Gradualia, Morley, Wilbye and Weelkes madrigal books, Fellowes's English Madrigal Verse

label_when: A type label alone on a line, or in parentheses under a title or beside the tune, naming the job the song served. It is usually followed by 'Solo'/'Chorus' or 'Shantyman'/'Crew' assignments, which are already listed.
sung_trap: Pull words in shanties are sung and often printed in CAPS or italics for emphasis ('Way, haul away, we'll HAUL away, Joe'; 'Heave and pawl'). The capitals mark the beat and are lyric, not a label. 'Capstan' and 'windlass' are sung nouns inside verse.
traditions: Davis & Tozer Sailors' Songs or Chanties (1887), Bullen, Terry, Whall's Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties, Sharp's English Folk-Chanteys, Lomax cowboy and work-song collections
examples: WHISKY JOHNNY (Halliard Shanty). Solo: Oh, whisky is the life of man, Chorus: Whisky, Johnny!

entries.term: Folk-song provenance metadata (singer, place, date, collector, noter)
variants: Sung by Mr. H. Burstow, Horsham, Sussex, 1893
Sung by Mrs. X (aged 74), Bridgwater, Somerset
Journal of the Folk-Song Society, vol. ii, p. 41
label_when: A line, often in small type or italics under a title or after the last stanza, giving the singer's name with age, place and year, and/or the collector with 'Noted / Collected / Taken down by'. A bare place name in parentheses under a spiritual's title (Slave Songs of the United States) is a locality tag.
sung_trap: Place names are sung in many songs ('In Charleston, Virginia, ...'). A locality tag is parenthesised, ends in a full stop and stands alone under the title. 'Sung by' in a lyric line ('The song that was sung by my mother') is sung, so the label needs a personal name followed by a place or date.
traditions: Slave Songs of the United States (1867), Fisk and Hampton jubilee books, Journal of the Folk-Song Society, Sharp/Baring-Gould/Broadwood collections, Lomax, Child and Greig-Duncan field notes
examples: (Port Royal Islands.)  /  Noted from Mr. Henry Hills, Lodsworth, Sussex, 1901.

variants: The children stand in a circle
One child stands in the middle
The child in the centre chooses ...
(All fall down.) as a printed cue
label_when: A 'Directions'/'The Game'/'Motions' heading and its prose paragraph, or a parenthesised imperative gesture at line end or on its own line, in children's song books, kindergarten books and collections of singing games.
sung_trap: Many action words are the lyric itself: 'Ring-a-ring o' roses ... we all fall down', 'This is the way we clap our hands', 'Turn, cinnamon, turn', 'Here we go round the mulberry bush'. They are sung when unparenthesised, metrical and rhymed. Label only parenthesised or bracketed imperatives and the prose paragraph under a Directions heading.
traditions: Newell's Games and Songs of American Children (1883), Gomme's Traditional Games (1894-98), kindergarten songbooks (Froebel, Eleanor Smith, Hill sisters), school songbooks, Mother Goose editions with motions
examples: THE MULBERRY BUSH. Directions: The children join hands and dance round, singing ... (Clap hands.)

entries.term: Country-dance, morris and sword-dance figure directions
variants: Longways for as many as will
Lead up a double and back
Down the middle and up again
label_when: Prose or abbreviated choreography in dance books and folk-play collections. Abbreviations such as 'cu.', 'wo.' and '1st man', bar counts ('8 bars'), and numbered figures under a tune title are apparatus.
sung_trap: Play-party songs and some square-dance calls are sung or chanted in rhyme ('Swing your partner, promenade all, / Skip to my Lou'). Keep metrical, rhymed call lines inside a song. Label prose figure descriptions, abbreviated forms (cu., wo.) and bar counts.
traditions: Playford's English Dancing Master (1651 onward), Sharp's Country Dance Book and Morris Book, sword-dance and mummers' play collections, American play-party and square-dance call books
examples: Longways for as many as will. -- Lead up a double and back. That again. Set and turn single.

label_when: A teaching label under a song title (Rote Song, Exercise, Grade), or a performer prefix for a child or a class in a Sunday-school exercise ('First Child.', 'Class.', 'Superintendent.') at line start followed by a recitation or response.
sung_trap: 'Class', 'school' and 'teacher' are sung nouns in school songs ('Our school is the best'). Label them only as a line-initial prefix ending in a full stop or colon. The verse a child recites after the prefix is recited lyric and should be kept. A prose pledge or salute is not lyric.
traditions: American graded school music series (Normal Music Course, Natural Music Course), Sunday-school songbooks (Bradbury, Lowry, Doane), Children's Day and Easter exercise pamphlets, British Tonic Sol-fa school books
examples: CHILDREN'S DAY EXERCISE. First Child. -- I bring a lily white and fair ... School. -- (Sing No. 12.)

entries.term: College and glee-club songbook apparatus (yells, class odes, fraternity heads, class-year tags)
variants: Rah! Rah! Rah! (as a printed yell)
Greek-letter fraternity heads: ΔΚΕ, Ψ Υ, Φ Β Κ, Σ Χ
label_when: Yell headings and yell blocks (chanted, but not song lyric), occasion headings for class and commencement odes, Greek-letter fraternity headings, and a class-year apostrophe tag ('92) right after a contributor's name.
sung_trap: 'Rah! rah!' and 'Hurrah' do occur inside sung college songs, and Alma Mater addresses are sung ('Alma Mater, dear to thee'). A yell is a separate block under a YELL/CHEER heading, built from spelled letters and staccato syllables ('Brek-ek-ek-ex, co-ax'). The class tag '92 is a 2-digit year after a name or a comma.
traditions: Carmina Yalensia, Harvard, Princeton and Cornell songbooks, Student Songs, fraternity songbooks, glee-club programmes (1860-1929)
examples: CLASS ODE. Tune -- Auld Lang Syne. Words by J. H. Smith, '92.

entries.term: Lodge, temperance and society odes and ritual labels
variants: So mote it be (as printed response)
label_when: Ode headings by ritual position (Opening, Closing, Installation) and officer prefixes (W. M., Chaplain., N. G.) at the start of a ritual exchange. The prose ritual between odes is non-lyric.
sung_trap: 'So mote it be' is the Masonic Amen and is often sung by all as the response. Treat it like Amen: lyric when it ends an ode's text or sits under 'All:', apparatus when it ends a spoken prayer. The pledge text is recited prose, not lyric.
traditions: Masonic, Odd Fellows, Knights of Pythias and Grange songbooks, Good Templar and Band of Hope melodists, Washingtonian and W.C.T.U. temperance songsters
examples: OPENING ODE. Tune -- Old Hundred. ... Chaplain. -- Let us pray.

entries.term: Public-reading and recitation occasion headnotes (Read at / Delivered before / Recited at)
variants: [Read at the Convention which formed the American Anti-Slavery Society ...
Read at the dedication of the Bartholdi Statue, New York
Read at the Annual Dinner of ...
Read at the Harvard Commemoration, July 21, 1865
Delivered before the Phi Beta Kappa Society
Spoken by Miss Fontenelle on her Benefit Night
label_when: A line under the title or in brackets, in italics or small type, beginning 'Read / Delivered / Recited / Pronounced / Spoken at/before/by'. The corpus has Whittier's '[Read at the Convention ...' and Rankin's 'Read at the dedication of the Bartholdi Statue, New York'.
sung_trap: 'Read' and 'spoken' occur inside verse ('the words he read'). A headnote begins its line with the past participle plus at/before/by, followed by an institution, event or date, and does not rhyme.
traditions: Occasional verse of Holmes, Whittier, Lowell, Rankin and Longfellow, Poems of American History, Phi Beta Kappa and Commemoration odes, Burns's prologues
examples: Read at the dedication of the Bartholdi Statue, New York

entries.term: Facing-page and interlinear original-language text (translations, bilingual libretti, Gaelic/Welsh with English)
variants: Latin text with English verse on the facing page
column merge: 'Gaudeamus igitur      Let us now in youth rejoice'
label_when: In facing or interleaved printings, the non-English column or block is not English lyric for this corpus. 'Original'/'Translation' headings and line counters are labels. A two-column OCR merge interleaves the two languages on one physical line. The corpus has Lovelace's 'with a Latin translation.' and 'The same in LATIN.'
sung_trap: Macaronic carols and English songs keep Latin or Gaelic refrains as SUNG lyric: 'In dulci jubilo', 'Caput apri defero', 'Gaudete', 'Puer nobis nascitur', 'Shule, shule, shule agrah', 'Eileen aroon', 'Cushla machree', 'Fal de ral'. These alternate line by line with English in one stanza, rhyme with the English lines, and carry no Original/Translation heading. Drop only a whole parallel block or column in the other language.
traditions: Greek Anthology and Horace translations, Moore's and Mangan's Irish, Brooke's Reliques of Irish Poetry, Highland song collections (Gaelic and English), Welsh Melodies (Brinley Richards), bilingual opera libretti (Covent Garden, Her Majesty's), student songbooks with Gaudeamus
examples: The Original. / Integer vitae scelerisque purus ... / Translation. / The man of life upright ...

entries.term: Latin, German and other original-incipit headings over translated hymns and psalms; breviary source tags
variants: From the Latin of St. Ambrose
From the Greek of St. John Damascene
From the German of Paul Gerhardt
label_when: A foreign-language incipit in italics or small caps directly under or above an English hymn or psalm title, or after the Psalm number in the Prayer-Book and Old Version psalters. A source-office tag sits in the credit block.
sung_trap: 'Adeste fideles', 'Gloria in excelsis' and 'Alleluia' are sung when they are the text of the stanza or refrain. An incipit heading is a lone line before an English text that does not continue in Latin.
traditions: Hymns Ancient & Modern, the English Hymnal, Neale's and Caswall's translations, Catherine Winkworth's Lyra Germanica, Book of Common Prayer psalter, Old Version and Scottish psalters

entries.term: Hebrew-letter section heads (Psalm 119, Lamentations, alphabetic acrostics)
variants: Hebrew glyphs: א ב ג ד ה
label_when: A Hebrew letter name alone on a line, in caps or small caps, before each 8-verse block of Psalm 119 (metrical and prose psalters, Watts's Psalm 119 parts) and Lamentations paraphrases.
sung_trap: 'HE.' collides with the He./She. dialogue prefix, and 'NUN.', 'PE.', 'MEM.' and 'AIN.' look like abbreviations. Read these as Hebrew heads only inside Psalm 119 or Lamentations, in alphabetical order. None of these words is sung.
traditions: Book of Common Prayer psalter, Coverdale and King James psalms, Old and New Version metrical psalters, Scottish Psalter (1650), hymnals' responsive readings
examples: ALEPH. -- Blessed are the undefiled in the way ...

entries.term: Prayer-Book psalter day-and-office divisions and selections
variants: Psalter, or Psalms of David, pointed as they are to be sung or said in churches
label_when: A heading line dividing a prose or pointed psalter into the 30-day morning and evening course, or a numbered 'Selection' heading in American Episcopal and other hymnals.
sung_trap: 'Morning' and 'evening' are sung words. A label combines an ordinal day with Morning Prayer or Evening Prayer, or 'Selection' with a numeral, on a line of its own.
traditions: Book of Common Prayer (1662 and American 1789/1892), cathedral psalters, Anglican chant books

entries.term: Scottish metrical Paraphrases and numbered paraphrase heads
variants: Translations and Paraphrases, in Verse, of several passages of Sacred Scripture
label_when: A numbered heading 'Paraphrase N.' with an optional scripture reference, in Scottish Presbyterian psalm-and-paraphrase books and the hymnals that reprint them.
sung_trap: 'Paraphrase' as a generic poem-title word is already listed. The numbered form is never sung.
traditions: Church of Scotland Translations and Paraphrases (1781), Scottish psalm books, Presbyterian hymnals in America

variants: Indulgence of 100 days, once a day
Stations of the Cross: First Station
Our Father, Hail Mary, Glory be (said)
Benediction of the Most Holy Sacrament
label_when: An indulgence grant (days, conditions, pope and year) printed under a hymn or prayer. Censorship formulas (Nihil Obstat, Imprimatur already listed). Devotional-sequence headings (Station, Mystery). Recitation counts in parentheses.
sung_trap: 'Pray for us' and 'Ora pro nobis' are SUNG litany responses after each invocation in a sung litany. Keep them when they alternate with sung invocations, and drop them only in prose prayers. 'O Salutaris' and 'Tantum Ergo' are sung texts when their verses follow.
traditions: Catholic hymnals (St. Basil's, Crown of Jesus, Westminster Hymnal, Roman Hymnal), the Raccolta, Faber's and Caswall's hymns, Catholic prayer-and-hymn manuals
examples: An indulgence of 300 days, once a day. (Leo XIII., 1886.)

entries.term: Long-poem divisions not otherwise listed (Night, Day, Week, Station, Month, Letter, Meditation, Vision)
label_when: A division word plus an ordinal or numeral, alone on a line, heading a section of a long poem (Young's Night Thoughts, Blake's Four Zoas 'Night the First', Du Bartas/Sylvester 'Weeks', Spenser's Shepheardes Calender months, Anstey's New Bath Guide 'Letter I.', Edward Taylor's 'Meditation').
sung_trap: 'Night', 'day', 'dream' and 'vision' are among the most frequent sung nouns. Label only with an ordinal or numeral (the First, I., 2.) and nothing else on the line, or in the 'Month. Ægloga N.' frame.
traditions: 18th c. long poems, Spenser, Sylvester's Du Bartas, Blake prophetic books, epistolary verse narratives, colonial American devotional verse

entries.term: Emblem-book structure (Emblem, motto, Pictura, Epigram, quotation blocks)
variants: S. AUGUST. Soliloq. cap. 20 (patristic quotation block)
label_when: An 'Emblem N.' heading, the scripture motto under it, the prose patristic quotations after the poem (with S. AUG., S. BERN. citations), and the 'Epig.' label before the closing couplet.
sung_trap: 'Emblem' is a common sung word. The corpus has 'Emblem of happiness,' (Hogg), 'Emblem of that which will not fade or die!' (Hemans) and 'Emblem of dread to tyrant holds'. Label only with a numeral or with 'Book N.'. The epigram couplet after 'Epig.' is verse and should be kept.
traditions: Quarles's Emblems (1635), Wither's Collection of Emblems, Bunyan's Book for Boys and Girls, Harvey's School of the Heart
examples: BOOK I. EMBLEM III. -- Psalm 13. 3. ... EPIG. 3.

entries.term: Epitaph inscription formulas and monument prose
label_when: In epitaph poems printed with their monument text: the capitalised prose inscription block (name, dates, age, erector, abbreviations such as D.O.M. or H.S.E.) before or after the verse. Lines set in centred capitals that follow monument conventions are apparatus.
sung_trap: 'Here lies' very often opens the epitaph VERSE itself ('Here lies our sovereign lord the king'). Keep it when the line is metrical and rhymes with the next. Drop it in a prose block with dates and age.
traditions: Epitaph collections, Oxford and Home Book of Verse epitaph sections, 17th-18th c. miscellanies, church-monument verse in county histories
examples: SACRED TO THE MEMORY OF / JOHN SMITH / WHO DEPARTED THIS LIFE / MAY 4, 1790, AGED 72 YEARS.

entries.term: Epistolary salutations and letter frames around verse
variants: Ellisland, 1790. Dear Sir, -- (prose letter preceding verses)
label_when: Prose salutation and closing lines, and the letter body around verses sent in correspondence (Burns, Cowper and Byron editions). A prose salutation sits alone on its line, ends in a comma or dash, and comes before an unmetered prose paragraph. The signature side is already listed.
sung_trap: Verse epistles open with sung or recited salutations inside the meter: 'Dear _____, I'll gie ye some advice,' (Burns, in the corpus) and 'Dear Smith, the slee'st, pawkie thief'. Keep a salutation that starts a rhymed metrical line. Label it only when the next line is prose.
traditions: Burns's letters and epistles, Cowper's letters, Byron's letters in collected works, Lamb, Swift and Pope correspondence editions
examples: Dear Sir, -- I enclose you a song which I composed lately ...

entries.term: Name and occasion blanks and alternative-word slots
label_when: A blank rule, the liturgical 'N.' or a parenthesised alternative word inside a lyric line, meant for the performer to fill. Count the line as lyric but drop the alternative in parentheses. A blank alone on a line, or inside an air/tune slot, is apparatus. The corpus has '[air: ___________________________________]' in Moore and 'Dear _____,' in Burns.
sung_trap: The line itself is sung. Only the parenthesised duplicate ('King (Queen)') is non-lyric. A blank rule inside a sung line stands for a sung name (or a censored word) and should be kept as one token, not counted as a separator.
traditions: Wedding and funeral hymns, national anthems, lodge and birthday songs, Burns's blanked names, Moore's unknown airs

entries.term: Riddle, enigma and charade answer lines
variants: Answer to the Riddle in our last
Solution of the Enigma in No. 12
label_when: After a verse riddle, enigma or charade, a line beginning Answer/Solution/Key, or a parenthesised one- or two-word noun phrase alone on the line, gives the solution. In periodical and songster reprints, answers to earlier puzzles are listed as prose.
sung_trap: 'The answer' is sung in verse ('The answer, my friend ...'). Ballad dialogue 'Answer.' and 'The Answer' headings are already listed. A riddle solution follows a riddle, is a short noun phrase, and does not rhyme.
traditions: Nursery-rhyme collections (Halliwell), Mother Goose riddles, Swift and Cowper riddles, songster and almanac enigmas, children's magazines
examples: In marble walls as white as milk ... Answer: An egg.

entries.term: Sheet-music genre subtitles not otherwise listed (supplementary)
label_when: A small-type line directly under a sheet-music or songster title naming the song's commercial type, often in parentheses or quotation marks, sometimes repeated on the cover and on the first page of music.
sung_trap: 'Love song', 'war song' and 'mother' are frequent sung phrases ('Sing me a love song'). A subtitle stands alone under the title, in Title Case, with no verb, before the credits block.
traditions: Tin Pan Alley sheet music (1890-1929), British music-hall sheet songs, Victorian ballad sheets, songsters
examples: DOWN BY THE OLD MILL STREAM -- Waltz Ballad

entries.term: Sheet-music cover blurbs, professional-copy notices and record/roll tie-ins
variants: The Song Sensation of the Season
Positively the Biggest Song Hit in Years
The Song That Made X Famous
On sale at all Woolworth stores
Ask your dealer for the record
label_when: Cover and first-page marketing text: superlative taglines, photo-inset captions, professional-copy stamps and catalogue numbers for records and piano rolls. Ad catalogue lines already listed; these are the remaining cover-blurb forms.
sung_trap: Taglines can quote a song's hook line in quotation marks ('The song with the "Oh!"'). Treat a quoted fragment in a blurb as apparatus unless it is in the lyric block. Word rolls print the lyric itself between roll codes: keep the words and drop the roll number and code letters.
traditions: Tin Pan Alley sheet music (Remick, Feist, Witmark, Shapiro-Bernstein), British Francis Day & Hunter, photoplay theme songs, Q.R.S. and Aeolian word rolls
examples: PROFESSIONAL COPY -- Not for Sale. Featured with great success by Al Jolson. Victor Record 18564.

entries.term: Back-cover and inside-cover thematic advertisements quoting other songs
variants: Try this over on your piano
