Songster back-page: 'The following popular songs are published by ...' with first verse printed
Copies of this song ... can be had at
label_when: On back covers and inside wrappers, a block headed by another song's title and 'Chorus' or 'Try this over', followed by 4-8 lines of THAT song's lyric under music and a copyright line. The whole block is apparatus for the item being staged: it is a different song, cut short.
sung_trap: The quoted lines are real sung lyric, but of another song. Do not merge them into the staged song. They follow its last stanza and end-mark, under a different title, and the block closes with a publisher copyright line. If the advertised song is wanted, it must come from its own sheet.
traditions: Tin Pan Alley and British music-hall sheet music (1900-1929), dime songster back pages, parlour sheet-music wrappers
examples: TRY THIS OVER -- 'When You Wore a Tulip' -- CHORUS: When you wore a tulip, a sweet yellow tulip ... Copyright MCMXIV by Leo Feist, Inc.

entries.term: Air: national-origin descriptors (supplementary to Irish/Scotch/Welsh Air)
label_when: After 'Air--' or as a standalone line under a title in Moore's National Airs and similar collections, naming the origin of the melody rather than the tune title.
sung_trap: Nationality adjectives are sung ('a Highland air', 'the Venetian moon'). A label stands alone under the title with 'Air' capitalised, and the line has no verb.
traditions: Moore's National Airs (1818-1827), Thomson's collections, Hemans's songs to national airs, Victorian drawing-room collections
examples: OFT, IN THE STILLY NIGHT. (Scotch Air.)  /  THOSE EVENING BELLS. (Petersburg Air.)

entries.term: Credentials, unit and affiliation tags after names (supplementary to honorifics)
label_when: Right after an author or composer name in a credit line, a degree, order, clerical title or military unit, set off by a comma. War-song anthologies (Southern War Songs, American War Ballads) often credit soldiers by company and regiment.
sung_trap: Regiment and company names are sung in war songs ('The Black Regiment' is a corpus title, and 'the Fifth Georgia' is sung). The tag form uses an abbreviation (Co., Regt., C.S.A.) and follows a personal name.
traditions: Hymnals and anthem credits, cathedral music, Civil War anthologies (Fagan, Eggleston, Browne), naval and military songbooks
examples: Words by Col. W. S. Hawkins, C.S.A., Prisoner at Camp Chase.

entries.term: Order-of-worship items not otherwise listed (Call to Worship, Ascription, Sentences)
label_when: The heading of a service item in a hymnal's orders of worship, or service-book headings listed as a sequence. Prose sentences under 'Offertory Sentences' are scripture, not lyric.
sung_trap: Choral responses ('Hear our prayer, O Lord') are SUNG short texts. Keep them when they are lineated under a Choral Response heading with music. Drop the headings themselves and the prose sentences.
traditions: American Protestant hymnals 1880-1929 (Methodist Hymnal 1905, Pilgrim Hymnal), Unitarian service books, Scottish and English nonconformist service books
examples: ORDER OF WORSHIP. Organ Prelude. Call to Worship. Hymn. Responsive Reading No. 12.

entries.term: Running quotation marks at the start of every line of a quoted passage
label_when: 18th and early 19th c. printing repeated the opening quotation mark at the start of every line of a quoted speech or epigraph. When the same mark opens three or more consecutive lines and only the last line closes it, the marks on the inner lines are artifacts: strip them, but keep the words.
sung_trap: Dialogue ballads open each new speaker's line with a genuine quote. Real opening quotes alternate with closing quotes inside the stanza. Running quotes have no closing mark on the intermediate lines.
traditions: Percy's Reliques, 18th c. miscellanies and magazines, early Wordsworth, Scott and Campbell editions, PG transcriptions that keep the convention
examples: “Now stay thy hand, thou bold baron, / “For I am but a maid; / “And ...”

variants: Click here to shop the Bartleby Bookstore
label_when: Any wiki template in double braces, any XML or TEI element in angle brackets, or a web-site navigation line or metadata field label ('Meter:', 'Topic:', 'Text Information'), left in a scraped or converted text. Some corpus files are staged from Kalliope XML (thabz/Kalliope), so its element names can leak.
sung_trap: Angle brackets and braces do not occur in sung text. 'Meter' and 'topic' as field labels end in a colon. 'Previous' and 'Next' are sung only inside a metrical line.
traditions: Wikisource, Bartleby, hymnary.org, CCEL, Mudcat/DigiTrad, Kalliope, TEI-encoded corpora (ECCO-TCP, EEBO-TCP)

entries.term: Invisible and control characters (BOM, soft hyphen, zero-width, OCR not-sign hyphen, CR)
variants: ﻿ (byte-order mark at file or line start)
¬ (not-sign used by IA/Google OCR for a line-break hyphen)
label_when: Strip or normalise everywhere. A '¬' at line end joins a hyphenated word across lines. A soft hyphen is invisible but splits word counts. A BOM before the first line can stop a header or label regex from matching. The corpus notes CRLF-to-LF staging for the Otterbein hymnal.
sung_trap: None of these is sung. The only trap is that stripping a soft hyphen or '¬' must not join two separate sung words: join only when the parts form a dictionary word.
traditions: Internet Archive and HathiTrust OCR, Google Books text, older PG files (ISO-8859-1, CRLF), Windows-converted e-texts

reader_notes.sections: CROSS-CUTTING DETECTION RULES. (1) A section label is apparatus; the section's BODY is lyric (verse prologue, epilogue, envoi, invocation, dedication, interlude). Exceptions where the body is apparatus too: a prose Argument, a prose Preface or Dedication, a 'SCENE.--' setting, a 'Spoken' stage aside if spoken text is not counted, instrumental cues (Symphony, Vamp, Dance, Break). (2) Three label shapes cover nearly every hit: (a) BARE LINE: the term plus at most a numeral/ordinal, a '(...)' qualifier, 'of/for/to ...' heading formula, and terminal '.', ':', '.--', '--' or em-dash, often in caps/small caps, usually with a blank line or stanza break around it; (b) LINE-INITIAL PREFIX: the term + '.--' / '--' / ':' / '.' then lyric on the same line (Burns 'Chorus.--', Elizabethan 'Cho. THEN', spirituals 'Solo. --', 'Fonn:'); strip only the prefix; (c) PARENTHESISED or BRACKETED inline/trailing marks ('(bis)', '(Spoken)', '(Dance)', '(2nd time)', '[Music: _CHO. of all._]'). (3) Sung-word discrimination: a candidate is lyric if it carries an article/possessive/adjective, a following verb or object, a following comma plus more lyric words, lowercase continuation without dash punctuation, or sits inside the metre of a stanza. The highest-risk sung words in this corpus (verified by grep) are Fit (30+ line-initial sung uses), Part (~20), Lament, Patter, Repeat, Answer/Reply, Verse, Fine, and Strain; also generically: air, round, break, end, close, bridge, song, burden, refrain (verb), chorus (noun), all, he/she, lay, port, catch, glee, act, scene, amen, hallelujah, noel/nowell. (4) What the corpus already stages: '[VERSE n]', '[CHORUS]', '[CHORUS n]', '[REFRAIN]', '[BURDEN]', '[PATTER]', '[URLAR]', '[URLAR n]', '[SIUBHAL]', '[SIUBHAL n]', '[CRUNLUATH]' are the staging tags; leftover printed labels still inside lyric bodies include 'Chorus.--' and 'Chorus--' (Burns), 'CHORUS.'/'CHORUS:'/'Chorus', 'Cho.' (madrigal texts), 'Refrain.--', 'PAUSE.'/'PAUSE I.'/'PAUSE II.' (Watts), 'Second Part. L. M.'/'C. M.' (Watts), 'Part I'/'Part II', 'ENVOY' x6, 'L'ENVOI', 'ODE.', 'Doxology.', 'Hymn 77.' and 'Hymn n:n. ...' headings, 'Psalm 147. 19 20.', 'HE.'/'SHE.' dialogue labels, bare 'I'/'II'/'III', 'Common Metre.'/'Short Metre.' (metre domain), '[Gothic: Eclogue.]' x13 and '[Music: ...]', '[Sidenote: ...]' digitization artifacts, and the direction sentence 'Repeat the first stanza to complete the tune.' (5) Character/speaker names in libretti and verse drama (DAEMON:, MEPHISTOPHELES:, CYCLOPS:, KO-KO, etc.) are a sister category (speaker labels); they use the same bare-line/colon shapes and should be detected by the same machinery, but they are not enumerated here. (6) Numbering mixes with every label: roman (I., ii.), arabic (1, 1., (1), [1]), ordinals in digits (1st, 2d, 2nd, 3d, 3rd, 4th) and spelled (First, Second, Third, ... Last), ordinal-after formulas ('Part the Second', 'Fit the Third', 'Canto Fourth', 'Duan First'), Latin ('Primus', 'Prima', 'Liber Primus'), and 'the Third and Last'. (7) Deliberately left out or only cross-referenced: tune names and 'AIR--\"X\"'/'TUNE--' designations, metre labels (L.M., C.M., S.M., 8s & 7s, P.M.), tempo/expression marks (Andante, ad lib., rit.), footnotes, page numbers, 'NOTES:' blocks, by-lines and source citations - these belong to the meter/tune, tempo, editorial and attribution domains. Also omitted as never printed as labels in English song/poem sources of the period: sonnet 'octave/sestet/volta' divisions (except teaching anthologies, very rare), 'bob and wheel', 'cauda'. Modern pop section names (pre-chorus, post-chorus, hook, outro, middle eight, bridge) are listed for completeness but should have zero native hits in 1600-1929 printings; a hit means modern editorial contamination. (8) Ambiguity to flag, not auto-strip: form-name lines that are the item's real TITLE (e.g. 'Prelude', 'Recessional', 'A Psalm of Life', 'Hymn to Intellectual Beauty') belong in TITLE, not body; 'Amen'/'Hallelujah'/'Noel'/'Selah' after a hymn or carol are usually sung; incipit lines ending in '&c.' are real lyric words acting as a repeat pointer.
reader_notes.stage and liturgy:
CROSS-CUTTING RULES.
(1) Prefix rule. Most labels in this domain are line-INITIAL PREFIXES that share a line with sung text ('Cho. THEN UNDERSTAND...', 'Choir.--O Tibbie...', 'Both. For a' the joys, &c.', 'He. -  When he looks...', 'CHA.  A slave!', 'Ans. Heat ye...'). Strip only up to and including the prefix's terminal punctuation ('.', ':', '.—', '--', '. -'); never drop the line. Speaker prefixes can also occur MID-line after a run of 2+ spaces (Lovelace: 'You must, lost fool, come in.    W.  Oh, let me in!').
(2) Punctuation test for common words. All / Both / He / She / Men / Girls / Boys / Women / Echo / Voice / Full / Leader / Answer each begin many sung lines. The label form is word + full stop or colon (optionally + parenthetical) + a NEW capitalised sentence or end of line. A comma, 'of', or a continuing verb or noun means it is sung. 'He.', 'She.', 'All.', 'Both.' as complete sentences essentially never occur in sung English.
(3) Parentheticals. They are sung far more often in this corpus than they are directions ('(Hurry!)', '(Hark to the thrush's trilling)', '(Butter and eggs...)'). Strip a parenthetical only if it is a 3rd-person present stage verb, a 'to X' addressee, an aside/within/off marker, a sound/music cue, or a one-word performer/dance cue. Keep it if it rhymes, scans, repeats as a refrain, or is in 1st/2nd person.
(4) Brackets. The 18th-century/Shakespearean unclosed '[' (e.g. '[Exeunt.', '_[Exit FRANCES._') collides with the harness's own structural tags ([VERSE n], [CHORUS], [BURDEN], [REFRAIN], [Sidenote ...]). Classify by content: a bracket containing Enter/Exit/Exeunt/Manet/Aside/Within, or a character name in caps, is a stage direction. The harness tags are structural and are not this checklist's concern.
(5) Italic markup. Underscore italics (_..._) mark directions and speaker tags in the staged text ('_Mrs. Thorpe (aside)._', 'SCENE II.--_Noon..._'). Italic alone is NOT sufficient, because the corpus also italicises sung refrains and emphasis ('(_Buy my cherries ..._)', '_greeting_'). Combine it with the rules above.
(6) Latin incipits and liturgical words. Amen, Alleluia, Hallelujah, Hosanna, Gloria, Kyrie eleison, 'Miserere Domine' are USUALLY SUNG. Treat them as labels only when they are a lone heading line followed by an English translation or a different text block, or when they appear in a 'use'/rubric line. Default an Amen to sung; flag bracketed '(Amen)' for policy.
(7) Spoken material. Prologues, melodrama, music-hall 'Spoken' patter and recitation lines are recited text: strip the label but keep the text, under the corpus policy that counts sung OR recited lyric. Purely prose stage descriptions, Dramatis Personae blocks, Arguments and rubrics are wholly apparatus.
(8) Single-letter ambiguity. 'V.' and 'R.' can be versicle/response, speaker initials (Lovelace V.) or author initials ('R. Burns', 'R.B.'); 'A.' can be Answer, Alto or the sung article; 'S. A. T. B.' are part letters; 'B.' and 'T.' are often initials. Decide from context: an alternating V./R. pair is liturgical; an initial followed by a surname is attribution (another domain); an initial followed by 2+ spaces and speech is a speaker.
(9) Corpus-attested look-alike sung lines to use as negative tests: 'Enter! fear not the bars', 'Act,--act in the living Present!', 'Scene of glory and dread!', 'Air with no breath of earth to stain it', 'Exit bid to every woe', 'Catch me, cowardly knaves', 'All under the willow-tree', 'All alone on the hillside--', 'Amen, Amen:', 'Miserere Domine.', 'Round the old tree.', 'a great Te Deum'.

HENRY LAWES.', 'R. Burns'), titles and dedications ('TO LUCASTA.'), and the harness '--- TITLE/SOURCE/NOTE:' header lines. reader_notes.directions and metre:
CROSS-CUTTING RULES
1. Position is the main discriminator. Almost every word in this domain is also ordinary English. A direction is (a) alone on its line, or (b) line-initial and followed by tune or label punctuation (':', '--', '.--', ' - ', or ', ' plus a quoted or italic proper title), or (c) line-final and enclosed in parentheses, brackets or italics after the sung line's terminal punctuation. It has no subject, no finite verb (except imperatives with a structural object: repeat, omit, sing verses, vamp), and does not take part in the stanza's meter or rhyme. A sung occurrence sits inside a clause, takes an article, possessive or object, and scans or rhymes.
2. Line-initial vs line-final matters for 'Air': 'Air--X' line-initial is apparatus; '...heavy Air:' line-final is sung (D'Urfey). Restoration printing capitalises nouns, so capitalisation proves nothing for pre-1750 texts.
3. When a label and sung text share a line ('Solo. -- Sin's rooster's crowed'; 'Chorus.--My heart's in the Highlands'; '_p_ Sleep, baby, sleep'; 'Rise, rise, etc.'), split them: annotate the label and keep the words. Never delete a whole line because it contains a direction token.
4. Some phrases never mean anything musical, so cheap regexes are safe for them: pp, ff, mf, sfz, fp, cresc., dim., rit., rall., accel., D.C. (but not 'Washington, D. C.', and not D.C.M.), D.S., Dal Segno, Da Capo, al Fine, al Coda, Tacet, Colla voce, Ad lib., 8va, Ped., M.M., the Italian tempo words (except 'Grave'), meter labels when not initials, digit-dot meter strings that match syllable counts, and lines made only of chord symbols or sol-fa letters.
5. Abbreviation collisions to guard explicitly: C.M./L.M./S.M./H.M./D.C./D.S./P.M. as personal initials, 'His/Her Majesty', 'post meridiem' or 'District of Columbia'; 'Ten.' (tenor/tenuto) vs 'ten'; 'Do.' (ditto) vs 'do'; '5s.' (shillings) vs '5s' (meter); 'Psalm 49. 6 9.' (scripture) vs '8.7.8.7.' (meter); 'D.C.M.' (Double Common Metre) vs 'D.C.' (Da Capo); 'Tune Uke' vs 'Tune:'; '(2)' speaker number (Barnes) vs '(2)' repeat count.
6. Tune names are singable words of OTHER songs ('Auld Lang Syne', 'Ye Banks and Braes', 'Over the hills and far away'). In tune-line position they are apparatus, even in ballad operas where 'AIR XVI. Over the hills and far away.' is followed by new words. Check that a title-hoisted first line is not counted twice.
7. Repeat directions say how many times to sing something, but the counted text should be what is PRINTED. Do not expand 'bis', 'twice', '&c.', 'D.C.' or 'Chorus after each verse' into duplicate text unless the project adopts an explicit expansion policy. Annotate the abbreviated return (the corpus already does this for '&c.').
8. Spoken and patter passages and the final hymn 'Amen' are policy questions, not pure apparatus. The label is apparatus, but the text under 'Spoken' is performed (recited), and the hymnal 'Amen' is sung. Tag them rather than delete them.

CORPUS FINDINGS FROM THIS SURVEY (read-only)
- eng_hymn_watts.txt:13301 stages 'To the tune of the 113th Psalm' as a --- TITLE; it is a tune line.
- eng_celtic_thomas_moore.txt:3320 hoists '(Time - the Ninth Century)' into [air: ...] together with 'Air - Cruiskeen Lawn'; the time-setting header is not tune information. Similar <line> nesting appears at line 320 ('Written on Returning a Blank Book').
- Inline Burns 'Tune--“...”' lines remain in body text at eng_celtic_robert_burns.txt:21183, 21705 and 21839; they should be apparatus.
- D'Urfey [Music: ...] blocks (eng_hall_thomas_durfey.txt) contain duplicated underlay words and part labels ('_First Nose._', '_CHO. of all._').
- Watts meter and part headers ('Hymn 3:26. 1st. L.M.', 'First Part. L. M.', 'Common Metre.', 'Short Metre.') and scripture-citation lines remain in body text in eng_hymn_watts.txt.
- '(Omit chorus.)' sits flush right in eng_american_carrie_bell_sinclair.txt:108.
- 'Solo. --' prefixes a sung line in eng_american_sidney_lanier.txt:104.

DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT (other domains): section and part names (Verse, Chorus, Refrain, Burden, Fytte, Canto, Part II, pibroch Urlar/Siubhal as headings); speakers and stage directions (Enter, Exit, Aside, character names); stanza and verse numbering; footnotes and editorial glosses; titles and by-lines beyond musical credits; liturgical rubrics (Doxology, Gloria Patri, Introit, Response, Minister/People); copyright, price and publisher lines on sheet music (except where they collide with meter forms); omission asterisk rows; page headers. Also left out: devices that cannot appear in printed pre-1930 English song sources (modern lead-sheet terms such as 'outro', 'hook', 'bridge (8 bars)', 'fade out', DAW and recording terms). Note that 'Bridge' and 'Release' as section names came into use only around the late 1920s and belong to the section-name domain.
reader_notes.editorial and bibliographic:
I sampled /home/user/CodexMusica/lyric-harness/corpus/song/eng_*.txt to ground this list (1,468 files in the directory, not ~1,344). Examples marked as corpus are real lines from it: '&c.' pointers (about 82 files), lettered and numbered footnote markers ('[ll][293]', '[lh]', '[bx]'), a sidenote ('[ye'), insertions ('burst[s]', '[be]', 'F[oe]minae'), notes ('[F] Orig. ed., _warty_.', '[MS. M. First published ...]', '_Memoir_, p. 84.]'), signatures ('R.B.', 'Robert Burns.'), datelines ('March, 1787', '1846.'), credit and occasion lines ('Written by W. H. Archbold ...', 'Altered from an old English song.', 'Written at the request of the committee ...'), and sung traps such as Scots 'sic', 'Anon shot by', 'By Goddes fay' and 'Composed by conventions and Counsellor Grey.'. The examples for loads still to come (G&S, music hall, Tin Pan Alley, more songsters and hymnals) are typical printed forms, not corpus lines.

RULES THAT APPLY ACROSS ENTRIES
1. Position and shape count for more than the word. Apparatus usually (a) stands alone on its line or in brackets or parentheses, (b) sits in a slot outside the stanza (under the title, after the last stanza, at the page foot, or in the margin after a wide run of spaces), (c) has no clause verb or rhyme, and (d) contains locators: numerals, roman numerals, p./vol./No., years, sigla, '&' plus 'Co.', street addresses or currency. A sung line with the same opening word ('By', 'From the', 'Old', 'Written', 'Words', 'See', 'Sold', 'Anon', 'sic', 'St.', 'fol', 'art', 'cap', 'lit') carries on into a metrical clause inside a stanza.
2. Markers attached to sung words (footnote digits and letters, *, †, ‡, [sic], glosses, sidenotes) are removed and the line is kept. Supplied text inside brackets ('[be]', 'burst[s]') is kept without the brackets. Whole-line apparatus is dropped.
3. A note can quote verse. Lines inside footnotes, variant sections, epigraphs, index-of-first-lines entries and illustration captions are verse-shaped, but they are not new sung occurrences.
4. '&c.' has two jobs. As a chorus pointer it means a sung repeat. Annotate it as an abbreviated return, as the corpus does, and do not count '&c.' or the incipit as new lyric. When spelled out and needed by the meter or rhyme, it is sung.
5. Several abbreviations collide with labels from other domains. Check what follows: p/pp/ff/tr without a number are dynamics or ornaments; C.M./L.M./S.M./P.M./H.M. are hymn meters, not initials; D.C./D.S. are navigation; Ch./Cho. is a chorus label; a lone I./V./X. is a stanza numeral; St. followed by a name is Saint; l. after an amount is pounds; d. after a figure is pence; Col./Capt./Rev. before a name may be sung in war and comic songs; Sc. may mean scene, scilicet or Scots; v. may mean verse, vide, versus or roman 5.
6. To tell a speaker label from a signature: labels like 'MARIA.', 'SHE.', 'BOTH.' come before speech and repeat. A signature or credit comes once, after or above the text.
7. Roman-numeral years (MDCCC..., MCM...) in copyright and imprint lines are not stanza numbers.
8. Bowdlerised sung words ('d--d', 'D--n', '****') are sung, not apparatus.

AMBIGUITIES TO FLAG, NOT AUTO-STRIP
- A postscript in verse (Burns epistles).
- Dedicatory poems.
- Spoken recitations inside music-hall songs.
- Prose links in chantefable pieces.
- Variant versions printed in full.
- Parenthetical sung asides versus glosses.
- Name lines that could be an address inside the song or a signature.
- 'Another', 'Englished' and 'Song' staged as TITLE lines in the corpus. These are the printing's headings and are left to the title domain.

DELIBERATELY LEFT TO OTHER DOMAINS (cross-referenced only)
- Part and section labels (Chorus, Verse, Refrain, Part II, Fytte, Act/Scene headings in libretti).
- Speaker and character labels, and stage directions.
- Tempo, dynamics and performance directions.
- Air/Tune/meter lines, hymn meters and tune names.
- Repeat and navigation signs (D.C., Fine, bis, 2x).
- End markers (Finis, The End).
- Titles and running heads, stanza and hymn numbering, page numbers and catchwords.
- Omission rows of asterisks and other digitization artifacts.
- Liturgical labels (Amen, Doxology).
I list a few of these only where they collide with apparatus abbreviations, such as '&c.' as a pointer, ditto, and the cross-reference, index and illustration entries.

DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED
- Post-1929 apparatus (ISBNs, modern copyright formats, Roud numbers, ASCAP/BMI lines).
- Phonetic and IPA apparatus.
- Abbreviations that do not occur in English song and poem printings.
reader_notes.print and digitization: Cross-cutting rules: (1) POSITION beats word. Most print artifacts are lines with no verb, no rhyme partner and no metrical fit, sitting at page, section or book boundaries (front matter, back matter, between stanzas mid-sentence). The repeated test for a word like fine/end/over/do/fol/bis/air/I/Mi is: alone on its line or bracketed or abbreviated with a period, AND no rhyme or syntax role. If it fills a rhyme slot or completes the sentence, it is sung. (2) Strip the token, keep the line: page anchors {12}/[Pg 12], footnote refs [8], margin line numbers, chord brackets, _italic_ and =bold= delimiters, braces, ligatures, long s, underlay hyphens and extenders are inline. Remove the artifact and keep the sung words. Whole-line labels (separators, running heads, signatures, catchwords, contents and index entries, PG boilerplate, credits, end markers) are annotated as a whole line. (3) Bracket spans can be multi-line ([Footnote ...], [Sidenote ...], [Illustration: ...]). Track the open bracket to its close, because the continuation lines carry no marker; the corpus still holds unclosed-looking Sidenote continuations. (4) Duplicated lyric in apparatus (first-line indexes, plate captions, back-cover thematic ads, errata, notes quoting lines, sidenotes) is the main way real lyric words get double-counted. Position and the trailing page or line reference decide. (5) Sung-vocable whitelist that must NOT be caught by notation rules: fa la (la), fal lal, fol de rol, tol de rol, la la, derry down, hey nonny, with a hey, ri-fol, too-ra-loo-ra, and solmization syllables when they sit in a rhymed refrain position across parallel stanzas. (6) Deliberate comic hyphen-splits at rhyme position (G&S, Calverley, music hall) are sung and must not be rejoined; printer hyphenation and turnovers must be rejoined. Concrete leaks found in the current staging, worth a targeted pass: eng_hymn_watts.txt (book-end markers, half-titles 'Hymns.' / 'Book 2.', 'The TABLE.' contents, 'The End of the Table.', 'ADDENDUM' heading, 'Transcriber's Note.'), notes-section glosses staged as TITLE records (=headword= lines, '19 ff.'), inline [N] footnote refs (Hemans and Poe editions), trailing margin line numbers (Whittier/Lowell-type long-line poems and a Swinburne-style edition), [Sidenote: ...] spans (Coleridge Mariner gloss, war-song dates), bare roman numeral lines, numbered Herrick/Lovelace contents-style headings ('181. A DIALOGUE...'), and 'etc.' chorus cues. Deliberately left out or deferred to sibling domains: section and part names (Part/Canto/Fytte/Act/Scene), speaker and voice labels, stage and performance directions, tempo and expression marks, tune and meter lines (Air:, L.M., C.M., 8.7.8.7), repeat signs as navigation (D.C., D.S., bis, Chorus repeat), bylines and source credits ('—From the Richmond Examiner'), liturgical labels (Amen, Doxology), and scholarly abbreviations (ibid., op. cit., var.). These are only touched here where a print convention creates them (e.g. Fine, bis, Do., etc.). Things that cannot occur in English printed song sources were not padded in (e.g. modern tablature diagrams beyond 1920s ukulele vamps, digital lyric-site boilerplate).

Chor.' solo-section label.

Cross-cutting rules: (a) position and punctuation decide. Label words are labels only at line start with '.--', '--', ':', '._' or a closing period and nothing else, or alone on a line; mid-line they are almost always sung (air 1,011, round 1,331, part 655, end 486, fine 282, echo 204, glee 205 sung rows). (b) Strip the prefix, keep the remainder: 'Chorus.--', '_Chor._', 'ROB.', '_Polly._', '(2)' and trailing line numbers are removed, and the verse after them is sung. (c) Italics and parentheses are NOT apparatus signals by themselves: italic lines are Durfey's sung burdens and parenthesised lines are Gilbert's sung asides. Only third-person action verbs, CAPS character names, credits or bibliographic vocabulary make them apparatus. (d) Check the rhyme before stripping a signature, a date or a Latin tag (Burns's 'concerns/Burns'). (e) Speaker-abbreviation homographs: _End._ (Endymion), _Matt._ (Matt of the Mint), _Her._ (Herrick or Hernandez), _V_. (Vicar), MAR./DES. (Margaret/Despard, also month abbreviations), _Item._ (sung). (f) Scots 'sic' is sung; only [_sic_] is apparatus.

Ambiguous between sung and not sung (flag for review, do not auto-strip): the &c. incipit line, whose incipit words are sung but which stands for an unprinted refrain; the bare-name-alone lines; ALL-CAPS short lines in war songs; the 'glee:--CHORUS.' wrapped tail; Burns's 'Subscripsi huic, / Robert Burns.'; the optional hymnal 'Amen'; 'Selah'; Campion's Greek-in-braces line; quoted epigraphs that are also the first sung line.

Deliberately left out: tablature, staff notation and chord symbols (none survive in the text corpus and none can be printed as words in these sources); non-English-language label systems beyond the Latin and Italian terms that appear in English printings; MIDI or recording metadata. Entries marked '(expected)' have 0 corpus rows but are standard in the incoming G&S (PG 808, about 349 numbers headed SONG/DUET/TRIO/CHORUS/FINALE with CAPS speaker prefixes and parenthesised directions), music-hall, Tin Pan Alley, hymnal and songster printings.
reader_notes.completeness critic:
Method: I grepped the 1,344 staged files read-only (PCRE). The corpus comes almost entirely from GITenberg anthologies: Poems of American History, Home Book of Verse, Oxford Book of English Verse, Modern Scottish Minstrel, Southern War Songs, Otterbein Hymnal, Elizabethan song-books, Beadle's dime songsters and the Barnum songster. One Moore file comes from Kalliope XML. As a result, most of the additions above are expected for the coming loads rather than present today.

Corpus-attested gaps:
- The staging format's own markup ([VERSE n] 46,151 rows, [BURDEN] 1,580, '# APPARATUS:' 4,295, '--- TITLE:', '[air: ___]', '[v.5]') was never listed as a category.
- Bracketed multi-line editorial headnotes ('[This song is said to ...', 21 lines starting '[This/These/The ').
- Restoration theatre-song title formulas ('A SONG in the Comedy call'd ... Set by ... Sung by Mrs. Bracegirdle'): this is the dominant D'Urfey heading shape.
- 'Read at ...' public-reading headnotes (Whittier, Rankin).
- Blank name slots ('Dear _____,' in Burns, '[air: ______]' in Moore).
- Sung look-alikes that ground the trap rules: 'Showing how ...' (T. D. English, Moody), 'discovered' (Gilbert), 'Emblem of ...' (Hogg, Hemans), 'Toast' (Burns, D'Urfey), 'Garland' (Trowbridge).

Probed and absent (0 hits) but kept because the coming printings contain them: Hebrew-letter Psalm 119 heads, shanty type names, college yells, lodge odes, indulgence notes, Playford figures, school exercises, word-roll and record numbers, wiki/TEI markup, '¬'.

Rules that cut across several entries:
1. 'HE.' is ambiguous three ways: He./She. dialogue prefix, Hebrew letter in Psalm 119, sung pronoun. Decide by context: alphabetical sequence inside Ps. 119/Lamentations, or dialogue alternation.
2. Back-cover thematic ads and songster back pages contain REAL lyric of OTHER songs. Detect them by position (after the end-mark, a new title plus a copyright line). Lexical tests miss them.
3. Libretto spoken dialogue is a whole block of non-lyric prose that a label-only checklist misses. Use number headings (AIR/SONG/No.) as the lyric boundaries.
4. In facing-text and macaronic material, drop parallel blocks in another language. Keep foreign-language refrains that alternate and rhyme with English inside one stanza.
5. For action songs, play-party calls, shanty pull-words in CAPS, 'Pray for us' litany responses and 'So mote it be', the words are sung. Only the parenthesised or prose-paragraph forms are directions.

Left out deliberately: anything already in the five lists, even where my wording would differ (e.g. Interlocutor, Olio, Child sigla, Imprimatur, Sternhold-style 'Another of the same', Dramatis Personae). Also left out: modern-era forms that cannot occur before 1929 (e.g. Nashville number system, tablature websites beyond those named). I did not split pantomime and burlesque into their own entry, because their apparatus (Transformation Scene, Harlequinade, 'Introduced in the pantomime') is covered by the existing tableau, 'Introduced by' and stage-direction entries plus the stage-position and programme entries added here.
